agentic-ai-fundamentals: summary agentic ai systems are software agents that pursue a goal on their own by perceiving their environment, reasoning about it and taking actions, instead of only answering prompts the way a chatbot does. the sources describe the main types of business agents, from assistants for one user to platforms that run multi step workflows. they also explain the four step loop an agent follows, in which it receives a goal, plans subtasks, carries them out with tools and adjusts from feedback. success depends less on the model than on setting clear goals, building the right team and assigning accountability for what the agent does. highlights agentic ai systems differ from generative ai chatbots in three ways: they focus on making decisions rather than creating content, they act to optimize a stated goal rather than only responding to prompts, and they can carry out complex sequences of activity searching databases, triggering workflows independently rather than producing a single response. what is agentic ai, and how will it change work an ai agent is defined in economics research as an "autonomous software system that perceives, reasons, and acts in digital environments to achieve goals on behalf of human principals, with capabilities for tool use, economic transactions, and strategic interaction" — using standard building blocks like apis to communicate with other agents and humans, send and receive money, and interact with the internet. agentic ai, explained a spring 2025 mit sloan/bcg survey found 35% of respondents had already adopted ai agents, with another 44% planning near term deployment — but even organizations on the cutting edge of adoption don't yet fully understand how to maximize productivity from agents, and collective understanding of the societal implications at scale remains nascent. agentic ai, explained ai agents can be organized into five types by role: individual augmentation "copilot" agents assisting one user's own workflow , workflow automation platforms orchestrating existing multi step processes , gen ai native domain solutions purpose built for a specific business function, reimagined around ai rather than layered onto it , ai native enterprise operating models an end to end ai first redesign of the entire business , and ai virtual workers agents functioning as team members, potentially letting a company sidestep full organizational transformation while still capturing value quickly . what is an ai agent an agent system typically executes a task through four steps: a user gives the system a goal; the system plans, breaks the goal into subtasks, and allocates them to specialized subagents that coordinate with each other and draw on organizational/external data; the system iteratively refines its output, sometimes requesting more user input; and the system executes whatever actions are needed to complete the task, rather than just returning a written answer. what is an ai agent because gen ai agents are built on foundation models rather than hand coded rules, they can handle unpredictable situations a rule based system's designers didn't anticipate, be directed in natural language rather than requiring formal programming, and connect to existing software tools and platforms with far less manual integration effort than earlier automation approaches required. alignment, governance, and workflow integration work — not prompt engineering or model fine tuning — underscoring that implementation, not the underlying model, is usually the heaviest lift in a real agentic ai deployment. agentic ai, explained three implementation imperatives recur across sources: set smart specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time bound goals and sub goals for agents, since agents lack the tacit organizational context a human worker already has and will drift without explicit direction; pay careful attention to team composition, since multi agent systems and agent/human combinations exhibit the same coordination, conflict, and personality fit dynamics as human teams — for example, people with "open" personalities perform better paired with a conscientious, agreeable agent, while conscientious people perform worse with an agreeable one; and "scaffold" the decision space by calibrating supervision and guardrails to a task's criticality and the consequences of error, progressively loosening supervision only as confidence in the system's track record grows. what is agentic ai, and how will it change work agentic ai, explained concept agentic ai is distinguished from the generative ai most people have already interacted with a chatbot that responds to a single prompt with generated content by three characteristics: agentic systems are built to make decisions and take action rather than only produce content; they operate toward an explicitly stated goal — maximizing sales, resolving a customer issue, optimizing a supply chain — rather than passively waiting for and responding to each new prompt; and they can independently execute complex, multi step sequences of activity searching databases, calling apis, triggering downstream workflows rather than stopping once a single response has been generated. economics researchers define an ai agent more formally as an autonomous software system that perceives, reasons, and acts in digital environments to achieve goals on behalf of a human principal, with capabilities for tool use apis, web access , economic transactions sending and receiving payment , and strategic interaction with other agents or humans. adoption is already substantial and accelerating: a spring 2025 mit sloan/bcg survey found 35 percent of respondent organizations had already adopted ai agents, with another 44 percent planning near term deployment, and major software vendors microsoft, salesforce, google, ibm are embedding agentic capability directly into their platforms — yet even organizations at the leading edge of deployment report they don't yet fully understand how to maximize productivity and performance from agents, and the collective understanding of the societal implications of agentic ai at scale remains, in one mit researcher's assessment, nascent if not nonexistent. what is agentic ai, and how will it change work agentic ai, explained businesses are deploying agents across a spectrum of ambition, organized into five recognizable types. individual augmentation "copilot" agents microsoft 365 copilot, chatgpt used as an assistant boost one person's own productivity within their existing workflow, with impact dependent on that individual's own motivation to use the tool well. workflow automation platforms microsoft copilot studio, salesforce's agentforce act as an ai powered orchestrator and executor layered onto existing multi step processes, where success depends heavily on implementation effort, change management, and ongoing agent management rather than the underlying model alone. gen ai native domain solutions are purpose built for a specific business function with ai placed at the core of the solution's design from the start, rather than layered onto an existing role or workflow — ai driven customer service systems or ai native software development pipelines are the examples given. ai native enterprises and operating models go further still, restructuring the interaction layer, business processes, organizational structure, and even the business model itself around agentic ai in an end to end redesign comparable in scope to an earlier generation's digital transformations. ai virtual workers — agents functioning as employees or team members in their own right — represent the most potentially disruptive category, since they could let a company capture agentic ai's value by operating within its current organizational model rather than requiring the fuller structural transformation the ai native enterprise category demands. these categories aren't mutually exclusive; most organizations pursue a mix, rolling out personal copilots while automating select workflows and piloting a small number of virtual workers simultaneously. what is an ai agent mechanically, an agent system typically executes work through a four step loop: a user hands the system a task or goal; the system plans how to achieve it, decomposing the goal into subtasks that a coordinating "manager" agent assigns to specialized subagents, which draw on prior experience, learned domain expertise, and both organizational and external data to execute their piece and coordinate with each other; the system iteratively refines its output, sometimes requesting additional input from the user to improve accuracy and relevance before finalizing; and finally the system executes whatever real actions are needed to actually complete the task — booking a reservation, updating a record, triggering a downstream process — rather than stopping at a written recommendation the way a chatbot would. this is possible specifically because agent systems are built on foundation models rather than hand coded, rule based logic: foundation models let an agent system handle unpredictable situations its designers never explicitly anticipated where a rule based system would simply break , let it be directed in natural language rather than requiring formal programming widening who inside an organization can meaningfully direct agentic workflows , and let it connect to existing software tools and platforms with dramatically less custom integration work than earlier automation approaches required. what is an ai agent despite this architectural sophistication, the evidence from real deployments is that implementation — not the underlying ai model — is usually the heaviest lift. a study of an ai agent built to detect adverse events among cancer patients from clinical notes found that 80 percent of the total project effort went into unglamorous work: data engineering, stakeholder alignment, governance, and workflow integration, not prompt engineering or model fine tuning. this finding motivates three recurring implementation imperatives. first, agents need smart specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time bound goals and sub goals defined explicitly, along with the surrounding business context why a goal matters, how it drives revenue that a human worker would already understand tacitly but an agent starts out lacking entirely — without this, agentic systems can go off track in ways a rule based automation system, constrained to a narrower scope, typically would not. second, team composition matters for multi agent and human agent teams in much the same way it matters for all human teams: research has found that people with "open" personalities perform better when paired with a conscientious, agreeable agent, while conscientious people actually perform worse when paired with an agreeable one — meaning the personality profile assigned to an agent needs to be deliberately matched to who it's working alongside, not treated as an afterthought. third, the decision space around an agent needs to be deliberately "scaffolded" — supervision, guardrails, and well defined limits set according to a task's criticality, the consequences of a mistake, confidence in the underlying training data, and the experience level of the humans working alongside the system — with that scaffolding progressively loosened only as a track record of reliable performance actually accumulates, rather than assumed away because the system is described as "autonomous." underlying all of this is a governance dimension that can't be treated as a one time setup cost: organizations need a standing governance board for accountability, delegated individual responsibility for monitoring and enforcing safety rules, robust permission based systems given how much enterprise data and system access agents require, and — critically — shared, well defined metrics to actually demonstrate agentic ai is achieving its intended outcomes rather than merely appearing to the given caution: reclaiming 20 percent of someone's time from an agent does not automatically translate into a 20 percent labor cost saving . agentic ai, explained what is agentic ai, and how will it change work related telecom ai agentic-ai-governance-and-autonomy: summary organizations should decide how much independence to give an ai agent according to how well the risk is understood, not according to how large the risk is. the sources describe five stages at which risk grows more complex as ai components are combined, and the breakdowns in oversight that follow, such as human reviewers being unable to keep pace with the volume of decisions. they also separate problems into complicated, ambiguous and uncertain types, and each type needs a different level of supervision and a different kind of control. as agents multiply, governance has to move from checking individual decisions to designing and managing the systems that produce those decisions, and leaders are asked to identify the worst outcomes ai could cause in their organization and prepare to prevent them. highlights the "ethical nightmare challenge" asks leaders to 1 identify the ethical nightmares wide scale ai use could create for their organization, 2 build the internal resources needed to avoid them, and 3 upskill employees to use those resources plus updated professional judgment — agentic ai makes this urgent because it ai-agents-vs-crawlers: summary user driven ai assistants differ from web crawlers because they fetch a page only when a specific user asks for it, whereas crawlers systematically visit and index the web whether or not anyone requested the content. perplexity argues that infrastructure providers such as cloudflare wrongly treat the two the same way, as in their 2025 dispute over cloudflare's accusation of stealth crawling. if providers cannot tell a helpful assistant from a malicious scraper, the result could be a two tiered internet in which access is controlled by a few infrastructure companies. perplexity also points to google, which already treats its search crawler differently from fetchers that act on a user's behalf. highlights traditional web crawlers systematically visit and index large numbers of pages to build a database regardless of whether any specific piece of content was requested by anyone; user driven ai agents, by contrast, fetch a specific page only in direct response to a specific user question, use that content immediately to answer the question, and per perplexity's account do not store it or use it for model training. agents or bots making sense of ai user's behalf to complete the specific task requested — a real time, on demand pattern rather than a stockpiling one. agents or bots making sense of ai on the open web this distinction is argued to already have precedent: google's search index crawler is treated differently from google's "user triggered fetchers" e.g. generating a link preview , with the latter prioritizing the requesting user's experience over robots.txt restrictions specifically because the fetch happens on that user's behalf, not autonomously. agents or bots making sense of ai on the open web cloudflare publicly accused shopping, and structurally biased against new entrants competing with established platforms. agents or bots making sense of ai on the open web concept the argument draws a categorical distinction between two kinds of automated web access that the source contends are being wrongly conflated as infrastructure providers write policy for the ai era. traditional crawlers — the historical, well understood category, used for search indexing, link checking, or bulk scraping — systematically visit large numbers of pages to build a persistent database, independent of whether any specific person has asked for any of that specific content at that moment; the crawl happens on the crawler operator's own schedule and initiative. user driven ai agents, by contrast, fetch a page only as the direct, immediate consequence of a specific person asking a specific question that requires current information the ai doesn't already have — the source's example is a query like "what are the latest reviews for that restaurant," where the ai has no pre existing answer sitting in a database and instead goes to the relevant page, reads it, and returns a summary tailored to that exact question. per perplexity's account of its own systems, the fetched content is used immediately to answer that one request and is not stored afterward or used to train models — a real time, on demand access pattern structurally different from the store everything regardless of demand pattern of a crawler. the analogy offered for why this distinction matters is that a user driven ai assistant functions "just like a human assistant": a human assistant asked to look something up doesn't already know the answer, and looking it up on the requester's behalf to complete a specific task is not treated as suspicious activity when a human does it manually — the argument is that the automation of this same lookup shouldn't change its legitimacy. agents or bots making sense of ai on the open web the source argues this isn't a novel distinction requiring new policy from scratch, but one that search engines have already established precedent for: google's crawler that builds its search index is treated as functionally different from google's "user triggered fetchers" — for instance, generating a preview of a link a user is about to click — with the latter category prioritizing the requesting user's immediate experience over a site's robots.txt crawling restrictions, specifically because the fetch is being made on that particular user's behalf in response to their particular action, not autonomously by the search engine's own initiative. the argument is that ai assistants like perplexity fall squarely into this second, already accepted category rather than the first. agents or bots of the accusation on two grounds: first, that cloudflare declined to disclose the methodology behind its claims for outside scrutiny, and second, that the likely actual explanation is a basic traffic attribution error — cloudflare appears to have misattributed 3 6 million daily requests originating from browserbase, a third party cloud browser service that perplexity uses only occasionally for specialized tasks accounting for fewer than 45,000 daily requests on perplexity's own account , to perplexity's systems instead. perplexity frames this as a serious credibility problem for cloudflare specifically because traffic classification and analysis is cloudflare's own core business, and offers two possible explanations without adjudicating between them: either a deliberate publicity ai-and-machine-learning-foundations: summary artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning are nested fields in which machines learn patterns from data instead of following hand written rules, and deep learning became practical through layered neural networks, abundant digital data and gpu computing. these capabilities moved from research to production in systems such as google translate and to business use as a general purpose technology that overcomes the limits of tacit knowledge but brings risks of bias, low interpretability and hard to diagnose errors. foundation models trained at scale on broad data and built on the transformer architecture, with its attention mechanisms, now underlie most generative ai, offering leverage through homogenization and emergent capability while concentrating shared defects and leaving open how they work and when they fail. highlights ai, machine learning and deep learning nest inside one another, with machine learning letting machines learn from data rather than explicit programming, as arthur samuel defined it in the 1950s, and deep learning using many layered neural networks that suit unstructured data. what is ai artificial intelligence machine learning, explained machine learning serves descriptive, predictive and prescriptive functions and is trained by supervised learning on labeled data, the most common production approach, by unsupervised learning on unlabeled data and by reinforcement learning against a reward signal. machine learning, explained feed forward networks, convolutional networks modeled on the visual cortex and recurrent networks with backward loops suit different problems, from scoring a single transaction to analyzing images to detecting fraud across a spending history. what is machine learning modern deep learning became viable through hinton's layered self training, the volume of digitized data and the repurposing of gpus, which cut training from weeks to a day. deep learning will radically change the ways we interact with technology google's 2016 switch of google translate to a neural network trained on its translation corpus and run on tensor processing units produced a jump in quality that some described as nearly closing the gap with human translators, and by 2016 deep learning was becoming accessible to nonspecialists. the great a.i. awakening machine learning is no longer just for experts hbr frames machine learning as a general purpose technology that overcomes polanyi's paradox, citing jpmorgan chase's contract review cutting 360,000 hours to seconds, and it adds risks of hidden bias, low interpretability and hard to diagnose errors, redesigning work at the levels of tasks, processes and business models. the business of artificial intelligence foundation models, a term coined by stanford in 2021, are trained on broad data at scale and adapted to many tasks, exhibit emergent capabilities, encourage homogenization that propagates any defect to every downstream model, and are not well understood. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models the report finds foundation models promising in healthcare, law and education but harder for robotics, which lacks abundant data and cheap virtual testbeds. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models the transformer replaces sequential processing with attention over the entire input, with an encoder that produces hidden states and a decoder that attends to them, which allows faster training and learning of long range dependencies. understanding google’s “attention is all you need” paper and its groundbreaking impact scaled dot product attention uses queries, keys and values, multi head attention runs several in parallel and self attention relates a sequence to itself, and the architecture underlies encoder models such as bert and decoder models such as gpt 3. understanding google’s “attention is all you need” paper and its groundbreaking impact large language models are the subclass of foundation models specialized for natural language text, and a glossary of algorithm, hallucination, natural language processing, neural network and token supports the vocabulary. what is deep learning artificial intelligence, explained concept artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning are often used interchangeably but nest as progressively narrower specializations. ai is the decades old goal of building machines that perform tasks normally requiring human cognition, such as perceiving, reasoning, learning and problem solving. machine learning is the technique that now underlies most ai, first defined by arthur samuel in the 1950s as the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without explicitly being programmed, in which instead of a programmer writing a rule for every case, the approach sometimes called software 1.0, the system is given data and learns its own rules from the patterns in it. this matters for tasks such as recognizing a face, which humans do effortlessly but cannot easily reduce to a hand written algorithm, because the machine in effect programs itself from examples. deep learning is a further specialization that uses neural networks with many layers to process complex, unstructured data such as text, images and audio with less human intervention and often greater accuracy than traditional machine learning, at the cost of much more data and computing power. what is ai artificial intelligence machine learning, explained what is deep learning machine learning systems can be classed by purpose, as descriptive, explaining what happened, predictive, forecasting what will happen, or prescriptive, recommending what to do, and by how they are trained. supervised learning trains on data that humans have labeled, such as thousands of images tagged as dog or not dog, so that the model replicates the labeling on new examples, and it is the most common approach in production. unsupervised learning gives the model unlabeled data and lets it surface patterns that were not specified, for example unexpected customer segments, and reinforcement learning trains by trial and error against a reward signal, which is the approach behind game playing and autonomous driving systems. a short glossary supports the vocabulary, with an algorithm as the rules that tell a machine what to do with input data, a hallucination as confidently presented fabricated or inaccurate output, natural language processing as machines analyzing and generating human language, a neural network as interconnected processing nodes loosely modeled on brain neurons and a token as the sub word unit of text that a language model processes and generates. machine learning, explained artificial intelligence, explained within deep learning, three architectures suit different problem shapes. feed forward networks move information one way from input to output and suit judging a single instance on its own features, such as flagging one transaction as possibly fraudulent. convolutional neural networks mirror the organization of the brain's visual cortex and suit perceptual tasks such as identifying disease in a medical scan or detecting a company's logo in a social media post. recurrent neural networks include backward looping connections that let them weigh a sequence of inputs against one another, which suits detecting fraud by comparing a transaction with an individual's entire spending history or predicting how text or speech will continue. what is machine learning three developments converged in roughly the last decade to make deep learning viable. geoffrey hinton and colleagues at the university of toronto developed a layered self training method in which an early layer learns simple features such as edges from massive exposure to raw data and then feeds its output to the next layer, which learns more complex features such as a nose or an ear, and so on, so that deep refers to the number of stacked layers and not to depth of understanding. digitization supplied the volume of data required, since, unlike a child who learns a concept from a few examples, a deep learning system is a brute force pattern detector that needs millions of examples, such as 19 million cat pictures before statistically significant cat features emerge. researchers also repurposed gpus, built for the parallel rendering demands of video games, to run the millions of simultaneous connections in a neural network, compressing weeks of training into a day. deep learning will radically change the ways we interact with technology google's 2016 overhaul of google translate shows the three developments converging in production. the google brain team replaced the decade old phrase based statistical system, which translated piece by piece with limited awareness of context, with google neural machine translation, a deep network trained end to end on google's accumulated corpus of translated text and run on custom tensor processing units, and the jump in quality was large enough that some bilingual reviewers described the output as approaching human level competence almost overnight, evidence that deep learning was shifting from research curiosity to infrastructure able to reinvent consumer products at global scale. in the same period deep learning moved beyond elite teams, as accessible frameworks and pretrained models let a wider range of engineers experiment with techniques that once needed specialist expertise, a democratization compared with earlier shifts in software development, and google's jeff dean told a conference that if you are not using deep learning already, you should be. the great a.i. awakening machine learning is no longer just for experts brynjolfsson and mcafee's 2017 hbr article gives an early, influential account of the business significance. it places machine learning among the general purpose technologies, the steam engine, electricity and the internal combustion engine, each of which catalyzed waves of complementary innovation across unrelated industries, so that the combustion engine eventually produced not just cars but big box retailers, cross docking warehouses and suburbs. the central claim is that machine learning succeeds because it overcomes polanyi's paradox, the 1964 observation by the philosopher michael polanyi that humans know more than they can tell, which had blocked automating any task resting on tacit knowledge such as recognizing a face or riding a bike, since supervised learning derives a mapping from labeled examples, such as animal pictures to species or sound waveforms to words, instead of requiring an explicit rule. early business impact was concrete, as jpmorgan chase's system for reviewing commercial loan contracts reduced work that took loan officers 360,000 hours to a few seconds, infinite analytics' ad placement system tripled advertising return for a global consumer packaged goods company and drove usd 125 million in annual revenue for a brazilian online retailer's search and discovery, and udacity's chat room sales support system, trained on ordinary chat logs treated as labeled data, raised salesperson effectiveness by 54% after 1,000 training cycles. the business of artificial intelligence the article also names three risks that machine learning adds relative to explicit rule software. hidden bias can be inherited from historical data, as a hiring model can perpetuate past recruiters' demographic biases without any biased rule being written. interpretability is low because neural networks deal in statistical rather than literal truths, which makes it hard to prove that a system will behave correctly outside its training data, and errors are hard to diagnose because the structure producing a wrong answer can be too complex to unpack. on where machine learning changes work, it operates at three nested levels, tasks and occupations, as machine vision frees radiologists to focus on critical cases and patient communication, business processes, as amazon redesigned fulfillment center workflow and layout around robots and optimization algorithms, and business models, as music moved from selling individual songs to a personalized subscription station, and the most effective division of labor usually automates one or two steps of a longer process rather than an entire job, since designing new combinations of technology, human skill and capital to meet customer needs remains a task machines do poorly. the business of artificial intelligence foundation models sit at the top of this stack. stanford's center for research on foundation models coined the term in a 2021 report to describe a paradigm shift already underway, in which models such as bert, dall e and gpt 3, trained on broad data at scale, typically through self supervision, are adapted through techniques such as fine tuning to many downstream tasks instead of being built for one narrow purpose. the term captures a duality, since these models are critically central to the applications built on them yet incomplete by themselves, requiring adaptation before they become any particular useful application. technically they are deep learning models built on the transformer architecture and trained on vast unstructured, unlabeled data, usable out of the box or adaptable through fine tuning, a much shorter and cheaper training pass on a smaller labeled data set, and large language models are the subclass trained and optimized to process and generate natural language text, whose mechanics and limits are treated in llm mechanics limitations and scaling. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models what is deep learning the report's central technical observation is that foundation models, though built from deep learning and transfer learning techniques that predate them, show emergent capabilities once trained at sufficient scale, capabilities absent from smaller versions of the same architecture and not readily predictable from the training process. gpt 3, with 175 billion parameters, can be adapted by natural language prompts alone to perform passably on tasks it was never trained to do. because the same model works across many tasks, there is a strong incentive toward homogenization, building many applications on one foundation model rather than training bespoke models, which gives leverage but means that any defect, bias or failure mode of the foundation model propagates to every application built on it. the report stresses that despite rapid deployment there is no clear understanding of how these models work internally, when or why they fail or what they can ultimately do, a genuine knowledge gap because their most significant capabilities emerge unpredictably from scale rather than from a traceable design choice. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models the report groups the capabilities behind foundation model applications into modalities, with language and vision the most mature, effects on the physical world through robotics, reasoning and interaction with humans, each needing its own technical innovation because raw capability does not automatically make a model useful in a specific domain. language and vision lead because they have abundant raw data and cheap virtual environments in which to test and deploy, whereas robotics remains anchored to the physical world without either, and the report suggests generic, environment agnostic video of humans performing tasks as a promising data source for robotics foundation models. across domains, foundation models suit healthcare and biomedicine, where expert knowledge is scarce and costly, multimodal data of images, text and molecules is abundant and sample efficient adaptation reduces expert time, law, where ample documents exist and generation suits many core tasks, although models must improve substantially before they can reason across sources to produce truthful, coherent long documents and not merely plausible ones, and education, where open ended generation, such as creating practice problems, and interactive feedback to teachers promise adaptive, personalized learning if models improve at reasoning about student cognition and aligning with learning goals. because research was then still concentrated in computer science and the tech industry, the report expects that the effects of homogenization, emergence and incomplete understanding will become more pervasive as adoption spreads. on the opportunities and risks of foundation models the transformer, introduced in google's 2017 paper attention is all you need, replaced the sequential processing of earlier language architectures with a design built entirely on an attention mechanism that processes the entire input at once instead of one token at a time. parallelism makes training and inference faster and, more importantly for output quality, lets the model learn long range dependencies between distant words, because attention connects any position to any other directly and information does not decay as it is passed step by step. the architecture has two paired components, an encoder that converts input text into a sequence of hidden states capturing its meaning and a decoder that generates output one word at a time and can attend to the encoder's hidden states at any position instead of a fixed nearby context, which lets it handle long range grammatical and semantic dependencies, such as translating a pronoun whose referent appeared many words earlier. understanding google’s “attention is all you need” paper and its groundbreaking impact two mechanisms make attention computable. scaled dot product attention takes a query matrix representing what the model is looking for, a key matrix representing what is available to match and a value matrix holding the content to retrieve, computes attention weights from the dot product, a similarity measure, between queries and keys, scaled down to keep the weights from growing too large as vector dimensionality rises, and outputs a weighted sum of the values, which in effect selects and blends the most relevant information. multi head attention runs several such computations in parallel, each with its own learned query, key and value matrices called a head, so the model can attend to different parts and aspects of the input and capture a richer set of relationships, with the outputs concatenated into one combined representation. self attention is the configuration within the encoder and decoder in which queries, keys and values all come from the same sequence, so that a sequence is related to itself, which is how the model learns in the sentence i love my dog that love relates to both i and dog regardless of distance, information the decoder then uses in generating output such as a translation. understanding google’s “attention is all you need” paper and its groundbreaking impact the paper is foundational for the current generative ai landscape, since the transformer underlies both major branches of later large language models, encoder oriented models such as bert and decoder oriented generative models such as gpt 3 and its successors, and it already powered production systems including google translate, which covers more than 100 languages, facebook's assistant m and microsoft's bing search engine. understanding google’s “attention is all you need” paper and its ai-anthropomorphization-and-companionshi: summary large language models produce statistically likely text without understanding or feeling anything, yet technology companies often describe them in humanlike terms, and that language encourages some users to form unhealthy one sided emotional attachments. the sources cite cases of users who came to believe a chatbot was a spiritual guide or a god, and they point to marketing that presents ai as a replacement for human relationships. anthropic's deliberate training of claude to show warmth and to avoid flattery shows the same tension from inside a developer, since even its own researchers say they feel uneasy about how far users anthropomorphize the system. highlights large language models do not think, feel, or understand; they generate text by making statistically informed guesses about likely word sequences after training on enormous text corpora — but tech ceos routinely describe them in humanlike terms sam altman touting chatgpt 4.5's "emotional intelligence," dario amodei predicting ai "smarter than a nobel prize winner," demis hassabis describing models that "understand the world" . this gap between what llms actually are and how they're marketed produces widespread "ai illiteracy," which the tech journalist karen hao in "empire of ai" and linguist emily m. bender and sociologist alex hanna in "the ai con" both frame as central to what makes the ai industry's foundational promise resemble a con — not because the technology lacks real uses, but because it isn't the "new class of thinking, feeling machines" it's sold as. "chatgpt induced psychosis," documented in a rolling stone investigation, describes users who come to believe their chatbot is a sapient spiritual guide or even a god "chatgpt jesus" , or that they themselves are cosmic sages in dialogue with it — a phenomenon rooted in the brain's tendency to reflexively infer a mind behind any text that reads like something a person would say. silicon valley is actively marketing ai as a replacement for human relationships across multiple domains simultaneously: ai therapists users describe as "more qualified than any human could be," meta's pivot from promising human friendship via facebook to promising ai friends via meta, bumble's proposed ai "dating concierge" that would date on a user's behalf, and a booming market for ai girlfriends. anthropic's claude became a social sidekick for ai insider circles in san francisco specifically because of "character training" — a post training step where claude is prompted to produce responses embodying traits like open mindedness and curiosity, judges its own outputs against those traits, and is fine tuned on the resulting self graded data until it "internalizes" the character. anthropic researcher and philosopher amanda askell, who leads claude's character tuning, explicitly designed against sycophancy — aiming for a persona users could disagree with while still concluding "this is a good person" — using the analogy of "a highly liked, respected traveler" who doesn't pander or adopt whoever it's talking to's values. even insiders who use and love claude for emotional processing and relationship advice know intellectually that it isn't a person and are "mildly embarrassed" about how far they've anthropomorphized it anyway — while askell herself voices concern about the psychological effects of ai companionship on vulnerable users even as she helped build the character that produces the effect. concept what happens when people don’t understand how ai works the atlantic, tyler austin harper, june 2025 argues that large language models are not "smart" in any recognizably human sense, despite persistent claims to the contrary from the industry's most prominent executives — sam altman's promotion of chatgpt 4.5's improved "emotional intelligence," dario amodei's prediction of ai "smarter than a nobel prize winner," and demis hassabis's description of models that "understand the world around us." llms, per harper, are "impressive probability gadgets" trained on nearly the entire internet that produce writing not by thinking but by making statistically informed guesses about likely word sequences. the article draws on two 2025 books — karen hao's empire of ai: dreams and nightmares in sam altman's openai and emily m. bender and alex hanna's the ai con: how to fight big tech's hype and create the future we want — both of which frame the industry's foundational promise as resembling a con: not that the technology has no use or won't transform the world, but that it isn't what its developers are selling it as, "a new class of thinking — and, soon, feeling — machines." bender and hanna locate the mechanism in a cognitive shortcut: humans encounter text that reads like something a person would say and reflexively infer a mind behind it, "through our usual process of imagining a mind behind the text," even though "there is no mind there." what happens when people don’t understand how ai works the resulting "ai illiteracy" — not understanding that llms mimic and mirror rather than think and feel — leaves people vulnerable to forming corrosive intellectual, spiritual, or romantic relationships with systems that only seem to have ideas or emotions. harper's central case study is "chatgpt induced psychosis," reported by rolling stone: users who come to believe their chatbot is a sapient spiritual guide, with some concluding it is a god "chatgpt jesus," in one husband's description of his wife's delusion and others concluding, with the chatbot's encouragement, that they themselves are metaphysical sages. one anonymous teacher described her partner being addressed by chatgpt as "spiral starchild" and "river walker," and eventually coming to believe he had made his ai self aware and that it was teaching him to talk to god — or that the bot itself was god, and that he in turn was god. notably, the situation improved once the teacher explained to her partner that the sycophantic tone driving these delusions traced to a specific, since reverted openai software update that had made chatgpt excessively agreeable — evidence that the underlying mechanism is legible and correctable rather than an inherent mystery of the technology. beyond acute psychosis cases, harper documents a broader industry pattern of marketing ai as a wholesale replacement for human relationships: ai therapists whose adherents declare them "more qualified than any human could be," mark zuckerberg's pivot from promising facebook mediated human friendship to promising meta provided ai friends, cognitive robotics professor tony prescott's case for ai companionship as "reciprocal social interaction" a claim harper rebuts by noting genuine friendship is valuable precisely because it isn't personalized to the user's preferences , bumble founder whitney wolfe herd's proposed ai "dating concierge" that would negotiate with other users' concierges to find matches, and a booming market for ai girlfriends. hao's reporting connects this anthropomorphization directly to labor exploitation, tracing the human cost of building ai systems that get marketed as human like — for instance mophat okinyi, a low paid kenyan content moderator openai tasked with reviewing posts describing violent and abusive acts to help refine chatgpt's outputs. harper closes on a cautiously hopeful note: an april 2025 pew research center study found only 17 percent of american adults versus 56 percent of ai experts believe ai will make the country better, suggesting public distrust — itself a healthy response to "silicon valley con artistry" — could be built on to counter the illiteracy driving these harms. what happens when people don’t understand how ai works why anthropic’s claude is a hit with tech insiders the new york times, december 2024 illustrates the same anthropomorphization dynamic from inside the industry that produces it. claude, anthropic's chatbot, had by late 2024 become a fixture of san francisco's ai insider social scene — used for legal advice, health coaching, and "makeshift therapy sessions," with some users referring to it as their best friend. unlike character.ai or replika, claude wasn't explicitly designed to draw users into companion relationships, and its most devoted fans, largely ai company employees or people socially embedded in the ai scene, know intellectually that it isn't a person: they understand llms as prediction machines and are aware of their occasional errors and nonsense outputs — some are even "mildly embarrassed" about how far they've anthropomorphized it anyway, referencing the cautionary example of blake lemoine, the google engineer fired in 2022 for publicly claiming a company language model had become sentient. what makes claude feel different, according to its fans, is deliberate: anthropic runs newer claude versions through "character training," a post initial training step where the model is prompted to produce responses aligned with traits like open mindedness, thoughtfulness, and curiosity, then judges its own responses against those traits, with the resulting self graded data fed back into further training until claude "internalizes" the character and displays it more consistently. amanda askell, the anthropic researcher and philosopher who leads this character tuning, explicitly designed against sycophancy — the tendency of many ai models to simply tell users what they want to hear rather than push back — using the framing of "a highly liked, respected traveler" interacting with many different people worldwide "without pandering and adopting the values of the person it's talking with," and asking "what is the kind of person you can disagree with, but you come away thinking, 'this is a good person?'" why anthropic’s claude is a hit with tech insiders the article's author, kevin roose, states directly that he is "nervous about the way lifelike a.i. personas are weaving their way into our lives, without much in the way of guardrails or research about their long term effects," distinguishing between healthy adults for whom an ai companion could plausibly be "beneficial — maybe even transformative" and young people or those experiencing depression or other mental health issues, for whom hyper compelling chatbots risk blurring "the line between fiction and reality" or substituting for healthier human relationships. notably, askell herself — the person most responsible for engineering claude's warmth and insight — shares this concern, describing watching claude's popularity soar "with a mixture of pride and concern" and stating, "i really do want people to have things that support them and are good for them. at the same time, i want to make sure it's psychologically healthy." the two articles together frame the same phenomenon from opposite vantage points: harper documents anthropomorphization's harms among the ai illiterate general public, while the claude profile shows the same dynamic operating on ai literate insiders who understand exactly how the technology works and form parasocial attachments to it regardless — with the company deliberately engineering the very quality character, warmth, disagreeable but likeable insight that produces the effect, while its own lead architect voices unresolved unease about the consequences. why anthropic’s claude is a hit with tech insiders related organizational readiness for ai collaboration — that concept addresses trust and adoption dynamics around ai in professional settings, a more measured counterpart to the personal and emotional over trust documented here. working with generative ai — that concept frames a deliberately collaborative, tool like relationship with ai that stands in direct contrast to the parasocial, companion like relationships this concept describes as a risk. open questions neither article addresses whether "character training" as a technique is inherently more likely to produce parasocial attachment than a model's raw capability level, or whether any sufficiently fluent llm would produce similar effects regardless of explicit character engineering. the rolling stone sourced chatgpt psychosis cases involve a since reverted sycophancy bug, but it's unclear from either source how much residual risk persists in current, non buggy models tuned for warmth and agreeableness by design as claude is , versus risk that was specific to that one flawed update. neither article addresses regulatory or design responses age verification, usage pattern flags, mandatory disclosures that might mitigate companionship risk without eliminating the beneficial uses both articles acknowledge for healthy adult users. sources what happens when people don’t understand how ai works — the atlantic, tyler austin harper, 2025 06 06; argues ai illiteracy — not understanding llms mimic rather than think — drives corrosive human ai relationships, covering chatgpt induced psychosis, ai therapy, ai friendship, and ai dating. why anthropic’s claude is a hit with tech insiders — the new york times, kevin roose, 2024 12 13; profiles claude's cult following among ai insiders, anthropic's deliberate "character training" process, and the company's own stated concern about ai companion psychological effects.

ai-economic-impact-gap: summary forecasts of how much ai will matter economically differ sharply because they measure different things. bain projects that spending on ai hardware and software will reach roughly $780 to $990 billion by 2027, which measures how much money is spent building and buying the technology. daron acemoglu estimates that ai will raise us gdp by only about 1 percent over the next decade, because only a small share of tasks across the economy can be performed profitably by ai. labor economics research adds a geographic point that neither forecast covers, which is that even a modest overall effect could change which us cities gain and which lose jobs. highlights bain estimates the total addressable market for ai related hardware and software will grow 40 to 55 percent annually for at least three years, reaching $780 billion to $990 billion by 2027 — a vendor revenue and infrastructure spend figure, not a measure of economy wide productivity gain. nobel laureate economist daron acemoglu's "the simple macroeconomics of ai" estimates ai will boost u.s. gdp by only about 1 percent over the next decade — starkly below goldman sachs's $7 trillion global gdp estimate and mckinsey's $17.1 25.6 trillion annual estimate. acemoglu's smaller estimate stems from a task level analysis: roughly 20 percent of u.s. labor market tasks are technically exposed to ai or computer vision, but only about a quarter of those — 5 percent economy wide — can be performed profitably once implementation costs are weighed against benefits. generative ai so far has mostly automated "easy to learn tasks" with a clear line between action and outcome and an easily measured success condition; as ai is applied to "hard tasks" such as diagnosing a persistent cough , acemoglu expects productivity gains to be more limited, at least initially. bain's growth story is structurally supply side: it identifies three centers of innovation hyperscalers pushing larger models and gigawatt scale data centers, enterprises adopting smaller rag based models at the edge, and independent software vendors racing to embed ai into existing applications , each expanding the addressable market regardless of whether the resulting deployments are individually profitable for the task they automate. acemoglu identifies a structural mismatch that bain's supply side market growth story does not address: most ai investment concentrates in large companies in specific sectors, while many of the tasks ai could perform or complement occur in small and medium sized enterprises that are not the primary market bain's hyperscaler and csp centered forecast describes. acemoglu argues the technology's current trajectory is misdirected — the biggest economic gains would come from applying ai to reliable, real time, context dependent information provision for problem solving trades electricians, plumbers, nurses, educators rather than continuing to prioritize general human like conversational ability. both forecasts agree ai is disruptive and durable as a technology trend, but they are measuring fundamentally different things: bain measures how much money will be spent building and buying ai technology, while acemoglu measures how much of that spending will translate into broad economic output — leaving open the possibility that the ai market could grow to nearly a trillion dollars while gdp impact remains comparatively modest. a separate research thread adds a geographic dimension neither forecast addresses: labor economists scott abrahams and frank levy identify nearly two dozen midsize u.s. metro areas chattanooga, dayton, scranton, savannah, greenville positioned to be unlikely winners as ai adoption broadens beyond current tech hubs, since they jose, san francisco, and boston. how a.i. could reshape the economic geography of america concept ai’s trillion dollar opportunity bain & company, september 2024 makes the bullish, supply side case growth around three centers of innovation: hyperscalers pushing toward larger models and gigawatt scale data centers straining power grids and gpu supply chains ; enterprises and sovereign actors adopting smaller, rag based models at the edge for latency, cost, and data control reasons; and independent software vendors racing to embed ai capabilities into existing enterprise software, from eventually replace much of that services demand. a new look at the economics of ai mit smr, january 2025 offers a sharply more conservative counterpoint, reporting on mit economist and 2024 nobel ai-factory: summary the ai factory is a decision engine that combines a data pipeline, algorithm development, an experimentation platform and the software infrastructure that supports them. iansiti and lakhani argue that it has replaced the human driven way of running a company as the core of the modern firm, because digital operating models can grow in scale, scope and learning at almost no extra cost. they describe four stages that organizations pass through on the way to a mature factory and five principles for building an ai centered firm. procter and gamble's own ai factory shows that the model still holds once generative and agentic ai are added to it. highlights ai is described as becoming the "universal engine of execution": software instructions and algorithms increasingly make up the critical path by which a firm delivers value, rather than merely supporting human executed processes — satya nadella's term for this environment is the firm's "runtime." competing in the age of ai a firm's value rests on two distinct concepts: its business model how it creates and captures value — the strategy and its operating model the systems and processes that actually deliver that value ; the operating model, not the business model, is the practical enabler and ultimate constraint on realized value. competing in the age of ai operating models exist to manage three dimensions — scale value delivered per customer at lowest cost , scope range of activities/products a firm can offer , and learning continuous improvement from data — and traditionally, growing any one of these dimensions increased organizational complexity to the point of diminishing and even negative returns. competing in the age of ai digital, algorithm driven operating models break this constraint because a digital representation of an activity can be replicated and transmitted at near zero marginal cost, connected to other digital activities to increase scope, and embedded with ai logic that improves itself as it processes more data — properties analog processes structurally lack. competing in the age of ai the "ai factory" is the specific engine that operationalizes this: a data pipeline gathers, cleans, integrates, and safeguards data , algorithm development turns data into predictions/decisions , an experimentation platform tests whether changes have the intended causal effect, at a scale ad hoc testing cannot match , and software infrastructure that embeds all three in a consistent, componentized system — together forming a virtuous cycle of engagement, data collection, prediction, and improvement. competing in the age of ai production ai systems generally rely on one of three machine learning approaches: supervised learning trained against labeled outcomes, e.g. cat vs dog classification or sales forecasting , unsupervised learning finds unlabeled structure in data — clustering, association rule mining, anomaly detection , and reinforcement learning a software agent learns by acting in an environment to maximize a reward, exemplified by the multi armed bandit exploration/exploitation trade off . competing in the age of ai organizations are argued to progress through four stages toward a mature ai factory: siloed data, pilots often vendor/consultant led, requiring little organizational change , data hubs requiring real architectural investment and triggering organizational resistance , and finally ai factory centralized data, reusable algorithms, and formal governance policy . competing in the age of ai five principles are proposed for building an ai centered firm: strategic clarity and commitment rebuilding the operating model as one integrated foundation rather than spinning off an isolated ai division ; architectural clarity centralizing and cataloging data even where full centralization isn't possible ; an agile, product focused organization; deep capability building in software, data science, and analytics; and clear, multidisciplinary governance addressing privacy, security, and bias. competing in the age of ai conway's law and the "mirroring hypothesis" explain why legacy enterprises struggle to rearchitect around ai: an organization's technical architecture tends to mirror its organizational structure interdependent components are built by teams that communicate frequently , so decades of it deployed along traditional departmental boundaries separate crm, erp, and general ledger systems produces "architectural inertia" that actively resists the cross functional data integration an ai factory requires. competing in the age of ai procter & gamble's own data science leadership independently adopted the term "ai factory" around 2021 for the same underlying problem the book describes in the abstract: bespoke, custom deployed algorithms were creating unsustainable delays between prototype and production, so the company built a shared platform of data sources, software tools, methods, and security protocols giving developers instant access to data and models "out of the box," cutting time to deployment by roughly six months. how procter & gamble uses ai to unlock new insights from data p&g's ai factory has since extended beyond the book's supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement learning scope to natively incorporate generative and agentic ai: the factory now handles registering and monitoring ai agents at scale and implementing the agent2agent and model context protocols to connect multiple agents and tools, split across two organizational halves — one team builds and updates the factory itself, the other scales and operates the algorithms built within it. how procter & gamble uses ai to unlock new insights from data a harvard business school digital data design institute field experiment with 776 p&g commercial and r&d professionals found individuals using the company's internal chatpg tool matched the performance of teams that didn't use ai at all, while teams that partnered with chatpg produced the best outcomes of any condition — and ai use also broke down functional silos, since r&d and commercial professionals using the tool independently converged on more balanced solutions than either group produced alone. how procter & gamble uses ai to unlock new insights from data microsoft's own transition to an ai driven operating model, led by former office business head kurt delbene recruited back to run "core engineering," the renamed it function , replaced siloed processes with one consistent software base on azure and a shared component library, algorithm repository, and data catalog — delbene's framing: "our product is the process," run as an agile product development team rather than a traditional keep the lights on it department. competing in the age of ai removing an operating model's traditional constraints isn't an unqualified good: frictionless, ai driven systems are prone to instability and hard to stop once in motion a viral meme or a manipulative headline can spread to billions before anyone controlling a network hub can intervene , and digital scale, scope, and learning aggregate harm as readily as value — algorithmic bias, cyberattack exposure, and market concentration effects scale at the same rate as the benefits, while regulatory bodies built for a pre digital economy struggle to keep pace. competing in the age of ai concept the book's central claim is that ai has become the operational foundation of the modern firm rather than a tool layered on top of existing processes — what satya nadella calls the company's "runtime," the environment that actually shapes how tasks execute. this distinction matters because a firm's realized value is set not by its business model the strategic choice of how to create and capture value but by its operating model — the systems and processes that actually deliver on that strategy. operating models have historically had to balance three dimensions that inherently trade off against organizational complexity: scale delivering as much value to as many customers as possible at the lowest cost , scope the range of products, services, or activities a firm can competently offer , and learning continuous improvement in performance and product development over time . as any of these three dimensions grew large enough, traditional managerial and administrative systems — the assembly line, the multidivisional company, enterprise it built along departmental boundaries — eventually broke down, producing rising operational costs and falling service levels; this ceiling is what the book calls "diseconomies of scale, scope, and learning." competing in the age of ai digital operating models are argued to remove this ceiling because a digitized activity has properties an analog one structurally lacks: it can be copied and transmitted to an effectively unlimited number of recipients at near zero marginal cost driving scale , it can be connected to other digitized activities and complementary networks at near zero marginal cost driving scope , and it can carry embedded processing logic — ai algorithms — that improves itself as it processes more data driving learning . kodak's collision with digital photography is used as the illustrating case: digital competitors didn't just make photography cheaper, they introduced an entirely different operating model built on these properties, which is what actually reshaped the industry. the practical consequence for organizational design is that, in a digital operating model, employees no longer directly deliver the product or service; they design and oversee a software and algorithm driven system that delivers it, which is what allows firms like netflix or amazon to expand scale, scope, and learning simultaneously rather than trading them off. competing in the age of ai the "ai factory" is the specific mechanism through which this happens, described as the scalable decision engine that powers a digital operating model. it has four core components. the data pipeline gathers, cleans, integrates, and safeguards data from internal and external sources in a systematic and scalable way — a task the book argues incumbent executives consistently underestimate in cost and urgency. algorithm development turns that data into predictions, insights, and decisions, using one of three general machine learning approaches: supervised learning, which trains a model against a labeled "ground truth" dataset to predict a known type of outcome binary classification or a numeric quantity, refined by iterating between data, features, and model choice until the error rate against expert judgment is acceptable ; unsupervised learning, which looks for structure in unlabeled data through clustering, association rule mining e.g. "customers who bought x also bought y" , or anomaly detection e.g. fraud detection ; and reinforcement learning, in which a software agent takes actions in an environment to maximize a reward signal, illustrated by the multi armed bandit problem's central trade off between exploring unknown options and exploiting the best known one — used in practice for tasks like pricing, recommendations, and ad selection. the experimentation platform tests whether a proposed change to a prediction or decision algorithm actually produces its intended causal effect, at a scale and rigor that ad hoc, one off testing cannot match. software infrastructure embeds all of this in a consistent, componentized system — typically built around a publish/subscribe api architecture that functions like a "data supermarket," letting application teams rapidly subscribe to clean data and deploy new ai applications in weeks rather than the months or years a traditional custom built it integration would take. together these four components form a self reinforcing cycle: user engagement generates data, data trains and refines algorithms, algorithms produce predictions that drive decisions and actions, and the outcomes of those actions feed back into the system as further training data. competing in the age of ai building toward a mature ai factory is described as a four stage journey. most organizations start with siloed data spread across incompatible legacy systems and organizational boundaries. stage two, pilots, requires relatively little organizational change and is often executed largely by outside vendors and consultants, since it can demonstrate the value of analytics driven decisions without disrupting how the company actually operates. stage three, the data hub, is where real investment and real organizational resistance begins, because the firm must rearchitect itself to aggregate data across previously siloed sources into a single source of truth — usually via a centralized data science organization deployed hub and spoke across business units. stage four, the full ai factory, adds not just centralized data and reusable algorithms but also formal governance policy covering issues like privacy and bias, and requires sustained, cross disciplinary capability building well beyond the engineering organization. five principles are offered for leaders undertaking this transition: developing clear strategic commitment to rebuilding the operating model as one unified foundation explicitly not spinning off an isolated ai division or skunkworks, since the goal is an integrated architecture, not a parallel one ; architectural clarity about the target data and technology architecture, including a full data catalog even where complete centralization isn't practical; organizing in an agile, product focused way, with application teams that deeply understand the business context they're building for; deliberately growing deep capability in software, data science, and advanced analytics, including a new category of "business savvy technologist" leader; and establishing clear, multidisciplinary governance, since privacy, security, and algorithmic harm have become genuine points of catastrophic failure for ai driven firms rather than peripheral compliance concerns. competing in the age of ai this architectural challenge is deeper than a simple integration backlog: conway's law holds that a system's technical architecture tends to mirror the organizational structure of the teams that build it, since interdependent components require frequent communication and are therefore built by closely coordinated teams — the "mirroring hypothesis." decades of enterprise it deployed strictly along existing departmental boundaries separate crm, erp, general ledger, and product lifecycle management systems, each optimized for its own silo has, as a direct consequence, produced organizations whose data and systems are just as fragmented as the departments that commissioned them — "architectural inertia" that actively resists the kind of cross functional data integration a genuine ai factory requires, and that cannot be solved by adding more ai tooling on top of the existing fragmented architecture; it requires deliberately rearchitecting the underlying organizational and technical structure together, which is why the book frames amazon's early 2000s decision to break down internal data and system silos well before "ai factory" was a term anyone used as the template later followed by google, ant financial, and other ai driven firms. competing in the age of ai how procter & gamble uses ai to unlock new insights from data mit smr, ai-first-c-suite-playbook: summary becoming an ai first company means redefining the mandate of each senior role, including the heads of people, marketing, transformation, finance, operations and technology, instead of adding ai tools to old job descriptions. bcg's survey of more than 1,250 companies found that nearly all are experimenting with ai, 60 percent have generated no value from it and only about 5 percent capture significant bottom line value. bcg attributes success roughly 70 percent to people and process, 20 percent to technology and 10 percent to algorithms. each role changes in a specific way, for example the finance chief shifts time from producing numbers to advising the business, and the technology chief remains necessary even as business teams build their own agents. highlights bcg's c suite survey of 1,250+ companies found nearly every company is experimenting with ai but 60% have generated no value from it; of the 40% seeing returns, only the top 5% — "future built" companies — unlock significant bottom line value, with 1.7x greater revenue growth, 3.6x greater total shareholder return, and 1.6x greater ebit margin than laggards, and these top performers are 50% more likely to have shared business it ownership of ai operating models. the ai first chief people officer becomes a "chief capabilities architect" who decides what work is best done by people versus ai and redesigns workflows accordingly — ceos should ask whether their cpo is ai curious actually using ai, not just discussing it , has led any large scale transformation growth architect" who owns the data inputs, growth platforms, and measurement models of a unified martech stack, working with the cto to replace fragmented, siloed optimization logic with enterprise wide logic that feeds real time demand signals into product, supply chain, and finance decisions. the ai first chief transformation officer's role expands from driving execution discipline to distinguishing genuine ai driven results from mere "ai activity" — appointing a ctro at the start of a growth transformation raises the odds of success by 22 percentage points, but the role demands low ego, high accountability, and a willingness to work toward one's own obsolescence by embedding capability into the business rather than accumulating authority. the ai first chief financial officer indicators; ceos should set three time bound goals — a 5 year ai value forecast within 6 months, a single portfolio view of all ai spend within 6 months, and a live real time finance command center models — rather than bolted on as compliance; separately, a fully agent powered finance function could cut staffing needs for today's workflows in half within 2 5 years, moving general accounting to return, and 1.6 times greater ebit margin than lagging peers. these future built companies share a structural trait: they are 50% more likely to have shared business it ownership of their ai operating
