governance research is based on interviews from 2022 to 2025 with senior governance, risk, compliance, data and product leaders at microsoft, barclays, kyriba, nasdaq, lloyds bank, danske bank and the abu dhabi department of finance, validated against disclosures and filings from more than 40 other financial institutions. it starts from a gap, since government and regulatory frameworks already state principles such as transparency, fairness and accountability, yet organizations struggle to translate them into day to day workflows and decisions. the proposed answer reframes governance from a compliance obligation into a strategic, adaptive capability, built on matching controls to the type of ai system and risk and embedding the controls in workflows, decision rights and accountability structures rather than adding a separate oversight function. scaling ai with adaptive governance choosing controls begins with recognizing two structurally different moments of risk. development risk covers problems introduced before a system goes live, namely biased or incomplete training data, models poorly aligned to the task and insufficient validation, as when an early credit limit model at one bank produced large swings in decisions from small changes in input data. deployment risk emerges when a model meets a dynamic environment and real operators, through data drift, in which quality degrades as live data diverges from training data, plausible but false outputs, and users over trusting output they cannot verify. nasdaq's market surveillance systems, which generate hundreds of alerts per second, show it, since the line between abnormal and illicit behavior is often blurred when illegitimate trading is designed to exploit a model's learned patterns and look compliant. scaling ai with adaptive governance two further dimensions of the system matter. the first is whether it is bounded learning or adaptive. bounded learning systems operate within fixed rules and parameters and improve by optimizing how the rules are applied, as credit scoring models and most pretrained generative ai that does not update during use do, while adaptive systems evolve by feeding production data back into their training and updating the relationships among variables, as algorithmic trading platforms and dynamic fraud detection do. the second is scope, whether errors stay within a function, as in anomaly detection in one transaction stream, or propagate across functions, geographies or industries, as in a cross border supply chain optimization platform, a difference the research calls exponential rather than incremental because errors in a wide system interact and amplify into second order effects absent from any component. crossing these dimensions with timing yields three layers of control, each necessary but insufficient on its own. scaling ai with adaptive governance rules based controls form the baseline for narrow, static systems whose logic is explicit and auditable, such as credit scoring, fraud detection and customer service chatbots. they embed norms and compliance requirements in the model design as constraints, supplemented by validation testing and anomaly monitoring. one bank deliberately uses a statistical rather than deep learning approach for its credit limit increase model so that decisions stay interpretable, and before any model is deployed the analytics team produces a model card covering data checks, meaning completeness, recency, balance and how drift will be detected, decision logic and edge case review, including explicit analysis of the gray zone around the threshold where a customer tips into an increase, and bias and discrimination testing for overfitting to profiles or disadvantage to groups. a model risk unit with credit and regulatory expertise reviews the card independently and internal audit verifies it before launch, and human judgment stays central, since one organization ran each new midmarket lending model against 100 sampled client files and had relationship managers compare their assessments with the model's, investigating divergences to decide whether the model had found an insight or was overfitting, with periodic sample reviews continuing after launch. scaling ai with adaptive governance ex post alignment controls form the second layer, needed when systems, especially deep neural networks, grow so complex that traceability and explainability lose effectiveness, because rules based controls depend on specifying decision logic that becomes more opaque as models become more sophisticated, and generative ai compounds this through stochastic behavior in which an identical prompt can yield different outputs. instead of explaining how a decision was reached, these controls test whether outcomes remain legitimate against ethical, regulatory and domain standards, shifting emphasis from preventing errors upfront to detecting misalignment as systems operate and scale. microsoft evaluates high stakes models against libraries of expert defined policies for fair and acceptable outcomes, with evaluators annotating outputs and independent reviewers validating shortfalls, partly automated through continuous monitoring and automatic flagging of deviations. algorithmic auditing is a core mechanism, first identifying failure scenarios and defining the full use case, who the system serves, who its decisions affect and for what purpose, and then monitoring those risks through decision outputs, input data and internal logic to surface disparate impacts, document recurring patterns and trigger corrective action. users must also be trained to treat probabilistic recommendations as informed signals rather than truth, knowing when to rely on a system, when to challenge it and how to spot biased output. scaling ai with adaptive governance at scale this layer needs structured human review. nasdaq's cross functional teams of compliance officers, data scientists and domain experts review flagged activity through case workflows, document the rationale for each conclusion and feed outcomes back to developers to recalibrate thresholds, with escalation committees stepping in when investigations suggest coordinated bad actors or systemic risk and audit trails capturing the chain from alert through decision to model adjustment. a global bank's fraud detection experience shows that misalignment often comes from workflow breakdown rather than model error, since alerts were routed to the wrong team, duplicated across units or left unresolved because no group owned the next step, and customer service staff sometimes contacted clients before fraud teams had validated an alert, which the bank fixed by mapping the workflow step by step, assigning clear ownership at each decision point and standardizing rules for when to suppress, investigate or escalate an alert. scaling ai with adaptive governance propagation risk controls form the third and most demanding layer. rules based and ex post controls both treat risk as confined to one system, focused on discrete errors or individual outputs, which is reasonable for isolated systems but leaves governance incomplete once systems are linked through real time data flows, apis and automated decisions. agentic ai makes the gap consequential, since systems that initiate actions, coordinate with other systems and pursue goals across domains can propagate an error from one system into others, and regulators are responding, with the bank of england flagging deep trading agents that could amplify market shocks or coordinate in ways that evade human detection, and parallel dynamics appearing in healthcare, where biased diagnostic models spread flawed heuristics across hospitals and insurers, and in supply chains, where procurement platforms amplify pricing errors across supplier networks. the risk is hard to govern because it is structurally invisible, since failures travel through hidden interdependencies, so a minor logistics api error harmless alone could combine with an unrelated payment gateway cyber incident to contribute to systemic breakdown. scaling ai with adaptive governance managing propagation risk requires a shift from a company centric to an ecosystem aware perspective with three activities, mapping interdependencies across organizational boundaries, monitoring shared infrastructure for cross organization vulnerabilities and institutionalizing anticipatory rather than reactive oversight. the european central bank's sectorwide cyber resilience stress tests show the idea at scale by mapping dependencies across clearinghouses, payment systems and financial institutions, monitoring shared infrastructure and simulating how a local disruption could cascade, practices the research says generalize to any interconnected environment. in practice it requires redistributing visibility, accountability and decision rights across an ecosystem and often a cultural shift toward data sharing, coordinated standards and co investment in shared oversight infrastructure with partners, competitors, regulators and sometimes open source communities, since no company can achieve resilience alone because resilience is a property of the wider system it depends on. scaling ai with adaptive governance identifying the right controls is not enough, and three practices implement them. first, risk control protocols must be hardwired into workflows, accountability structures and incentives, with oversight flowing into planning, audit and leadership review cycles instead of sitting in a separate compliance layer. one bank's ai use case committee documents for every approved use case the risk tier, based on customer impact, regulatory impact, data sensitivity and model type, the mandatory controls for that tier, such as independent validation, sample testing and post deployment review frequency, and the decision rights over model changes, then encodes them in the credit approval system so relationship managers cannot bypass validation or review without sign off from both business and risk. second, organizations need mechanisms for conclusive judgment across heterogeneous expertise, methods and risk tolerances, not consensus or homogenized judgment, since domain differences reflect legitimate differences in expertise and appetite. siloed knowledge undermines rules based controls, which joint model reviews and shared model cards address, and ex post controls break down when teams hold misaligned risk thresholds or incompatible validation methods, which shared evaluative routines such as incident and near miss analysis, drift monitoring and structured comparison of intended and actual outcomes address by giving analytic teams, experimenters and use case owners common reference points, avoiding both premature shutdown and paralysis. propagation risk governance needs the same, with shared rules of engagement, escalation rights and lasting decision authority, or interdependency mapping stays a one off exercise. scaling ai with adaptive governance third, governance must be a living learning system, since ai risks mutate and controls that do not evolve fall behind, which requires assigned responsibility for reviewing incidents and near misses, documenting what went wrong and translating the lessons into revised policies, recalibrated thresholds and stronger controls. the overarching argument is that competitive advantage will come from governing ai better rather than adopting it faster, by placing oversight where decisions are made, risk propagates and value is created. bcg's applied ai index report treats governance as an enabler of value, recommending that boards articulate and review ai risk appetite and keep an enterprise wide inventory of agents with transparency into the most consequential, and noting that agents that combine data, tools, permissions, memory and other agents can cause risks to emerge dynamically and compound at machine speed. scaling ai with adaptive governance the formula for agentic ai value bcg bcg's survey finds that 42% of companies expect agents to act healthcare and the public sector identified three structural gaps rather than simple lack of good intentions. the three obstacles slowing responsible ai the accountability gap is the most stubborn, since organizations publish principles but few define who is responsible for embedding them day to day, so responsibility is widely shared but rarely owned. it starts with how principles are written, as one adviser observed that companies define principles from what they already do, which legitimizes current practice without asking for change, and persists in execution, where fairness assessments compliance, privacy or risk departments downstream of product decisions, consulted only after the product is built, so ethics becomes a speed bump instead of a source of trust, pilots stall over usage ai-in-corporate-boardrooms: summary most corporate boards give ai a low priority and rarely use it, yet a few pioneering boards already use it to narrow the information gap between directors and management, to run scenario planning and, in one case, to seat a virtual non voting observer. directors who meet only a few times a year use tools such as chatgpt to prepare for meetings, benchmark performance and draft questions. a 2024 focus group of more than 50 board chairs suggests that the main concerns, namely leaks of confidential information, bias from limited data and an over reliance on past patterns, are more manageable than most directors assume. the recommended route is learning by doing, starting with one on one conversations to gauge each director's comfort and then practicing together as a board. highlights in 2014, hong kong based deep knowledge ventures gave an algorithm formal voting power on its vc board — dismissed at the time as a gimmick — but a decade later, focus groups with 50+ board chairs from companies including nestlé, shell, and novo nordisk found most directors still ranked ai as a low priority, well below issues like global context or ceo relations, with most using ai occasionally for personal needs but rarely for board work. nonexecutive directors face a structural information gap: they meet only a few times a year, often serve multiple boards, and traditionally close the gap through site visits, subcommittees, and board books — but a properly trained llm can analyze far more data than any director could manually, continuously monitor risks for early warnings, and condense information into formats directors can process in the limited time available. a danish nonexecutive director calls chatgpt her "sparring partner," using it to structure management presentations, find benchmarks, formulate boardroom questions, and run simulations — reporting improved meeting preparation and organizational understanding alongside a lighter workload. boards rarely practice genuine scenario planning despite widespread belief in its value, typically citing complexity and limited resources — ai needs far less time than a team of human experts to identify and assess potential changes in underlying variables, and one board used an llm to generate three scenarios for a proposed eastern european acquisition, concluding the investment exceeded its risk appetite and rejecting the deal. the logical next step — ai actually participating in boardroom discussion — is already happening: in 2024 uae's largest publicly traded entity appointed a virtual human, "aiden insight," as a non voting board observer whose contributions go into the official minutes, while g42's boardnavigator tool listens to live board conversations and offers real time insights and recommendations. three risks dominate director concern, and all are more manageable than assumed: information leaks are a data governance problem that predates ai and has known mitigations guardrails, procedural access rules, vendor no training on customer data guarantees , not an inherent ai risk; sample bias ai reflecting the biases embedded in its training data, illustrated by a european industrial company's expensive safety strategy that missed contractor managed operations excluded from the original employee survey is mitigated through regular data audits and demographic specific ai queries; and anchoring in the past is countered by using reasoning models capable of causal not just correlational explanation, so boards can identify and challenge specific outdated assumptions a model's recommendation relies on. a three stage learning by doing process moves a board toward genuine ai fluency: creating engagement through one on one conversations gauging each director's literacy and comfort level, paired with personalized training; practicing collective experimentation by having the entire board use the same general llm for two or three meetings before graduating to an enterprise trained governance coach and eventually firm specific data access; and maintaining momentum by building ai progress into director evaluations and having the chair model sustained personal commitment, including visible openness about their own learning struggles. concept how pioneering boards are using ai hbr, stanislav shekshnia and valery yakubovich, july 2025 opens with a decade old cautionary bookend: in 2014, hong kong based deep knowledge ventures formally appointed an algorithm to its vc board with real voting power on investment decisions, an appointment widely dismissed at the time as a publicity gimmick. a decade later, despite remarkable advances in the underlying technology, board level adoption has lagged: focus groups the authors conducted from june to september 2024 with more than 50 board chairs, vice chairs, and committee chairs from public and private companies across europe, asia, and north america including asm, lazard, nestlé, novo nordisk, randstad, sandoz, and shell found participants ranked ai relatively low in importance — well beneath global context or ceo/shareholder relations — and reported using ai occasionally for personal needs but rarely, if ever, for their board work, with one chair admitting it had "never occurred to me to consider ai for preparing for a board meeting." even so, a meaningful minority of participants described genuinely positive experiences, and the authors argue that recent advances in ai technology and the normalization of virtual human business interfaces mean an ai participant in boardroom discussion no longer feels like a gimmick. how pioneering boards are using ai the article identifies three distinct ways ai is already contributing to board work, with adoption deepening at each level. assisting individual board members addresses the structural information gap nonexecutive directors face: they typically meet only a handful of times a year, often serve on multiple boards simultaneously, and are structurally detached from day to day operations despite making consequential decisions — a documented challenge across a 17 country european study from 2016 2020. traditional mitigations site visits, employee meetings, subcommittees, board books help but don't fully close the gap; a properly trained llm can analyze far larger data volumes than a director could manually to surface patterns and trends, continuously monitor risks for early warning, and condense complex information into formats directors can actually process given their limited time. one danish nonexecutive director on five boards described chatgpt as her "sparring partner," using it to structure management presentations, benchmark performance, formulate discussion questions, and run simulations, reporting both better meeting preparation and a lighter overall workload; a swiss board chair similarly feeds board books to chatgpt before meetings to generate discussion questions and decision options. supplying the entire board with better information extends this to genuine scenario planning — a practice most directors say they value but few boards actually undertake, typically citing complexity and resource constraints as the barrier. ai needs far less time than a team of human experts to identify and assess potential changes in underlying variables research the authors cite shows this is exactly how llms improve human forecasting performance ; one austrian board chair described a board member asking an llm to produce three scenarios for a proposed eastern european acquisition, after which the board concluded the investment exceeded its risk appetite and rejected the deal — with the more durable outcome being that management began supporting all subsequent proposals with formal scenario analysis. a finnish board used chatgpt to sanity check its own strategy retreat conclusions the llm confirmed answers similar to the board's own , and a dutch board chair used claude 3.7 sonnet the same way, with the ai confirming three of four board conclusions and prompting deeper debate specifically on the fourth. ai can also analyze the board's own process — one swiss industrial company's board uses ai to track speaking time, group dynamics, and conversational tone, generating specific recommendations like redistributing airtime among directors or avoiding dismissive phrases like "no brainer." joining the board is the most advanced and most novel form of adoption: in 2024, uae's largest publicly traded entity, ihc, appointed "aiden insight," a virtual human built by abu dhabi's g42, as a non voting "board observer" whose contributions are recorded in official minutes, while g42's separate boardnavigator tool listens to live board conversations, identifies key discussion points, and offers real time data, recommendations, and frameworks. current ai board participants have real limitations — a lack of emotional and situational awareness makes it hard for them to participate without explicit prompting or to argue for their own recommendations under pushback, which the authors note may stem from safety programming unlikely to be "unlearned." how pioneering boards are using ai three risks dominate director concern, and the article argues each is more tractable than commonly assumed. information leaks — the fear that feeding sensitive board materials into an ai tool effectively opens confidential deliberations to competitors — are, per the authors, not actually a consequence of using ai at all but a preexisting data governance risk that companies already know how to manage through software guardrails, procedural access rules, and employee data security training that can straightforwardly extend to board members; major vendors like openai already guarantee enterprise customer data isn't used to train foundational models, and sap goes further by building smaller, client exclusive models trained only on a single customer's proprietary data. sample bias is a more genuine concern, since ai recommendations directly reflect whatever biases are embedded in training data — illustrated by a european industrial company whose board approved an expensive, comprehensive health and safety strategy built from an employee survey that, in retrospect, excluded contractor managed operations entirely; incidents there rose even as the company's own operations improved. mitigations include regular data audits and bias detection protocols at the technical level, and, more valuably, direct user awareness — prompting an ai to break down its analysis by gender or ethnic group specifically to surface latent skew, where demographic markers exist to do so. anchoring in the past is a particular risk for boards, whose job is often to change rather than preserve the status quo; one belgian food company ceo explicitly distrusts ai for strategic choices on the reasoning that "strategy is about the future, and ai knows nothing about the future" — though the authors note his own human instincts are equally anchored in past experience, just less legibly so. the most effective countermeasure is using the newest generation of "reasoning models," whose responses are built through explicit chains of causal reasoning rather than pure correlation, letting a board identify precisely which variable or assumption a given recommendation depends on and directly debate whether that assumption still holds for instance, challenging a borrowing reduction recommendation premised on rising interest rates if the board's own read of the environment points the other way ; boards can also proactively request ai generated scenario analyses and simulations to project forward rather than simply extrapolating from historical data. how pioneering boards are using ai because few current directors were trained to use ai and many came of age before the digital era, the authors recommend a deliberate three stage learning by doing process rather than expecting fluency to emerge organically. creating engagement starts with the chair holding one on one conversations with each director to gauge their literacy and interest, sharing the chair's own experience and attitude, and surfacing both real and imagined risks explicitly so directors understand they can be managed — followed by personalized training tailored to each director's learning style, ideally through one on one tutorials with an internal ai coach that emphasizes personal and collective board effectiveness rather than pure interface mechanics. practicing collective experimentation moves from individual comfort to shared board practice: for two or three meetings, directors sign onto the same general purpose llm and design their own prompts before and during meetings, debriefing afterward to share lessons — once the board finds this genuinely useful, the company can graduate to an enterprise llm trained on corporate governance best practices that functions as a performance coach, and eventually grant the tool access to firm specific data incrementally, starting with a single upcoming board topic rather than a full data dump; the chair should explicitly resist bypassing collective decision making in favor of pushing ai adoption through personal authority, since whole board ownership of the decision and its consequences is itself part of the goal. maintaining momentum requires making a board's progress with ai part of postmeeting and annual evaluations, recognizing directors and boards that engage regardless of outcome, and — critically — sustained personal commitment from the chair, who should model continued learning and openly acknowledge their own struggles rather than promoting ai for others while personally avoiding it, since visible chair vulnerability is what gives other directors permission to experiment openly themselves. how pioneering boards are using ai related organizational readiness for ai collaboration — the general change management discipline for ai adoption this concept applies specifically to the unique constraints part time engagement, fiduciary responsibility, information asymmetry of corporate boards. ai strategy — the executive fluency building process covered there operates one organizational level below this concept's board specific fluency building process, and the two share a similar staged, learning by doing structure. algorithmic auditing and ai failures — a complementary account of ai risk prediction failures vendor overselling, evaluation inflation relevant to the sample bias and anchoring risks this concept identifies for board level ai use specifically. open questions the article doesn't address how board composition itself might need to change as ai native, digitally literate directors become more common — whether boards should actively recruit for ai fluency now, or whether the three stage training process is sufficient to bring existing directors up to speed indefinitely. aiden insight and boardnavigator are both presented as early, largely successful examples, but the article doesn't address governance failure modes specific to ai board participants — for instance, how a board should handle a case where an ai observer's recorded minutes contradict human directors' recollection of a discussion. sources how pioneering boards are using ai — hbr, stanislav shekshnia and valery yakubovich, 2025 07 01; a 50+ board chair focus group study of ai use in corporate boardrooms, covering individual director assistance, whole board scenario planning, ai board observers, risk management, and a three stage adoption process.
ai-in-corporate-finance: summary ai consistently outperforms human managers at tactical finance tasks such as allocating short term budgets, forecasting and analyzing variances, but strategic financial planning under uncertainty still depends on human judgment. its tactical results depend on being given the right strategic context, because it optimizes narrowly for whatever metrics it is handed. most finance functions remain stuck at the pilot stage, and the main reasons are leadership practice and culture, since a profession built around avoiding errors tends to resist experimentation. finance teams that embed ai successfully share four leadership practices. redesigning entire processes, such as order to cash, shows far larger potential gains than automating the existing steps. highlights a management simulation testing ai against seasoned managers on budgeting decisions for a hypothetical automotive parts manufacturer found ai consistently outperformed humans at optimizing tactical budget allocation by learning from past performance data. ai's tactical budgeting performance depended heavily on the quality of the strategic context it was given: when participants selected kpis poorly aligned with strategic goals, ai optimized narrowly for those flawed metrics rather than compensating for the misalignment, illustrating the "surrogation effect" where over optimizing a proxy metric produces decisions misaligned with actual strategic intent. uber's finance function illustrates the tactical/strategic split working in practice: ai driven financial platforms handle real time tactical budget adjustments across 600+ cities, but local teams routinely override ai predictions using market knowledge to keep tactical decisions aligned with long term goals — a balance credited as pivotal to uber's first ever $1.1 billion operating profit in 2023. despite years of heavy ai investment, cfos privately report the same pattern: proofs of concept that never leave the sandbox, promising pilot models that sit unused once quarterly pressure hits, and dashboards that are refreshed but rarely shape actual decisions. the reason similar ai technologies transform other corporate functions but not finance is not primarily a technology gap data quality, tool integration, model trust — it is that finance's professional ethos is built around avoiding surprise and defending a single "right" number, which actively discourages the exploratory, uncertainty embracing behavior ai adoption requires. four recurring leadership practices distinguish finance teams that successfully embed ai: staying alert to weak external signals as shared team responsibility not a specialist task , running small bounded experiments evaluated by what was learned rather than only by accuracy, replacing single point forecasts with multiple explicit scenarios tied to concrete decisions, and actively diffusing local ai enabled practices across teams and geographies rather than letting them stay isolated wins. a cfo's influence on ai adoption operates less through direct technology decisions and more through the tone set day to day: demanding guaranteed roi before any pilot starts reliably kills experimentation, while showing genuine interest in what a team learned from a trial — even one that didn't outperform the existing model — legitimizes the exploratory work ai adoption actually requires. both sources converge on the same underlying principle even though they examine different mechanisms: ai's value in finance is not self executing — it depends on humans supplying the strategic framing, context, and organizational permission that determines whether ai's tactical strength gets pointed in a useful direction. hackett's modeled "ai world class" benchmarks claim a performance gap of up to 75% between organizations that redesign work around ai and those that automate existing processes, spanning 16 end to end processes. the ai enterprise performance gap hackett group in order to cash, modeled ai world class performance cuts process costs 52 59% and staffing per $1 billion of revenue 56 64%, raises automated credit scoring from 41% to 97% and electronic order receipt from 29% to 68%, shortens dispute resolution from 48 to 27 days and cuts average delinquent days from nearly 10 to about 1.5. the ai enterprise performance gap hackett group hackett reports engagements delivering a 60% faster booking cycle through quote to cash redesign and more than $20 million of potential annual revenue recovery from ai agents extracting contract terms in contract to payment, and advises a four step path of baseline, prioritization, future state operating model and roadmap. the ai enterprise performance gap hackett group concept how ai can help your company set a budget hbr, november 2024 supplies a specific, empirically tested answer to where ai should and shouldn't lead in finance. the article opens with a puzzle: companies like unilever, basf, and covestro have invested heavily in ai budgeting tools yet still struggle with forecasting accuracy amid volatile costs and inflation. the authors' answer is a tactical versus strategic split. tactical budgeting — short term resource allocation, cost management, performance tracking — is well defined and data driven, and ai should simply replace human decision making there, since it is faster, more consistent, and free of human bias. strategic budgeting — long term planning, aligning resources with a future vision under genuine uncertainty — remains a domain where ai struggles, subject to the "surrogation effect" from michael harris and bill tayler's 2019 hbr work in which ai narrowly optimizes whatever performance indicator it's given, even when that indicator is poorly aligned with the actual strategic goal. the authors tested this empirically via a management simulation: seasoned managers and an ai algorithm both made budget allocation decisions for a hypothetical automotive parts manufacturer across multiple cycles. ai consistently outperformed human participants when given a well defined strategic context clear goals, well chosen kpis , but underperformed when managers themselves had selected kpis misaligned with their stated strategy — ai faithfully optimized the flawed metric rather than correcting for the misalignment. uber is offered as a real world illustration of getting this balance right: ai driven platforms handle real time tactical budget adjustments across the company's 600+ cities, while local teams retain authority to override ai predictions based on market knowledge, a combination credited as pivotal to uber's first ever $1.1 billion operating profit in 2023. why ai isn’t transforming finance yet mit smr, june 2026 addresses the broader and, in some ways, prior question the budgeting article leaves implicit: given that the tactical/strategic logic is reasonably well understood, why do most finance functions still fail to realize it in practice? drawing on multiyear research with cfos and more than 300 senior finance survey respondents, the authors argue the constraint is leadership practice, not technology maturity. finance's professional identity is built around reliability and avoiding surprise — a great deal of the function's ethos is shaped by "the imperative of not being caught out" — which sits in direct tension with the exploratory, uncertainty embracing behavior ai adoption actually requires. the article identifies four recurring leadership practices, illustrated through anonymized vignettes, that distinguish finance teams that successfully embed ai: shared vigilance a manufacturing company's finance team built a weekly ritual of surfacing external signals as collective responsibility rather than a specialist task ; routine experimentation a consumer services company's finance director reframed pilots as bounded learning trials judged by what was learned, not just accuracy, which the cfo reinforced by asking "what did we learn that we could not have learned otherwise?" even after an underperforming trial ; scenario based strategic conversation a utilities provider's finance team replaced single point forecasts with multiple explicit scenarios, shifting executive discussion from "which number is right" to "what should we do if this scenario starts to materialize" ; and active diffusion of local practices a retail group's store level anomaly detection routine spread from one country to others once the organization created space for teams to share how they worked, not just what they delivered . the cfo's role in all four patterns is described as "indirect and decisive" — less about specific technology decisions than about the tone set through everyday questions, since demanding guaranteed roi before any pilot starts reliably kills experimentation, while genuine curiosity about what a team learned legitimizes it. read together, the two sources describe complementary layers of the same underlying challenge. the budgeting article specifies a concrete allocation of labor between ai and humans within one finance process — ai should lead tactical execution, humans must supply strategic framing — and demonstrates empirically what happens when that framing is absent ai optimizes the wrong thing faithfully . the finance leadership article explains why so few organizations actually achieve that allocation in practice: not because the logic is unclear, but because finance's control oriented culture and the cfo's everyday leadership tone determine whether teams feel safe enough to do the experimentation, signal scanning, and scenario thinking that supplying good strategic framing to ai actually requires. the hackett group's june 2026 study argues that finance's value comes from end to end process redesign rather than isolated task automation, because upstream improvements such as better credit decisions and cleaner orders reduce downstream collections and dispute work and compound across the process. collectors in the modeled world spend 75% of their time contacting customers rather than 41%, which hackett frames as a redesign of the role. it notes sg&a costs outpacing revenue growth across much of the fortune 200 and positions chief financial officers at the center of transformation, and says most ai business cases focus on individual productivity rather than process change. the ai enterprise performance gap hackett group related ai work and organization redesign — that concept covers the general thesis of ai pressuring organizational and leadership practice to change, of which this concept's finance function specific leadership findings are one domain instance. the process redesign methods there are the general version of the finance specific redesign hackett describes. gen ai organizational learning and knowledge — that concept covers organizational learning mechanisms for gen ai more broadly, complementary to this concept's finance specific experimentation and diffusion practices. open questions neither source addresses how the tactical/strategic split described in the budgeting article should be operationalized within the four leadership practices described in the finance transformation article — for example, whether "routine experimentation" as described applies equally to tactical ai deployment where the budgeting article argues ai should simply lead or is really only relevant to the strategic side. the budgeting article's management simulation used a single hypothetical company scenario automotive parts manufacturing ; neither source addresses how the ai outperforms on tactical tasks finding might vary across industries with different volatility profiles or regulatory constraints. the figures are modeled comparisons of peer median and "ai world class" scenarios from hackett's proprietary benchmark data, not observed outcomes from a defined sample, and the report is complimentary research from a firm marketing related services. the study covers transactional order to cash processes, not the strategic planning tasks where earlier sources in this concept find human judgment still decisive, so it does not test that boundary. sources how ai can help your company set a budget — hbr, 2024 11 14; a tactical versus strategic budgeting split, tested via management simulation, with uber as a real world example why ai isn’t transforming finance yet — mit smr, stijn viaene, kristof stouthuysen, and bjorn cumps, 2026 06 02; four leadership practices vigilance, experimentation, scenario thinking, diffusion that determine whether finance functions actually embed ai, based on multiyear cfo research the ai enterprise performance gap hackett group — the hackett group, june 2026; benchmark modeling of ai driven order to cash redesign.

ai-industry-vocabulary-2025: summary four terms captured how people inside the ai industry talked about the technology in 2025, namely reasoning models, evals, synthetic data and vibes. reasoning models work through multi step problems by backtracking and revising, at a much higher computing cost than earlier models. evals are batteries of automated tests that decide whether a frontier model is safe and capable enough to release. synthetic data is training material produced by one ai model for another, which became necessary as the supply of human written text ran out and carries the risk of passing on errors. vibes refers to judging a chatbot by its qualitative feel instead of benchmark scores, and projects such as chatbot arena and vibecheck try to measure it. highlights "reasoning" refers to a model's ability to work through multistep problems, backtracking and revising as needed, rather than producing an answer in one pass — openai's o1 and o3 models and deepseek's r1 the model that "shook up silicon valley" in january 2025 exemplify this category, taking a minute or longer to answer a question but showing their intermediate steps and handling more complex problems as a result. reasoning models cost substantially more to operate than earlier ai models because of the additional computing power required per query, and whether that added capability translates into genuine economic value remains, in the words of ai researcher melanie mitchell, "still an open question." "evals" evaluations are batteries of automated tests — such as probing whether a model can be prompted into hacking a computer network or providing bioweapon synthesis instructions — that determine whether a frontier ai model is safe to release; the practice remains entirely voluntary, run by ai companies themselves alongside third party labs and government bodies like the uk's ai safety institute, with no binding requirement that a company disclose or act on unfavorable results. "synthetic data" — training data generated by one ai model the "teacher" for another the "student" — has become necessary because most advanced models have already consumed essentially all freely available human generated text on the internet; deepseek used synthetic data from one of its own models to train another, and openai separately investigated whether deepseek had also queried openai's models to generate training data in violation of openai's terms of service. synthetic data carries a specific risk: because large language models can hallucinate, an inaccurate "teacher" model produces training data that makes the "student" model dumber rather than smarter, requiring careful human monitoring of the outputs used for training. "vibes" or a "vibe check" refers to judging an ai chatbot's output by qualitative feel — whether responses are concise or overwrought, pandering or confrontational — rather than by quantitative benchmark scores; openai's president publicly endorsed vibe checks as "great evals" in their own right, not merely an informal supplement to formal testing. uc berkeley's chatbot arena crowdsources vibe checks at scale: users see anonymous, randomly paired responses from different ai models to the same prompt and vote on which they prefer, and the resulting rankings from more than two million votes since the project's 2023 launch are closely watched across the ai industry as an informal but influential measure of model quality. a research project called vibecheck attempts to formalize this qualitative judgment into measurable dimensions — ranking chatbots along continuums like serious versus humorous and formal versus informal — on the argument that these qualitative properties have a measurable, real impact on how people judge ai models even though they resist reduction to a single correctness metric. concept ai buzzwords you need to know now wsj, february 2025 defines four terms that captured specific, concrete shifts in how frontier ai models were being built, tested, and judged as of early 2025, moving beyond the more foundational ai/ml/deep learning vocabulary that had already stabilized by that point. "reasoning" describes models capable of working through multistep problems with backtracking and revision — the article's example is coordinating an all hands meeting by cross referencing calendars and room availability, a task humans perform with what feels like effortless common sense but that requires genuine multistep planning. openai's o1 and o3 models and deepseek's r1 exemplify this category: they take noticeably longer to respond than earlier models, in exchange for handling more complex problems and exposing their intermediate reasoning steps, at meaningfully higher computational cost per query. whether this translates into commensurate economic value remains genuinely contested — the article quotes ai researcher melanie mitchell's explicit skepticism that reasoning capability will necessarily prove economically valuable at the cost required to run it. "evals" evaluations are the ai industry's term for the automated safety testing that determines whether a frontier model is fit to release, probing for dangerous capabilities such as facilitating computer intrusion or providing instructions for synthesizing weapons. the article is careful to note the practice's current limitation: evals remain entirely voluntary, conducted by the ai companies themselves increasingly alongside third party labs and government bodies like the uk's ai safety institute, quoted describing evals as "early tripwires ahead of more advanced capabilities" , with no binding requirement that a company disclose unfavorable results or forgo releasing a model that fails them — a structural incentive problem the article flags explicitly. "synthetic data" addresses a scaling constraint: since most advanced models have already consumed essentially all freely available human generated text online, researchers increasingly train new models on data generated by an existing "teacher" model for a "student" model to learn from, a technique deepseek used in developing its own models and that openai separately investigated deepseek for potentially having used against openai's own models in violation of its terms of service. the technique carries a specific risk given llms' propensity to hallucinate: an inaccurate teacher model produces training data that makes its student model measurably worse, not better, requiring careful human oversight of synthetic training data. finally, "vibes" captures a notable shift in how ai insiders themselves judge chatbot quality: increasingly by qualitative feel is a response concise or overwrought, pandering or confrontational rather than exclusively by quantitative academic benchmarks. the article treats this as a legitimate methodological development rather than a lapse in rigor, quoting openai president greg brockman's public endorsement that "vibe checks are great evals" in their own right. uc berkeley's chatbot arena operationalizes this at scale — presenting users with anonymous, randomly paired model responses to vote between, accumulating more than two million votes since its 2023 launch into industry watched rankings — while a research project called vibecheck attempts to formalize the underlying qualitative judgment into measurable dimensions serious versus humorous, formal versus informal , arguing that these "soft and fuzzy" properties have a demonstrable, measurable impact on how people actually judge ai models even though they resist reduction to a single correctness score. related ai and machine learning foundations — the foundational ai/ml/deep learning vocabulary and history this concept's more recent, frontier model specific terminology builds on top of. measuring ai project value and quality — that concept covers formal evaluation methodology for genai applications in more depth than this concept's brief treatment of "evals" as an industry term. open questions the article does not address how "vibes" based evaluation should be weighed against formal evals when the two disagree — for instance, whether a model that passes safety evals but performs poorly on vibe checks or vice versa should be considered ready for release. no source in the vault addresses whether synthetic data training and the teacher/student dynamic it depends on faces the same model collapse risk researchers have identified when ai generated content increasingly pollutes the training data available for future models. sources ai buzzwords ai-safety-research-and-evaluation: summary ai safety cannot be meaningfully assessed or guaranteed at the level of a model alone, because whether a use is harmful usually depends on the deployment context that the model cannot see. this implies that misuse defenses belong mainly at the downstream attack surface, that open versus closed release should be judged by marginal risk, and that red teaming should track adversary capability and be led by third parties. because the resulting system level evaluation depends on independent researchers, the sources also propose a legal and technical safe harbor that would protect good faith evaluation of deployed models from lawsuits, account suspension and rate limiting. highlights ai safety questions generally cannot be asked or answered at the level of a model alone, because safety depends on the deployment context, which contradicts the widely held but rarely stated assumption that safety is an intrinsic model property. ai safety is not a model property a model asked for a persuasive, urgent email cannot tell phishing from marketing, because the malicious link or attachment is content it never sees, so blocking phishing at the model level would mean blocking email writing in general. ai safety is not a model property the same pattern appears for bioweapon related information, where a model cannot separate general synthetic biology questions from bioterrorism, and for disinformation, where true but misleading information can be up to 50x more effective than false information at increasing vaccine hesitancy. ai safety is not a model property narrow exceptions exist where content is intrinsically harmful regardless of use, namely ai generated child sexual abuse material and verbatim memorized copyrighted output, and the argument applies most directly to misuse rather than to bias, accidents, reward hacking or prompt injection. ai safety is not a model property four recommendations follow, that misuse defenses sit mainly outside the model, that open versus closed release be judged by rigorously assessed marginal risk, that red teaming track the advancing frontier of adversary capability as an early warning system, and that third parties with better aligned incentives lead it. ai safety is not a model property the model property framing persists partly because it is administratively convenient, giving companies a clean release criterion and courts a cleaner liability question, while the real distribution of responsibility across models, deployment context and downstream defenses is messier. ai safety is not a model property independent post release evaluation, or third party algorithmic auditing, is essential for accountability and has already found low resource language vulnerabilities, safety measure bypasses and many jailbreaks that internal red teaming missed. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming the terms of service of major ai companies generally prohibit such research, enforceable through account suspension or legal action with limited transparency and no formal appeal, and existing bug bounty safe harbors cover traditional security research but not broader safety and trustworthiness work. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming the proposed remedy combines a legal safe harbor against laws such as the cfaa and dmca section 1201 with a technical safe harbor against account suspension and rate limiting, available only to good faith research that follows responsible disclosure, assessed after the fact. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming the legal risk is real, since openai moved to dismiss the new york times lawsuit partly by framing the times' research into the model as unauthorized access, while openai and cohere have since extended protection toward model vulnerability and academic safety research. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming concept the first argument challenges what its authors call a pervasive, rarely examined assumption in the ai safety field, that safety is a property of the model itself, checkable and fixable through alignment training and red teaming applied to the model in isolation. the assumption shapes behavior across the field, since companies invest heavily in pre release red teaming, researchers work to patch the brittleness of alignment techniques, some advocates push to restrict open weight models on the theory that they pose unique risk, and policymakers look for a training compute threshold above which intervention is justified, landing somewhat arbitrarily on 10^26 flops for lack of a principled alternative. the authors argue that these efforts are inherently limited, because, with a few exceptions, safety questions cannot be meaningfully asked or answered at the model level. safety depends on the context and environment of deployment, and a deployment context has to be specified before a safety question is even well formed. ai safety is not a model property three examples show that the safety relevant information lives in context rather than in the model. a phishing email is structurally just a persuasive email, and what makes it an attack is the destination of a link or the payload of an attachment, content the generating model never had, so the only way to make a model refuse phishing emails is to make it refuse persuasive emails in general, which breaks legitimate uses such as marketing. concerns about models helping bioterrorists have the same structure, since most synthetic biology information is already public, a claim the authors source to rand, and the hard parts of an attack, namely sourcing materials, culturing pathogens safely and disseminating them, lie outside what a model could gate, while nearly all of the model's assistance would look like ordinary bioengineering education. disinformation shows the pattern from another angle, because even a hypothetically perfect model that refuses every request for false information remains useful to a campaign, since true but misleading information is far more effective, up to 50x in one cited study of vaccine hesitancy, so an adversary can obtain accurate content, such as a summary of a real news story, and add the misleading framing outside the model's view. ai safety is not a model property the authors bound the scope of the argument. it applies most directly to misuse, both malicious, as in the examples above, and non malicious, such as students using a model to cheat on homework, where the model again lacks the context to know whether a task is an assignment. other failures, namely bias and toxicity, accidents, reward hacking and adversarial inputs such as prompt injection, are different problems to which the argument applies less strongly, and no separate analysis is offered. a few misuse cases are genuine exceptions because the content is intrinsically problematic regardless of use, such as ai generated child sexual abuse material, where the content itself is the harm rather than something downstream, and verbatim reproduction of memorized copyrighted material, and for these model level refusal makes sense. ai safety is not a model property four recommendations follow. first, defenses against misuse should sit primarily outside the model, at the downstream attack surface where misuse becomes harmful, and the best defenses against phishing, whether a human or an llm wrote the email, remain email scanners and url blacklists that have improved for roughly two decades, whereas relying on alignment is predicted to produce both false negatives, misuse the model fails to prevent, and false positives, with the model acting as an overzealous censor of innocuous requests, because it lacks the context to tell them apart. second, the debate over open versus closed release should be reframed around rigorously assessed marginal risk, the additional risk that a model's release adds relative to existing models and non ai technology and to defenses that already exist outside the model, and the authors cite their own contribution to such a framework, which found low marginal cybersecurity risk from open models for automated vulnerability detection but substantial marginal risk for enabling non consensual intimate imagery. ai safety is not a model property third, red teaming should be refocused, since the answer to whether a model can be misused is essentially always yes, and its more useful function is tracking the advancing frontier of what adversaries can accomplish with current models, for example whether a model can now automate an entire multi step cyberattack chain, so that it works as an early warning system that informs which downstream defenses to build, rather than as a gate on whether a model ships. fourth, red teaming for misuse capability should be led by third parties with incentives distinct from the developer's, because a developer has a structural disincentive to build and disclose the most effective offensive pipeline on its own model, since success would force it to admit publicly that it is releasing something it knows can be misused without a way to prevent it, whereas a company that does not look hard avoids the admission. ai safety is not a model property the authors suggest that the safety as a model property framing has persisted because it would be convenient if true. it would let companies make a clean technical determination that a model is safe enough to release, let researchers apply a familiar toolkit of alignment methods and give courts and regulators a cleaner liability question, under which companies are liable only when model level guarantees fail. accepting that there is no purely technical fix for misuse means that responsibility is distributed messily across models, deployment context and downstream defenses, with no consensus on how to allocate liability, a harder problem than the one the framing lets everyone pretend to solve. ai safety is not a model property system level safety depends on independent evaluation, and the second argument starts from a premise shared across ai companies, academic researchers and civil society, that independent risk assessment of deployed models is an essential accountability mechanism, distinct from and complementary to pre release red teaming done internally or by a few hand selected experts. independent post release evaluation, sometimes called third party algorithmic auditing, has a record of surfacing what internal testing misses, including vulnerabilities in low resource languages, techniques for bypassing safety measures and many jailbreaks that coax a model past its restrictions. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming the structural problem is that the terms of service of popular models, including those of openai, google, anthropic, inflection, meta and midjourney, generally prohibit exactly this research. they are written to deter malicious actors, but in practice they also discourage good faith safety research, because companies retain the right to suspend accounts or pursue legal action, with limited transparency into enforcement and no formal mechanism for justification or appeal, and losing an account can derail unrelated research that depends on it. as a result only a small group of researchers selected by the companies have clear legal authorization to evaluate models already deployed to millions of users. existing protections do not close the gap, since bug bounties with legal protections at openai, google and meta are scoped to traditional security issues such as unauthorized account access, and companies such as meta and anthropic reserve discretion over whether a researcher acted in good faith, a standard that can itself chill legitimate research. cohere, which explicitly permits intentional stress testing and adversarial attacks with appropriate disclosure, and openai, which expanded its safe harbor to model vulnerability and academic safety research in response to an early draft of the proposal, are partial exceptions, although the exact scope of their coverage remains ambiguous. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming the remedy has two complementary parts. a legal safe harbor would protect good faith, public interest evaluation from liability, in particular under the us computer fraud and abuse act and section 1201 of the digital millennium copyright act, both historically used against security researchers and both live risks in ai, as openai's attempt to dismiss the new york times lawsuit partly by framing the times' research as unauthorized hacking shows, and the proposal is modeled on a knight first amendment institute proposal for research on social media platforms. a technical safe harbor would address enforcement mechanisms such as account suspension and rate limiting, which operate independently of legal risk and can deter research even when a researcher is confident of winning in court. both are bounded, applying only to research that follows established vulnerability disclosure practices, assessed after the fact, so research done in bad faith or without responsible disclosure would fail the test and enforcement against malicious misuse stays intact, since bad faith actors never had protection. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming the technical safe harbor is harder to implement than it sounds, because it requires distinguishing legitimate research from malicious activity in something closer to real time, before the after the fact legal test can apply. the proposal suggests scaled up, impartially reviewed researcher access programs, with review in advance or promptly when a suspension looks unfair, ideally involving independent third parties rather than leaving the determination solely to the company being scrutinized. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming related algorithmic auditing and ai failures — that concept is a parallel critique from the same source and author, focused on real world deployment failures of ai risk assessment systems rather than model level safety framing. telecom ai technology — that concept gives a domain specific example of the human in the loop, audit oriented risk management that the technical safe harbor concept parallels. open questions the first essay does not say who should bear the cost of the downstream defenses it recommends, such as email scanners and content provenance systems, beyond noting that developers should morally bear some of it without any current legal mechanism requiring it. ai safety is not a model property the source does not report whether any company beyond openai and cohere adopted the proposed safe harbor commitments after the open letter, or how account suspension review would be resourced and staffed in practice. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming sources ai safety is not a model property — arvind narayanan and co authors' argument that ai safety depends on deployment context rather than being a fixable property of the model alone, with recommendations for red teaming and misuse defense. a safe harbor for ai evaluation and red teaming — sayash kapoor and 22 co authors' open letter and accompanying paper proposing legal and technical safe harbors for independent ai safety and trustworthiness research.

risk against demand, favor a quick, industry specific first pilot that creates measurable value and then concentrate on a deep and narrow domain rather than many shallow pilots, while mit cisr's four stage maturity model links higher maturity to above average financial performance. cgi and kpmg explain how to cross the pilot to production gap through an operating model, modernized it, data use case. the earliest is a 2x2 matrix for generative ai that plots risk, how likely and damaging fabricated or inaccurate output would be, against demand, whether a real, sustained need exists beyond the hype. the insight is to consider the two jointly, since both vary across industries and functions, and the high demand, low risk quadrant, with marketing copy, internal learning content, text review and editing and brainstorming, is where investment should concentrate first, because errors have limited consequences, a human typically reviews the output or the content is not fact heavy, and demand already exists. marketing illustrates it, since it needs constant idea generation, audience tailored messaging and text rich content, is rarely fact dense in ways that create risk and has ai project once a starting point exists, andrew ng addresses what makes a strong first pilot, whose purpose is partly to create value and more importantly to convince skeptical stakeholders to invest in ai capability. a good pilot delivers a quick win, ideally in six to twelve months, and running two or three parallel pilots raises the odds of at least one clear success. it is sized correctly, neither so trivial that success convinces no one nor so large that it stalls, and it is specific to the organization's industry rather than a generic capability, since a horizontal use case, such as a credibility to bring in google maps as a second project, each success compounding until google brain became central to google's ai transformation. he advises treating ai as automation of discrete tasks rather than entire jobs, since a radiologist's job includes reading x rays, operating equipment, consulting colleagues and surgical planning, and automating just the reading is far more tractable than automating the entire role, appointing a cross functional leader who bridges ai and domain knowledge, keeping the team small at typically 5 to 15 people, doing business value and interior designers and volume of quality data. stop running so many ai pilots third, prioritize efficiency before growth within the domain, since cost reduction is faster and builds the executive concerns differ, since false flags are a major headache for customers whose accounts are frozen and a moderate business worry, while an undetected fraudulent transaction harms the company but leaves other customers indifferent. each cell is judged on the likelihood of the risk, the number of people affected and the severity, informed by data and by legal constraints such as anti discrimination law, and then colored red for existential risks where a stakeholder could be gravely harmed or a hard constraint is violated, yellow for moderate ethical concern and green for no worries. the matrix fairness, addresses the harder question inside many fairness concerns, whether an observed disparity reflects legitimate discrimination, a difference explained by factors that belong in the decision, disorder sufferers facing direct harm from bad advice and neda's own institutional trust, which was in fact damaged, and the article argues that red teaming aimed at that cell and benchmarking against curated, evidence based question and answer pairs could plausibly have caught the problem. it notes that tessa is not isolated, citing a new york city government chatbot that told users landlords did not have to accept rental assistance tenants and employers could take a cut of tips, both illegal, and tax preparation chatbots from turbotax and h&r block that gave faulty advice. auditing
