or incomplete — one popular model, for instance, miscategorized the affordably priced ballantine's scotch as a "prestige" product. in response, pernod ricard launched an ongoing program to monitor and improve what the researchers call "share of model" — the measure of how often and how favorably a brand appears in ai generated results relative to its competitors — regularly prompting popular ai models with questions about its products, cataloging the responses, and iteratively adjusting website and advertising copy specifically to correct how the models describe its brands danone runs a comparable ongoing monitoring program . this shift, the authors argue, is the direct successor to the decades long discipline of search engine keyword optimization, now applied to an environment where a growing share of consumers research and increasingly complete purchases through ai intermediaries rather than traditional search: a july 2025 survey of 750 us consumers found 60% expect to use agentic ai to complete purchases within the next 12 months, and major platforms openai partnering with stripe, paypal, walmart, and shopify to enable in chat purchasing are actively building the infrastructure to make that shift concrete. the authors identify three coexisting, non mutually exclusive modes of ai mediated brand consumer interaction that companies must navigate simultaneously: brand agents, in which a company's own ai engages directly with customers capital one's auto navigator chat concierge can check dealership inventory, schedule test drives, and estimate trade in values, letting customers complete most of a car buying journey before ever visiting a dealership ; consumer agents, in which an independent ai acts on an individual's behalf across multiple brands claude's "computer use" capability navigating screens and completing purchases functions as something closer to a personal digital representative than a brand tool ; and full ai intermediation, in which agents interact autonomously on both sides of a transaction with minimal human involvement at all chatgpt's agent autonomously searching opentable, selecting a restaurant, and completing a reservation . to navigate this landscape, the authors propose a three stage adoption framework. stage one is determining whether deploying an ai agent makes sense at all for a given context, since research spanning 119,000 participants found consumer receptiveness to ai agents is high in low stakes, routine, predictable outcome domains illustrated by amazon's decade long evolution from the physical dash button through subscribe & save to the fully autonomous alexa+ ai, which can interpret an intent like "restock my groceries" and execute the full multistep task chain unassisted but notably lower in personally meaningful purchases, domains where visible human effort itself signals care gift giving, personal messages , high stakes decisions where people want to retain direct control healthcare, per boston university and salesforce survey research , subjective rather than objective judgment calls, and luxury or premium experiences where customers are explicitly paying for human guidance as part of the product itself lamborghini's ceo has deliberately resisted autonomous driving features specifically because the brand's value proposition is the visceral experience of driving, not being driven — the authors note this choice needn't be binary, illustrated by ag1's hybrid strategy of training its ai agent on brand voice and real time customer data for routine support interactions while keeping community building interactions like responding personally to every customer review strictly human, a program that achieved 99% ai agent interaction quality scores while measurably freeing human staff for complex, empathy requiring cases. stage two, once customers are receptive to ai agents generally, is persuading them to use a brand's own agent rather than an independent, third party alternative — a genuinely uphill battle, since consumer agents hold structural advantages in both perceived trust people naturally trust agents they personally control, viewing them as unbiased advocates analogous to a fiduciary financial adviser, whereas brand controlled agents are reasonably suspected of serving the company's interests over the customer's and data breadth an independent agent like chatgpt can draw on a user's accumulated history across every brand and domain, not just one company's data . the authors argue brands can offset this disadvantage by leveraging what independent agents structurally cannot replicate — deep, proprietary, real time product data sephora's ai draws on color iq technology differentiating 140,000 skin tones and first party profiles from more than 34 million beauty insider loyalty members, driving triple the purchase completion rate and a 30% reduction in returns and human in the loop escalation paths unavailable to a purely independent agent servicenow's agent autonomously resolves 80% of incoming queries and automatically escalates the remaining 20% to human experts, cutting complex case resolution time by 52% — while noting that responsible ai signaling itself measurably drives adoption: a salesforce survey found 72% of consumers demand transparency about whether they're interacting with ai or a human, and the authors' own three large scale discrete choice experiments with 3,268 uk participants found responsible ai features like privacy and auditability were consistently among the most influential factors in ai product adoption decisions — in one pension planning app study, embedding responsible ai features into the product design lifted predicted adoption from 2.4% to 63.2%. stage three addresses the reality that many consumers will nonetheless choose to rely on independent agents regardless of how well a brand's own agent performs, creating a distinct strategic imperative: ensuring a brand is visible to, and ultimately recommended by, those independent consumer agents. instacart's rapid, repeated adaptation illustrates the discipline required — building both an in app chatgpt powered search tool and a separate chatgpt plug in enabling users to add ingredients to a cart directly from a recipe conversation inside chatgpt itself, then launching a custom gpt when openai introduced that capability, maintaining presence across each new integration surface as the underlying platform evolved. harvard business school research the authors cite documents specific technical levers for shaping how ai agents perceive and recommend a brand, including "strategic text sequences" — algorithmically generated text, often nonsensical to human readers, added to a product page that measurably increased one fictional test brand's likelihood of being surfaced as an llm's top recommendation — and the emergence of next generation reasoning models that expose their own decision criteria, letting brands understand and align with the actual factors price, compatibility, reviews driving a given recommendation; separately, carnegie mellon research found that even simple prompt wording changes substituting synonyms in an otherwise identical query shifted brand recommendation likelihood by as much as 78.3%, underscoring that understanding how consumers actually phrase their ai queries — not just what products they're searching for — is now foundational to brand marketing content strategy. the authors also point to emerging technical standards brands are beginning to adopt proactively, particularly llms.txt, a machine readable format already used by cloudflare, hubspot, and stripe that structures product information specifically for ai agent parsing, with early adopters reporting measurable increases in both ai generated and organic traffic, and flag the likely future emergence of pay to play monetization models within ai mediated marketplaces analogous to search engine advertising, which will require brands to maintain visibility while navigating evolving transparency regulations around paid ai placement. preparing your brand for agentic ai related platform business models — the "share of model" discipline and agentic commerce brand strategy covered here are the brand side response to exactly the ai agent bypassing interfaces dynamic that concept describes eroding platforms' advertising and transaction fee revenue note: create this concept when that source is processed in a future batch . agentic ai enterprise transformation — pwc's finding there that trust in ai agents drops sharply for high stakes, autonomous use cases directly parallels this concept's finding that consumer receptivity to brand agents is lowest precisely in high stakes, personally meaningful, or luxury purchase domains. open questions none of the three sources reconciles a direct tension between the disclosure panel's finding that ai use should be disclosed, especially for consequential decisions and the agentic brand strategy research's finding that brands should build "human in the loop" and proprietary data advantages into their agents to compete with independent consumer agents — it's unclear whether aggressive ai agent deployment for competitive reasons is compatible with the disclosure panel's ethical recommendation to go beyond minimum legal disclosure requirements. de freitas's five pitfalls are grounded in controlled experimental studies simulations, hypothetical scenarios, survey vignettes ; none of the three sources addresses how reliably these lab measured effect sizes translate to real, high stakes brand crises in the wild, beyond the single cruise case study used to motivate the research. sources artificial intelligence disclosures are key to customer trust — mit smr and bcg's responsible ai expert panel on when and how companies should disclose ai use to customers. don’t let an ai failure harm your brand — hbr's seven year, seven study research program identifying five psychological pitfalls that amplify brand damage from ai failures. preparing your brand for agentic ai — hbr's three stage framework for brand strategy in an agentic commerce era, including the "share of model" discipline.
cloud-and-saas-business-economics: summary the cloud changed the economics of the technology industry in three ways. it shifted growth to a few leading providers, moved financial risk from customers to suppliers and made ongoing consumption, not the initial sale, the driver of revenue. the concept explains how established technology companies that were not built for the cloud can still capture growth by harvesting their older products, acquiring new capability and changing their sales channels. it describes the five customer segments that adopt cloud at different speeds and for different reasons, and a discipline called consumption development that closes the gap between the value a product could deliver and the value customers actually realize. it also explains how software as a service performance is judged, through the rule of 40, five operating benchmarks that distinguish companies that beat it and a growing set of alternative metrics that investors must read critically. highlights bain projected cloud would account for 60% of all global it industry growth through 2021, a tailwind captured mostly by the leading providers, as aws delivered more than half of amazon's operating income and azure grew 76% in a single 2018 quarter. how technology incumbents can realize their cloud growth ambitions from 2013 to 2017 all but three legacy technology categories underperformed expectations, with high end enterprise servers falling 11% against a forecast 3% decline, which showed cloud was cannibalizing incumbent categories. how technology incumbents can realize their cloud growth ambitions bain's playbook for non cloud native incumbents is to harvest legacy product line cash to fund hybrid and multicloud offerings, acquire fast growing capability, and evolve sales and channel models to match how customers now buy cloud. how technology incumbents can realize their cloud growth ambitions bain's five faces of the cloud are transformational, heterogeneous, safety conscious, price conscious and slow and steady customers, and the last, which waited out the early adopter phase, was projected to be the largest segment by 2022 and to account for half of spending growth. revisiting the five faces of the cloud under cloud and saas pricing, the supplier bears the financial risk of a sale because revenue accrues only as customers consume the product, which makes driving consumption existential for the vendor and creates a consumption gap between potential and realized value. consumption economics consumption development has three components, namely intelligent listening from instrumented usage data, consumption innovation that simplifies and guides users instead of adding features, and in product upsell, with a 10:1 rule of ten helpful non revenue offers for every revenue generating one. consumption economics customer support and service organizations are proposed as the best positioned owner of driving consumption because they have the lowest cost per interaction, global infrastructure, product knowledge and ownership of self service channels. consumption economics companies that beat the rule of 40, where growth rate plus profit margin exceeds 40 percent, are on average three times more valuable in enterprise value to revenue than those that fall short. the five habits of highly successful software companies bain and opexengine found five operating benchmarks that distinguish rule of 40 winners, namely employee retention the most important , sales and marketing efficiency, customer lifetime value relative to acquisition cost, opex discipline and efficient growth from the existing customer base. the five habits of highly successful software companies investors must decode alternative metrics such as annual recurring revenue, remaining performance obligations, net retention rate, contribution, adjusted ebitda and total addressable market, and bill gurley's 1998 warning about selling dollar bills for 85 cents shows why such measures deserve skepticism. the cloud is already confusing—the metrics make it worse concept the economics of the cloud market can be read from three vantage points: how the market grew and who captured the growth, how vendors should target customers who move at different speeds, and how the move to consumption based pricing changes what a technology company must do to earn revenue. bain's january 2019 sizing of the shift projected that cloud would represent 60 percent of all global it industry growth through 2021, split across public cloud infrastructure and enabling services 9 percent annual growth, reaching $127 billion , infrastructure and platform as a service 29 percent, $117 billion and saas 16 percent, $159 billion . the tailwind was captured overwhelmingly by the leading providers, with aws growing more than 40 percent a quarter and delivering over half of amazon's operating income by the third quarter of 2018 while azure grew 76 percent in the same quarter. how technology incumbents can realize their cloud growth ambitions the flip side was a difficult period for incumbents outside the leading cloud vendors. from 2013 to 2017 every legacy technology category except three underperformed growth expectations, with high end enterprise servers declining 11 percent against a forecast decline of 3 percent, so the shift was substantially cannibalizing incumbent categories instead of merely supplementing them. the one bright spot, midrange and volume servers, buoyed partly by white box manufacturers and partly by a resurgence in branded gear from dell, hp and lenovo, offered a transferable playbook. incumbents should harvest cash flow from legacy franchises specifically to fund new hybrid and multicloud offerings rather than just defending the old business, use acquisitions to obtain capability in fast growing cloud segments where they have little organic exposure, and evolve the sales and channel model to match how customers now buy and consume cloud services, rather than selling cloud adjacent products through a motion built for on premises deals. bain's closing warning is that the shift is structural and not cyclical, so incumbents that read short term stability as safety are setting up a later reckoning. how technology incumbents can realize their cloud growth ambitions bain's second installment narrows from market sizing to customer targeting with a five segment taxonomy first developed in 2011 and revisited with 2019 data. transformational customers, the early adopters that set the market's pace, prioritize performance and scalability over cost, but some are finding a ceiling, since a predictable workload running at 80 percent utilization increasingly favors on premises economics over pay as you go. heterogeneous customers, typically mature businesses with forward looking but risk aware it leadership, deliberately split workloads across saas, infrastructure and platform services and retained on premises systems based on fit instead of pursuing wholesale migration. safety conscious customers have real demand but have been held back by private cloud offerings too costly or complex to meet their need for a dedicated, non shared environment, a segment vendors could unlock by improving private and public cloud interoperability. price conscious customers have been most sophisticated at capturing savings, because they treat migration as a chance to audit and rightsize computing and storage, uncovering fragmentation and duplication, and bain's client work found rightsizing can cut costs by 30 to 60 percent, a gain lift and shift migrations reliably miss. slow and steady customers waited out the early adopter phase and commit over three to five years, and were projected to become the largest segment by 2022, accounting for half of spending growth, which makes them the most important segment for a vendor seeking growth. together with the sizing analysis, the segmentation gives incumbents the discipline for executing their playbook: a rising tide does not lift all boats evenly, so success depends on choosing which face of the cloud to serve rather than riding overall growth. revisiting the five faces of the cloud the vendor's problem runs deeper than targeting, because the move to cloud changed who bears risk. j.b. wood, todd hewlin and thomas lah argue that three roughly simultaneous shifts, the 2008 to 2009 recession, cloud computing and the smartphone, permanently changed how technology companies must generate revenue by moving financial risk in a sale from customer to supplier. under on premises licensing the customer paid upfront and bore the risk that the product would go underused, whereas under the cloud and saas model of no usage, no money, the supplier earns only as the customer actually consumes the product, so driving ongoing usage becomes existential. this is framed against the consumption gap, the growing distance between the value a product could deliver and the business value customers realize, which arises because vendors can add features and complexity faster than customers can absorb them. revenue is built from many small micro transactions, such as an added user, an unlocked feature or extra capacity, so growth depends on three behaviors, namely getting existing users to adopt more advanced capability, getting new users onto an application and getting existing accounts to adopt additional applications. consumption economics no single department can own consumption, since a company wide capability is required, but the authors identify customer support and service as the best positioned existing asset, because it already has the lowest per interaction cost of any customer facing function, global infrastructure, deep product knowledge and ownership of the self service channels through which consumption guidance would flow. their proposed account services organization blends that service capability with inside sales responsibilities focused on recognizing and acting on consumption opportunities. on the development side, consumption development has three components. intelligent listening replaces upfront market requirements documents with real time usage data from products deliberately over instrumented with listening posts, on the logic that what customers do inside a product is a more reliable signal of what to build than what they say they want. consumption innovation shifts investment away from the traditional speeds and feeds race of adding features and toward simplifying the product and guiding individual users along a consumption roadmap, a tiered presentation of features similar to how games reveal capability as a player shows readiness. in product upsell embeds recommendation engines and offer management inside the product to surface the next relevant feature, content or purchase in real time, modeled on e commerce patterns such as customers who bought this also bought. the design guidance is a 10:1 rule, ten purely helpful no revenue offers for every revenue generating one, because consistently helpful guidance builds the trust that makes a later commercial offer more likely to be accepted. consumption economics the same source cites don norman to explain why feature overshoot persists even though it is understood: customers in every segment keep requesting features specific to their own use, competitors keep shipping capabilities that create pressure to match, and engineers want to build visibly impressive functionality regardless of whether it serves most users. unused features are not harmless, because they clutter the interface, add cost across the product's life through installation, customization, maintenance and support, and slow adoption of the smaller set of features that drive most of the realized value. the wider shift from selling products to selling outcomes is described elsewhere as a move from business to business to business for business pricing, in which vendors price for the customer's realized outcome rather than for the transfer of a product or license, which structurally requires the same ongoing, usage driving engagement that consumption development provides, because a vendor paid for outcomes has a direct stake in whether the customer consumes and benefits from the product. consumption economics b4b investors judge this new model with the rule of 40, the principle that a software company's growth rate plus profit margin should exceed 40 percent, and bain finds the market rewards it decisively, since companies beating the threshold are on average three times more valuable in enterprise value to revenue. bain and opexengine analyzed 2019 financial data for nearly 80 saas companies and found that those beating the rule scored consistently higher on five operating benchmarks. the most important was employee retention, because customer satisfaction correlates with employee satisfaction and leaders protect both, a point bain noted needed to account for pandemic era changes in staffing, workspace, travel and safety. second was efficient sales and marketing spend, tracked through the magic number, the ratio of revenue growth to sales and marketing spend, which measures whether the sales organization is geared to growth and not merely to maintenance. third was a better ratio of customer lifetime value to acquisition cost, reflecting good targeting and products that sustain value, with digital investment stripping acquisition cost and digital native saas companies holding a structural edge over incumbents. fourth was disciplined operating expense, with efficient product development, ruthless culling of weak pipeline items to concentrate on the most promising ones, productive sales teams, contained administrative costs and continued investment in customer success. fifth was efficient growth from the existing base, meaning more new revenue from upgrades and cross selling and better limits on churn than peers. in the context of the early pandemic, when most enterprise it budgets were being cut but many buyers planned to raise saas spending, particularly in security and collaboration, bain judged that companies already strong on these benchmarks were positioned to sustain growth. the five habits of highly successful software companies barron's widens the lens from the rule of 40 to the vocabulary of alternative metrics cloud companies use about themselves, which investors must read critically. the article opens with venture investor bill gurley's 1998 warning that alternative performance measures let companies produce impressive looking revenue by effectively selling dollar bills for 85 cents, aimed even at the now standard price to sales ratio, which proved prescient before the dot com crash, yet complex metrics never disappeared and multiplied as cloud companies grew more sophisticated. it defines the terms investors most need to decode. annual recurring revenue is useful for companies that blend subscription and term contracts because it smooths up front recognition on term deals. remaining performance obligations are contracted work not yet recognized, a forward looking signal distinct from recurring revenue. net retention rate is a same store sales style measure of revenue growth per existing customer, with a high figure, such as the 168 percent of one profiled company, signaling that existing customers want more. contribution is transaction level profitability before fixed costs, sometimes paired with a take rate for marketplaces. adjusted ebitda strips out stock based compensation and one time items, and total addressable market is the most marketing oriented and the easiest to inflate. recurring revenue and net retention are also the inputs to the growth rate calculations behind the rule of 40, so this vocabulary is needed before the five benchmarks can be applied. the cloud is already confusing—the metrics make it worse related cloud value realization and maturity — the buyer side counterpart to this concept's price conscious segment finding: both independently converge on the conclusion that rightsizing and genuine organizational change, not simple migration, is what separates real cloud savings from disappointed expectations. cloud strategy and migration — that concept covers the workload level cost/benefit analysis capex vs. opex, which workload types actually pay off that underlies why different customer segments in this concept adopt cloud at such different rates and for different reasons. cloud computing foundations — this concept's account of shifting supplier risk under cloud pricing complements that concept's coverage of overprovisioning and data center economics under the older on premise model. customer centricity — that concept shares the underlying logic that ongoing customer value realization, not the initial sale, is what should drive resource allocation, though this concept focuses on product embedded mechanics rather than portfolio level clv. platform business models — the in product upsell / real time recommendation pattern described here parallels the "match" function platforms use to connect users with relevant value units. customer personalization strategy — a telecom specific parallel discipline for using customer data to guide real time, in context offers. ai disruption of saas business models — this pre ai era rule of 40 framework is the baseline saas performance metric that ai driven consumption pricing covered there is now forcing incumbents to rethink, since usage based revenue behaves very differently from the subscription revenue the rule of 40 was originally designed to measure. tech company operating model redesign — bain's own later research there on operating model redesign for sustained tech company growth extends this earlier financial metrics focused analysis into questions of organizational structure and decision making speed. ai investment bubble — that concept's capex to revenue gap analysis for ai infrastructure spending is a direct analogue of this concept's skepticism toward metrics like tam that can make growth look more substantial than the underlying cash flows support. open questions the bain vendor strategy and segmentation pieces date from 2019 and the rule of 40 research from 2020, so they predate the acceleration of cloud adoption during the pandemic, and the sources do not show how the five segment taxonomy or the growth sizing held up through it. the sources recommend that vendors focus on one customer segment but do not discuss the trade offs of serving several segments at once. the five operating benchmarks, especially the magic number and the ratio of lifetime value to acquisition cost, are built around per seat subscription economics, and it is unclear whether they remain as predictive once consumption based, ai driven pricing becomes widespread or whether a revised set will be needed. the underlying 2019 dataset of nearly 80 saas companies is not broken out by company, so the findings cannot be independently verified from the article, and the 2021 barron's glossary does not rank the metrics by how easily each can be presented misleadingly. sources how technology incumbents can realize their cloud growth ambitions — bain & company, mark brinda, 2019 01 15; cloud market growth sizing and a three move playbook harvest, acquire, evolve sales channel for non cloud native technology incumbents. revisiting the five faces of the cloud — bain & company, mark brinda, 2019 03 12; a five segment customer taxonomy transformational, heterogeneous, safety conscious, price conscious, slow and steady for targeting cloud vendor go to market strategy. consumption economics — j.b. wood, todd hewlin, and thomas lah's consumption gap diagnosis and consumption development discipline intelligent listening, consumption innovation, in product upsell . b4b — supplementary source on the shift from b2b product pricing to outcome based "b4b" pricing. the five habits of highly successful software companies — bain and opexengine's 2019 data analysis of the five operational benchmarks that distinguish rule of 40 beating saas companies. the cloud is already confusing—the metrics make it worse — barron's, cloud-computing-foundations: summary cloud computing is the shared, standardized and automated delivery of computing resources as a service, and it rests on a small set of foundations that business leaders need to understand. these include three nested service models infrastructure, platform and software as a service , the public, private, hybrid, multicloud, community and government deployment models, the microservice and container architecture that defines a cloud native application, and the standards that make interoperability and portability possible. together they explain why hybrid environments have become the practical default and why how an application is built matters more than where it runs. highlights cloud delivery is organized in three nested layers: infrastructure as a service provides a virtual server, platform as a service adds abstracted middleware and development tooling that hides the operating system, and software as a service provides a complete multi tenant business application. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.1 understanding the cloud multi tenancy, in which many customers share one running instance while their data stays isolated, is what makes public cloud and saas economics work, and it gives saas vendors a strong incentive to invest in uptime because one glitch affects every customer. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.9 using software as a service a hybrid cloud requires that private and public resources actually work together on a shared problem, so disconnected prototypes or divisions that each use their own single public cloud do not count as hybrid. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.1 understanding the cloud multicloud is the coordinated use of two or more public clouds, and its aspiration of automatically moving running workloads between providers by policy had not yet been realized when the source was written, although containers are making it more achievable. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.1 understanding the cloud cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.7 introducing all types of clouds bain's 2019 analysis projected worldwide public cloud revenue above $275 billion by 2021 against at most $75 billion for private cloud, yet enterprises chose public cloud mainly because it is cheaper, richer in features and easier to integrate, so the real competition has shifted to hybrid offerings. public vs. private cloud the market says hybrid data sovereignty, the principle that stored data is subject to the laws of the country where it physically resides, is a durable reason some workloads stay in a data center or private cloud however mature public cloud security becomes. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.1 understanding the cloud moving an aging monolithic application to the cloud unchanged captures none of the cloud's real benefits, because value comes from decomposing an application into independently deployable microservices packaged in containers. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.6 a closer look at cloud services kubernetes, created at google and open sourced in 2014, became the dominant container orchestration platform and the central open source standard for interoperability, because it runs on any public cloud, private cloud or on premises infrastructure and so limits vendor lock in. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.6 a closer look at cloud services cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.5 standards in a multicloud world cloud standards form through four routes multinational bodies, industry consortiums, ad hoc groups and de facto adoption , and data portability is harder to solve than application portability because data comes in varied forms and its handling is governed by its owner. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.5 standards in a multicloud world mckinsey reports that the global saas market reached roughly $3 trillion by 2022, that generative ai reached about 2% of the enterprise software market in one year a share saas took four years to reach , and that product led growth works best when combined with sales led growth as product led sales. what is saas concept cloud computing is best defined functionally, as the shared, standardized and automated delivery of computing resources applications, compute, storage, networking, development platforms and even business processes as a service. standardization gives consumers consistent interfaces, and automation provisions and releases resources according to business rules, resource availability and security demands; without both, a cloud would be merely remotely hosted infrastructure. multi tenancy is the architectural pattern that makes the economics work, because many customers share the same underlying infrastructure and software instance while their data and configuration remain isolated, so the provider avoids replicating dedicated hardware or software for each of them. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.1 understanding the cloud delivery is organized in three layers, each built on the one below. infrastructure as a service supplies a virtual server equivalent to a physical one, including an operating system, in public pay as you go, self service and private policy gated forms. platform as a service adds abstracted middleware, development tooling and deployment services so that the operating system is hidden from developers. software as a service is a complete multi tenant business application, such as salesforce, google's g suite or adobe creative cloud, where the customer cares only about functionality, performance, availability and security. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.1 understanding the cloud software as a service changes both the architecture and the economics of software. because every customer of a multi tenant application shares one code base, customers avoid the capital expense of scaling their own infrastructure, maintenance and updates are bundled into the subscription, and a business can configure the application's behavior without touching the underlying code, which keeps upgrades simple, although heavy process customization makes them harder. a single technical fault can affect every customer at once, so vendors have an unusually strong commercial reason to invest in uptime and continuity. salesforce.com illustrates how such a business grows. marc benioff's "no software" pitch won small businesses first, because the absence of capital expense and the month to month commitment made switching low risk, and large enterprises followed more slowly, often buying through sales and marketing budgets rather than formal it procurement. salesforce then opened its platform, branded force.com and later customer 360 platform, to independent software vendors, which let partners such as veeva systems build a pharmaceutical crm with built in regulatory reporting on its infrastructure and customer base. in effect, a saas vendor that opens its platform is offering a paas, which gives partners faster time to market and access to qualified customers the source's analogy is a food court in exchange for dependency risk if the vendor changes its apis, so vetting api stability is essential due diligence. delivering the expectation of unlimited resources also requires genuinely cloud native architecture rather than a lifted legacy application, and the requirement that saas stay available while features are deployed is what drives continuous deployment and devops. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.9 using software as a service platform as a service is defined by what it removes from the developer's concern. the platform supplies networking, file systems and input and output as abstracted services, so applications need no operating system expertise and port more easily between platforms than infrastructure as a service applications port between operating systems. organizations must also decide whether to manage their own paas environment, which gives more control and more operational burden, or to use a vendor managed one. paas is tightly coupled with two practice shifts: devops, which merges development and operations so that customer facing features ship as soon as they are ready instead of in numbered releases, and agile development, in which small cross functional teams work in sprints of two to four weeks, ideally staffed with full stack developers, so that some teams deliver a feature in two or three days. three variants serve different needs. public paas aws elastic beanstalk, azure app service, red hat openshift, google app engine is the fastest route to deployment and the largest scale, private paas runs inside a company's data center for regulated industries whose auditors need in person access or whose data must stay in a particular country, and open paas is built on open source software to avoid single vendor lock in and support multicloud strategies. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.10 standing on platform as a service the deployment models differ mainly in ownership, access and control rather than technology. a public cloud is owned and operated by a third party for use by others, and some customers pay a premium for dedicated, non multi tenant instances when governance rules forbid sharing infrastructure. a private cloud is owned and operated by or exclusively for one organization, sits behind a firewall and is built around governance, security and compliance, and public vendors increasingly sell appliance versions of their services aws outposts is the example that can be installed in a customer's own data center, which blurs the line between private cloud and public technology run locally. public clouds subdivide into commercial clouds backed by service level agreements generally written to protect the vendor, with carve outs for the outages that cause many real incidents , open social community clouds such as facebook and linkedin low security, no sla and no guarantee the community will persist , open technical community clouds such as github, and government clouds, which are segregated variants meeting stricter isolation and vetting requirements because a government data breach can become an international incident. private clouds subdivide into privately owned and managed clouds a financial services firm acting as its own cloud provider to partner banks , vendor appliances behind the customer's firewall, and commercial contractual private clouds run by a third party under a formal sla. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.7 introducing all types of clouds the terms hybrid and multicloud are often used loosely, but the source draws a precise line. a hybrid cloud requires that private and public resources work together toward a shared goal, for example a public development platform sending data to a private application or a saas analytics service ingesting data from several clouds, while a disconnected public cloud prototype, a saas application with no data flow back to the data center, or divisions that each standardized on their own single public cloud are explicitly not hybrid. multicloud is a strategic pattern rather than a cloud type, namely the coordinated use of two or more public clouds, motivated by developer choice, vendor risk diversification, cost and performance arbitrage and resilience against any one vendor's pricing or reliability. its endpoint, automatic movement of running workloads between providers by policy, was still unrealized because multicloud management tooling and application portability were immature, and in practice multicloud usually arises accidentally when teams or acquisitions choose different vendors. cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.1 understanding the cloud cloud computing for dummies 2nd edition . ch.7 introducing all types of clouds cloud adoption does not remove the data center. most medium and large companies still run one for systems of record such as accounting and inventory, and virtualization, which decouples software from hardware, has been the main lever for streamlining it. many organizations deliberately evolve the virtualized data center into a private cloud as a staging area for cleaning up virtual machine sprawl and making applications cloud ready, and after migrating to the public cloud the modernized private cloud becomes the foundation of a hybrid environment. data sovereignty, legacy applications that are not cloud ready and workloads with no business case for migration keep other systems in place. overprovisioning is a further cost driver in traditional data centers, which are commonly sized well beyond actual peak demand as a hedge against outages, inflating energy costs relative to the compute used, an inefficiency that elastic, on demand allocation is designed to remove. cloud computing for public cloud had pulled decisively ahead, but the dominance reflected trade offs more than preference, since many enterprises would have preferred a private solution and chose public cloud because it was cheaper, richer in features and easier to integrate than private alternatives, which are often too costly or hard to manage internally. private cloud vendors therefore now compete by emphasizing integration with public services, even for customers in highly regulated industries. security plays a dual role, remaining a top cited worry while also motivating adoption among executives who believe providers protect against breaches and privacy failures better than their own operations could. disappointments persist unevenly: cost is the largest source of dissatisfaction, because expected savings often fail to materialize, and dissatisfaction with compliance and regulatory issues rose roughly 50 percent between 2016 and 2018 even as satisfaction with security and reliability improved, which shows the parts of the value proposition maturing at different rates. public vs. private cloud the market says hybrid mckinsey's 2025 account of the saas market adds its current economics. the global market reached roughly $3 trillion by 2022 after nearly a decade in which software market capitalization grew at twice the pace of the broader market, but growth slowed as enterprises cut it spending in response to higher interest rates, pushing boards to ask what the best use of capital is and leading many companies to adopt the rule of 40, under which growth rate plus free cash flow rate should reach at least 40 percent. generative ai has disrupted software faster than saas did, with large enterprises spending roughly $15 billion on it in 2023 and reaching about 2% of the enterprise software market in a year, a share saas took four years to reach. mckinsey expects generative ai to make customers switch vendors more often as they chase new capabilities, so saas companies must keep pace with development and defend client relationships rather than assume renewal, and it advises leaders to reimagine their category rather than add ai features, to reallocate r&d in line with a 10 to 20 percent ai revenue contribution within five years, and to revisit pricing, packaging and proprietary data strategy. product led growth, which puts the product rather than a salesperson at the center of acquisition and expansion, is rarely successful alone, and the more durable pattern is product led sales, which layers it onto sales led growth so that incumbents can reach smaller customers cheaply while larger prospects still experience the product before signing a large contract. only 6% of global software revenue is earned by non technology companies despite widespread ambition, and mckinsey identifies six success factors for building a new saas business inside such a company: iterate quickly with a minimum viable product, exploit existing proprietary data and digital assets anheuser busch inbev built a b2b e commerce platform for retailers from its own data , plan for scale from day one, recruit scarce saas talent from wider pools such as open source communities and hackathons, tie pricing and selling to product usage data, and protect funding through the period before results appear. what is saas cloud native architecture builds applications as collections of small, independently deployable microservices that communicate only through standardized apis. each microservice serves one narrow function and is developed and deployed by a small team, which simplifies development, makes changes smaller and less risky, lets individual services scale up or down on their own demand, and lets other teams reuse a fully tested service without revalidating it. this is why lifting and shifting an aging monolith captures almost none of the cloud's advantage: the application keeps the same tangled dependencies it had on premises, and the benefit comes from decomposition rather than relocation. containers make microservices practical. a virtual machine abstracts the physical server, with each machine running its own full operating system, while a container abstracts the operating system itself by packaging application code with its dependencies, so it runs predictably across environments and is far smaller and faster to start. because one application may consist of hundreds or thousands of containers, orchestration platforms automate installation, scaling, health checks, versioning and rolling updates across a cluster. speed rather than one size fits all rigidity. architect enterprise — applications and services for impact concept forrester's central argument is that cloud has already overwhelmed the traditional shared services it operating model, yet most organizations — even after a decade or more of cloud usage — have never deliberately redesigned their operating model to match, instead accumulating one informally as decisions piled up over time. the legacy shared services model relied fundamentally on hierarchy, triage, and rationing, because on premises data centers simply couldn't scale fast enough to meet the competing demands of every internal and external stakeholder simultaneously; virtualization provided some relief but never resolved the underlying problem of allocating scarce resources across competing priorities. cloud removes that structural constraint entirely by aligning platforms, applications, and data directly with the specific needs of the users, partners, and customers who actually consume them — but forrester's research finds that early edition cloud operating models, built when usage was lower and complexity was lower, now genuinely require rework given today's scale, the proliferation of managed cloud services databases, cloud native platforms , and the recent explosion of ai workloads specifically. to replace the obsolete shared services model, forrester applied its general operating model framework to cloud specifically, producing a six layer cloud operating model framework meant to function as a blueprint any organization can adapt to its own circumstances, rather than a template to copy wholesale. design your cloud operating model the framework deliberately starts with customers, not technology. layer one requires organizations to explicitly define both their internal stakeholders — developers, business users, and the cross functional set of groups security; operations; governance, risk, and compliance; procurement; c suite executives whose initiatives touch cloud, each with a distinct interest in what cloud provides them — and their external stakeholders, since serving customers and partners must sit at the center of a cloud operating model given how much cloud and mobile technology have already raised baseline service expectations in both b2c and b2b contexts; cloud can serve external stakeholders by rapidly shipping new features, lowering cost, improving resilience, or simply facilitating partner collaboration that happens outside the traditional corporate firewall. layer two builds on this foundation to define cloud value specifically: the journeys stakeholders actually undergo to obtain cloud services mapped using customer journey and orchestration tools, to reveal friction points and opportunities for real time enhancement ; the concrete cloud offering itself — which specific services, platforms, and instances are available via self service, including associated slas, training, and repository resources, prioritized based on genuine stakeholder and business need rather than it's own preferences while still exercising enough oversight to prevent inappropriate, overly expensive, or non compliant service adoption ; a value proposition that goes meaningfully beyond positioning cloud operations as a passive, secure/compliant "broker" — since old operational habits like take it or leave it attitudes and overly hierarchical manual approvals will otherwise persist and undermine cloud's actual advantages — instead aggregating and genuinely inspiring stakeholders around near term, measurable business impact; and the actual experience delivered, since legacy shared services it was notorious for long lead times even on basic infrastructure requests, meaning a modern cloud experience needs to deliberately embrace automation, self service, and fast availability of new offerings while still preserving a white glove option for genuinely complex requests. design your cloud operating model layer three shifts from defining what cloud should deliver to documenting how the organization will actually deliver it, through five specific capability elements. activities need to be fully outlined and mapped to higher level workflows value streams, workstreams, lifecycle streams using business capability maps, since cloud's expanded capacity for action carries a real risk of service sprawl and chaotic, undocumented activity if left unmanaged. metrics require rethinking rather than simple carryover from the data center era: legacy measures like uptime, mean time to resolve, resource usage, and developer velocity still matter, but cloud's shared responsibility model complicates something as basic as an uptime metric, pushing teams toward root cause analysis and observability/aiops tooling specifically to distinguish platform caused outages from other failure modes, alongside a blended mix of business level okrs/kpis and more tactical operational metrics like deployment flow. skills remain a persistent constraint even as cloud services grow more abstracted and automated — organizations need to identify which specific cloud roles matter most for their context cloud administrator, cloud architect, solution architect, with cloud infrastructure engineer and cloud security engineer as natural next additions, plus non operational roles like cloud vendor management professional and finops practitioner , augmenting internal capacity with third party managed services where staffing limitations require it. competencies are related but distinct from skills: certain competencies genuinely need to live inside the organization, while others can reasonably be sourced from partners or a cloud provider's own support teams — and forrester specifically cautions that passing a vendor certification exam doesn't automatically mean someone is prepared to assume the real world responsibilities that certification implies, meaning organizations still need to assess actual readiness rather than treating certification alone as sufficient. and underlying technologies need to be catalogued explicitly — the specific cloud platforms and services in use, plus the surrounding ecosystem of governance tools, project management and collaboration software, portfolio visualization, developer platforms, and incident management software that together constitute the organization's genuinely full cloud technology stack. design your cloud operating model layer four addresses organizational structure directly, since cloud providers have effectively remade enterprise it in their own image — welcome when it means access to new services and a sharper focus on innovation, but something organizations still need to deliberately align with their own priorities rather than accept passively. five elements make up this layer: reporting lines, where cross functional technical roles may need a "two in a box" structure that keeps them accountable to business requirements while still connecting them to a technical manager who can assess skills and support career development; definition of work, moving away from legacy it's narrow, siloed functional definitions the canonical example being a server team standing up virtual machines with no visibility into what applications actually run on them toward genuine clarity about scope and ownership, achieved through pragmatism, collaboration, and formal training rather than idealized org chart design; operating units, where cloud centers of excellence and a cloud business office can facilitate coordination beyond formal reporting lines, paired with more tactical cloud platform teams, while the organization decides deliberately how centralized those units should be; location, where cloud increasingly enables virtual placement of an operating unit to best match stakeholder needs rather than defaulting to physical co location, subject to real national, regional, or business structure constraints where they genuinely apply; and interactions, where forrester identifies four distinct patterns describing how operating units actually affect each other's ability to deliver value — independent autonomous delivery of a new cloud service , coordinated multiple units working toward a shared goal, like a zero trust security program , contracted minimal cooperation delivery against a specified scope, like new networking capacity , and collaborative broad, guardrail supported coordination for something like a revamped, multi service customer engagement program — with cloud's underlying infrastructure unity making consistent interaction patterns more achievable than they were under fragmented, siloed data center era it. design your cloud operating model layer five addresses governance, framed as an organization's effort to reassert autonomy over its own it resources even as it hands substantial capability and control to external cloud providers. security starts from zero trust as the near universal foundational model, built on solid identity and access management practices, leaning on the inherited security properties of ephemeral, cloud native workloads, and paying careful attention to the shared responsibility model that defines which security obligations sit with the provider versus the customer at every layer of the stack. compliance requires embedding grc and security functions directly into the cloud operating model itself, starting from a baseline checklist that goes beyond standard controls to address cloud specific risks — since even substantial vendor provided regulatory documentation won't automatically align to an organization's own control framework, especially as the quantity and nature of cloud services keeps expanding generative ai deployment being the current frontier . decisions require a formal decision framework and catalog, since the early, informal days of cloud famously let business users stand up new services outside it entirely with nothing more than a credit card — a dynamic that still creates constant pressure toward decentralization, genuinely valuable when it avoids data center era bottlenecks but genuinely risky if left completely unchecked. transparency needs to shift decisively away from the narrow, hierarchical, and bureaucratic grc interactions typical of the private data center era toward real time dashboards and readily auditable artifacts that let both engineers and the c suite understand current status quickly — while still maintaining a strict separation of duties between grc stakeholders and cloud operations itself. and accountability requires cloud era raci charts that are meaningfully different from their data center era predecessors in both the pace of interaction and the sheer number of participants involved in each category, with cloud specifically empowering architects to assert genuine responsibility "r" while broadening who needs to be accountable and consulted as cloud services and their business impact continue expanding over time. design your cloud operating model layer six, leadership, closes the framework by addressing what the cloud operating model needs from the people actually running it, across six dimensions. vision matters more now than in cloud's early days, when adoption mostly meant standing up a specific service unavailable on premises managed databases, a vmware lift and shift ; the advent of cloud native technologies serverless, kubernetes and now cloud based ai workloads demands a genuinely expansive vision that ties the cloud operating model to broader organizational goals, such as a traditional bank explicitly using cloud to stay competitive against fintech rivals. strategy is the day to day operational reference point that translates that vision into practice — a us based regulated company expanding internationally, for instance, might make multicloud adoption an explicit part of its strategy specifically to address regulator concerns about vendor concentration while also satisfying sovereign cloud requirements abroad. culture needs to genuinely interlock cloud with the organization's broader culture rather than exist as a separate technical initiative — most companies blend their existing culture with devops driven momentum toward a more empowered, collaborative model, since the underlying cloud technology is itself designed to support exactly that kind of culture if the organization actually embraces it. performance needs to be measured against the organization's own broader goals and its chosen it style — forrester identifies four: the enabling style stabilizing, operating, and protecting existing it resources, such as a straightforward vmware to cloud migration , the amplifying style optimizing business outcomes at scale by tapping native cloud services for new global reach , the cocreating style delivering new products faster, such as standing up customer facing web apps rapidly in cloud based development environments , and the transforming style technology led innovation, such as cloud ai infrastructure and managed services — with automatic adoption of whatever cloud service is newest explicitly rejected as a valid performance strategy on its own. corporate values need to extend to the cloud provider relationship itself, since choosing a primary cloud provider carries genuinely long term implications and an organization needs to be comfortable with that provider's own positions on privacy and responsible ai use, alongside its own sustainability, accessibility, and inclusive hiring commitments shaping how cloud services actually get adopted and deployed. and motivation closes the framework by recognizing that a cloud operating model needs to actively motivate the people working within it — freeing it personnel from shared services rigidity to build genuinely empowered platform teams that interact more productively with the business — illustrated by a us federal agency that built its finalized cloud strategy around explicitly motivational documents connecting the agency's cloud strategy directly to its core mission, using compelling visuals and language specifically to get individuals and leaders genuinely excited about participating rather than simply complying. design your cloud operating model a the remedy is to treat migration as a chance to rationalize workloads, by assessing usage patterns and peak demand to inform downsizing, identifying storage patterns and proximity requirements, and rationalizing core processor counts to reduce processor tied licensing, which commonly surfaces fragmentation, duplication, incomplete records and zombie servers that were never decommissioned. done well, rightsizing cuts costs by 30 to 60 percent, and a tso logic analysis found that a company with 105,000 server instances and 20 terabytes of on premises storage would have faced a 22 percent cost increase from a direct match rehost but a 36 percent reduction from rightsizing first. savings also vary by workload, because nonproduction workloads gain more than production ones their volatile usage matches cloud elasticity and nonvirtualized workloads gain more than virtualized ones virtualization has already captured some of the utilization gains . the implication is that rehost and poorly executed rehost are not the same strategy, and even the easiest option requires real workload analysis. optimize, don’t ‘lift and shift,’ when migrating to the cloud microsoft's glossary places the 7 rs within a broader taxonomy of data migration, of which cloud migration is only one of five overlapping categories, the others being storage migration, database migration usually requiring conversion because the format changes , application migration and business process migration, such as moving data during a merger or product launch. it also distinguishes migration, which moves data from one place to another, from conversion, which transforms data from one format to another so a new system can read it. strategies such as refactor and repurchase often require both, and a project can include conversion as one step without the sequencing being obvious in advance. microsoft outlines a standard three phase process that generalizes across all seven strategies, namely planning, which discovers and maps existing data, assesses organizational impact and designs the approach and rate, implementing, which builds the solution and transfers data while monitoring for quality problems, duplicates and anomalies, and validating, which audits the migrated data for accuracy before the old system is decommissioned. what is data migration bcg frames the planning problem from a program risk angle. spending with the three largest public cloud providers rose 337 percent over five years to $211 billion in 2023, and organizations that execute the transition well can cut infrastructure costs by up to 40 percent, raise productivity by up to 50 percent and speed time to market by up to 60 percent, yet a smooth migration remains difficult. five traps commonly derail transformations even when the business case is sound. treating the cloud as another data center through application by application lift and shift forfeits the productivity gains of platform services, an integrated devsecops team and infrastructure as code tooling. failing to plan and manage costs leaves organizations accustomed to a capital based data center model without the skills or monitoring to stop volatile operating spend from spiraling. neglecting the timing of legacy decommissioning makes costs escalate while both environments run in parallel. losing control to the cloud provider or systems integrator, chosen mainly on projected savings rather than proven experience migrating complex legacy workloads, extends timelines and leaves the organization unable to build its own capability or challenge its partners. letting parallel programs proliferate across uncoordinated vendors erodes standardization, procurement economies of scale and internal skills. cloud transformation, without the risk five corresponding success factors counter the traps. the first is treating the transition as a business transformation rather than an infrastructure program, anchored in a communicated vision for speed to value and resilience and in well governed decisions about what, when and how to migrate. the second is a migration factory approach, in which each workload type gets a defined migration pattern that is piloted and then scaled in parallel across teams while lessons are fed back into the pattern. the third is active management of consumption through a finops function spanning business, technology and finance, which guards against over consumption and against under consumption that forfeits discounts tied to committed spend. the fourth is strict vendor oversight with internal staff making the key decisions, partners working alongside rather than in their own silo, agile contracts with shared productivity incentives and deliberate investment in in house skills. the fifth is a proactive program assurance capability from the outset rather than a risk function that intervenes too late. bcg formalizes these into a de risking framework with five elements, scope and objectives, business value and economics, governance and organization, solution and deliverables, and planning and execution, each carrying explicit go or no go questions to be answered at three checkpoints: pressure testing the strategy before the transition begins, testing scalability after a minimum viable product migration and before moving the remaining workloads, and promptly reassessing if execution stalls. it estimates that committing roughly 3 percent of the program budget to this assurance can save more than 30 times its cost, and it advises executives to demand complete answers on how scope aligns with business objectives, how risk will be managed, how value will be shown within budget, whether architecture governance is defined across the delivery lifecycle and whether the organization is building cloud skills for the long term rather than completing a one time migration. cloud transformation, without the risk a companion set of do's and don'ts turns this planning into tactics. the do's are to build toward cloud native architecture from the start rather than retrofit it, to establish data consistency and a common data catalog before integrating across silos, to choose and standardize cloud services deliberately, favoring vendors that support portability standards such as kubernetes, istio and docker, to build a unified service management view across all deployment models, to plan for portability, including an inexpensive way to move data out of a vendor relationship, before a problem forces the issue, and to treat security as a first class element of the plan. the don'ts are to avoid relying on a single vendor, since any vendor can suffer a catastrophic outage, which argues for replicating critical applications across regions or providers, to avoid over committing to bulk license discounts before confirming that usage will reach the committed volume, because vendors rarely let a contract be scaled down, to avoid assuming the cloud removes it's duty to monitor vendor performance, since the business blames it for an outage whoever's infrastructure failed, to avoid letting the on premises data center atrophy,
