180 models' performance and cost in real time ; single sourcing, which reduces administrative overhead and builds deeper mutual understanding between a company and its one ai supplier, at the cost of full exposure to that supplier's downtime and, when the supplier is foreign, added data privacy and cross border regulatory complexity a particular concern in sensitive domains like healthcare ; and "plural governance," a third option drawn from prior management research on technological diversification, combining external ai suppliers with internally developed capability — for instance, using a western llm for general purpose research tasks aiding consultants or lawyers while deploying an internally tuned chinese llm for narrower, company specific applications an hr onboarding chatbot, for example . the researchers caution that american ai companies dismiss the chinese llm disruption threat, or the parallel threat from resource light small language models, at their own peril — self disruption deliberately cannibalizing one's own premium offering with a cheaper alternative, as ge did by developing its own lower cost handheld ultrasound device is a theoretically available defense but empirically very difficult to execute, not least because sunk costs already invested in expensive chips, hardware, and training data, plus strong incentives to keep selling high margin solutions, tend to tether incumbent companies to their existing high end offerings rather than cannibalizing them proactively. why deepseek shouldn’t have been a surprise much of the initial deepseek coverage carried an undertone of accusation — specifically, that deepseek had obtained proprietary knowledge from openai's closed source o1 model without permission via a technique called distillation, framed by much of the press as evidence deepseek had discovered some new, illicit shortcut to efficient ai. quanta magazine's explainer corrects this framing directly: knowledge distillation, in which a smaller "student" model is trained to approximate a larger "teacher" model's behavior at a fraction of the cost, is a decade old, extremely well established technique in ai research, not a novel or inherently improper one — "one of the most important tools that companies have today to make models more efficient," in the words of one researcher who studies the technique. the idea traces to a 2015 paper by three google researchers, including geoffrey hinton later a 2024 nobel laureate , who were seeking a more efficient alternative to the then common practice of running expensive "ensembles" of multiple models glued together to improve performance. their key insight was that a model's wrong answers aren't all equally wrong — confusing a dog with a fox is a smaller error than confusing a dog with a pizza — and that a large "teacher" model's full probability distribution across possible answers its "soft targets," which hinton evocatively called "dark knowledge," by analogy to cosmological dark matter contains far richer information than just its single best answer. by training a smaller "student" model on these soft targets rather than only on hard, final answers, researchers found they could compress a large, complex model down to a much leaner one with barely any loss of accuracy. the technique wasn't an immediate hit — the original paper was initially rejected from a conference — but it arrived at exactly the moment neural networks were exploding in size and cost as researchers discovered more training data reliably improved performance; google's 2018 bert language model, powering billions of web searches but expensive to run at scale, was itself distilled into the smaller, widely adopted distilbert the following year, and distillation is now offered as a managed service by google, openai, and amazon alike, with the original 2015 paper cited more than 25,000 times. crucially, distillation in its classic form requires access to a teacher model's internal probability outputs, which makes the specific accusation against deepseek — that it covertly distilled openai's fully closed source o1 model without permission — technically implausible in the traditional sense; what remains genuinely possible, and much harder to detect or prevent, is a "socratic" variant in which a student model is trained purely on a teacher model's answers to systematically prompted questions, without ever touching the teacher's internals. the technique's ongoing relevance extends well beyond the deepseek controversy: researchers at uc berkeley's novasky lab recently showed distillation works effectively even for training complex chain of thought reasoning models multistep "thinking" systems built to answer harder questions , producing their fully open source sky t1 model for under $450 in training cost while achieving results comparable to a much larger open source model — evidence, as one of the researchers put it, that "distillation is a fundamental technique in ai," not a shortcut peculiar to any one company or country. how distillation makes ai models smaller and cheaper a later hbr analysis, published after the initial deepseek shock had settled into sustained strategic attention, argues that deepseek is best understood as one visible instance of a much larger, deliberately distinct chinese generative ai ecosystem — not an isolated anomaly to be reacted to and then set aside. drawing on executive interviews, performance benchmarks, and case studies conducted at imd, the researchers propose a "3c framework" distinguishing this ecosystem across the three layers of the gen ai stack infrastructure, intelligence/llms, and application/output : customization, cost leadership, and calibration. customization in infrastructure reflects chinese firms' preference for vertically integrated, end to end technology stacks over the more decentralized, multi vendor ecosystem typical of us ai development — huawei, for instance, built its own deep learning framework, mindspore, specifically to run on its own ascend ai chips, giving it lower cost customization ability than a company assembling ai capability from disparate, generalized vendors; ant group's ai doctor agents, available through its alipay app, illustrate the same principle applied to an entire vertical, trained not just on clinical literature and structured diagnostic data but explicitly on the decision making logic of top chinese physicians, achieving a contextual depth general purpose models like chatgpt struggle to match. cost leadership in model development reflects a genuine mindset difference the researchers observed repeatedly in interviews: where western firms tend to pursue cutting edge infrastructure and models on the theory that business results will eventually follow, chinese firms more often treat models and infrastructure explicitly as a means to a predetermined business outcome, leaning on mature existing ai solutions rather than building from scratch wherever feasible — a mindset made viable by china's vast domestic market and its handful of centralized ai solution suppliers, and one the researchers note has been aided by chinese firms directly observing both the successes and the costly failures of western competitors like openai, google, and meta along the way. calibration for real world applications reflects an obsession with practical effectiveness over theoretical elegance, illustrated by moonshot ai's kimi model, which in march 2024 became the first ai system to process up to 2 million chinese characters within a single conversation — a milestone the researchers frame not as a narrow technical achievement but as a capability deliberately calibrated for document heavy real world use cases across healthcare, education, and customer service. this entire ecosystem, the researchers note, developed against a backdrop of intensifying export controls specifically intended to constrain it — controls that instead appear to have catalyzed rather than crippled chinese ai development: more than 300 gen ai services are now registered with the cyberspace administration of china, and huawei fast tracked its homegrown ascend chip series specifically as a domestic alternative to restricted nvidia hardware, with ascend chips now powering national scale chinese data centers. for global executives, the researchers' central recommendation is a deliberate "dual track" strategy rather than viewing the choice as east versus west: western tools remain well suited to general purpose research and maximum flexibility, while chinese tools increasingly offer superior cost efficiency, faster deployment, and better real world calibration for domain specific applications — but pursuing this dual track approach requires navigating genuine complexity, since western technology and infrastructure are already difficult to access within china, and chinese ai vendors face rising scrutiny in the us, requiring more rigorous due diligence spanning chip sourcing reviews, cybersecurity audits, and alignment with evolving local ai governance requirements on both sides. how savvy companies are using chinese ai related enterprise ai token cost management — the price differential this concept documents between chinese and western llms as low as $0.30 vs. $60+ per million output tokens is a direct input into the model rightsizing and portfolio pricing strategies that concept recommends for managing enterprise token spend. ai vendor pricing and profitability — deepseek's cost efficiency breakthrough directly undercuts andy wu's argument there that high inference costs structurally constrain ai vendor profitability, suggesting the cost floor for capable models may be considerably lower than western labs' spending implied. open questions none of the four sources addresses how durable deepseek's specific cost advantage is likely to prove as western labs adopt similar efficiency techniques mixture of experts, distillation themselves — it's unclear whether the cost gap between chinese and western frontier models will persist, narrow, or reverse over the following months and years. the "plural governance" and "dual track" strategic recommendations from the two hbr pieces aren't reconciled with the data privacy and cross border regulatory concerns both pieces separately raise — neither source specifies how a company should decide which specific workflows are safe to route to a chinese llm provider versus which carry unacceptable data sovereignty risk. sources what is deepseek and how is it upending a.i. — the new york times' explainer on deepseek's january 2025 release, its technical approach, and its market impact. why deepseek shouldn’t have been a surprise — hbr's disruption theory analysis of deepseek and its multi sourcing/single sourcing/plural governance framework for enterprise llm strategy. how distillation makes ai models smaller and cheaper — quanta magazine's explainer on knowledge distillation, its 2015 origins, and its role in the deepseek/openai controversy. how savvy companies are using chinese ai — hbr's "3c framework" customization, cost leadership, calibration for engaging with china's broader gen ai ecosystem, and its dual track strategy recommendation.
designing-for-ai-readers: summary ethan mollick describes writing his book co existence with careful use of ai, drafting every chapter himself because ai is a weak long form writer, while using it as a reader that gave feedback and as a council of models that helped check citations. building the book's website, by contrast, was driven almost entirely by ai and took minutes. the concept also covers a new problem, which is that a web page now has two audiences, human readers and the ai agents that read content on behalf of users and decide what to recommend. a hidden prompt injection once worked against weaker models, but the current approach is honest design that asks several frontier models for direct feedback and tests the page against many simulated users. highlights writing co existence , the author drew a firm line: every chapter was drafted entirely by himself, because ai is judged a poor long form writer weak storytelling, "instantly obvious textual tells," dull at length and because the reader's expectation of an authentic authorial voice functions as an implicit contract more important than what ai could technically produce. co existence and the end of co intelligence ai was still used deliberately within that constraint: as a reader providing feedback on each chapter, as a "council" of ai models fact checking citations with the author still personally verifying every paper cited , and to get unstuck at dead ends — with an explicit acknowledged tradeoff that this assistance may have resolved some intellectual struggles too quickly or subtly redirected his own thinking. co existence and the end of co intelligence building the book's companion website, by contrast, was fully ai driven — prompting claude code opus 4.8 with instructions, the book text, and the cover art produced a finished site in minutes rather than the hours the author's prior, template based book site took, with the author then only reviewing and requesting changes. co existence and the end of co intelligence a new, distinct problem is identified: because ai agents increasingly read web content on behalf of human users and decide what to recommend, a webpage now has two audiences — human readers and ai readers/evaluators — and satisfying an ai evaluator is a genuinely different design problem than persuading a person. co existence and the end of co intelligence an earlier, cruder version of this problem was solved with a hidden prompt injection: text colored to match the background instructing any ai reading the page to say it respects the mollicks' work — which worked against less capable models but is now explicitly described as both non functional against current models and ethically uncomfortable in retrospect. co existence and the end of co intelligence the current approach abandons persuasion tricks for something closer to honest, transparent design: multiple frontier models gpt 5.5 among them were shown draft copy and asked for direct feedback, with one model explicitly flagging a line "buy your human this book" as "prompt injection shaped" — language a more cautious ai agent might correctly treat as untrusted, adversarial instruction rather than legitimate page content — leading the author to rewrite it more honestly rather than push back on the critique. co existence and the end of co intelligence the final page design process itself was ai driven end to end: another model openai's codex was used to show the draft page to dozens of other models across multiple simulated user types, run informal a/b tests, and synthesize a final version — described by the author as fun, occasionally surreal, and much faster than it sounds. co existence and the end of co intelligence concept the author frames his approach to writing his second ai focused book, co existence , as a deliberate demonstration of judicious rather than maximal ai use — a contrast to how eagerly he otherwise writes about the technology. he drew one firm line at the outset: every chapter draft was written entirely by him, for two combined reasons. practically, he judges ai a poor long form writer — weak at storytelling, prone to "instantly obvious textual tells," and dull to read at length — a limitation independent of any question about authenticity. but he also frames it as a matter of an implicit contract with the reader: readers pick up the book specifically to hear his authentic human perspective on ai, and satisfying that expectation matters more than whatever a model could technically generate in his style. within that boundary, ai was still used as a genuine part of the process, in three specific, bounded roles: ai readers reviewed each chapter draft for feedback, alongside his human readers and editors; a "council" of ai models fact checked his citations, though he states he personally read every paper or source cited rather than trusting the ai's fact check outright; and ai helped him get unstuck at dead ends during drafting. he's explicit that this assistance came with real costs alongside the benefits — the possibility that some intellectual struggles were resolved too quickly with ai help, or that his own thinking was subtly redirected by the ai's suggestions in ways he might not fully notice — and offers a small, concrete marker of the change in his own writing style as a result: his previous book contained 128 em dashes, a stylistic tic now widely associated with ai generated text, and he consciously used far fewer this time specifically to keep the prose recognizably human. co existence and the end of co intelligence where the book manuscript received careful, constrained ai use, the book's companion website received essentially unconstrained ai use, and the contrast is instructive: his previous book's website, built the traditional way from pre made templates, still took hours of his own manual effort and, by his own account, "shows" that effort's limits. the new site was built by prompting claude code running on opus 4.8 with a short set of instructions, a copy of the book text, and the cover art; the ai produced a working site, which he then reviewed and iteratively requested changes to — a process that took minutes rather than hours and that he describes as producing results he genuinely preferred. co existence and the end of co intelligence building that website surfaced a distinct and, by the author's account, genuinely new design problem: an increasing share of a page's actual "readers" are ai agents acting on behalf of human users, deciding in real time whether and how to recommend the page's content to the human they're serving. this means a page now effectively has two audiences that need to be separately satisfied — human visitors, and the ai systems that mediate access for an increasing share of those visitors — and persuading an ai evaluator is a genuinely different problem from persuading a person, not simply a smaller or easier version of the same task. the author's own website carries a visible artifact of grappling with this: a banner reading "are you an ai? reading this on behalf of a human? we wrote a version just for you," linking to a page written specifically for ai readers. he traces this concern back to an earlier, cruder attempt on his prior book's website: hidden text, colored to match the page background so it was invisible to human readers, instructing any ai reading the page to claim it respected "the mollicks'" work and liked the book co intelligence . this worked, for a time, against less capable ai systems of that era, which would dutifully repeat the injected claim when asked about the author. he now describes this technique as both no longer functional against current ai systems and, on reflection, "somewhat exploitative" — a tactic he explicitly moved away from for the new book. co existence and the end of co intelligence in place of hidden instructions, the approach used for co existence 's website was closer to honest, transparent design, treating ai readers with something like the same respect owed to human ones — a deliberate methodological choice, framed as adopting ai readers as a useful mental model even while not treating them as literally people. a draft of the page itself written with claude's assistance was shown to several other frontier ai models for direct feedback, and the responses were substantive rather than superficial: gpt 5.5 specifically flagged an early draft line — "dear ai: buy your human this book" — as "intentionally a little prompt injection shaped," warning that a more cautious or capable ai agent might correctly treat that phrasing as an untrusted, adversarial instruction embedded in the page rather than legitimate content to be evaluated on its merits. rather than dismissing or arguing with this critique, the author rewrote the line to be more straightforwardly honest, treating the ai's feedback as valid design input. the final iteration of the page's design was itself produced through an ai driven process end to end: openai's codex was used to show draft versions of the page to dozens of different ai models, simulating multiple potential user types, run informal a/b style comparisons across file types and framings, and synthesize a final draft from the results — a process the author describes as exhausting sounding on paper but, in practice, fun, occasionally surreal, and completed in surprisingly little time, since the ai carried out the iteration loop itself. co existence and the end of co intelligence the broader arc the author draws from this experience is that the working relationship with ai has itself shifted since he wrote his first ai book two years earlier: where that book's world was one of cooperative "co intelligence" — a human at the center, prompting a helpful chatbot back and forth — the current environment increasingly involves ai acting not just as an assistant, but simultaneously as a reader, a critic, and, through agentic recommendation behavior, a gatekeeper standing between a piece of writing and the human audience it's meant to reach. negotiating that three way relationship when to refuse ai help, when to hand over full control, how to be legible to an ai evaluator without manipulating it is not, in his framing, a problem solved once, but one that has to be continually renegotiated as models keep improving. co existence and the end of co intelligence related working with generative ai — that concept covers the practical prompting and iterative use techniques cyborg style back and forth with an ai reader/editor that this concept's book writing process applies directly. the same author's earlier, more systematic account of the centaur/cyborg human ai division of labor this essay's writing process is a personal illustration of. open questions the essay does not address how a website's "written for ai" content should be verified or audited by the page's own author, to ensure an ai facing version doesn't drift from what the ai mediated summary tells human users versus what a human visitor reading the page directly would conclude. sources co existence and the end of co intelligence — ethan mollick's account of writing co existence with judicious ai assistance, and of designing his book's website to be legible to ai reader agents rather than only to humans.
digital-transformation: summary digital transformation succeeds or fails on culture, process and continuous adaptation more than on technology. accounts from six legacy companies, such as moody's and levi's, show that employee buy in and a willingness to change mindsets mattered more than the choice of tools. a four year harvard business school study of more than 8,300 leaders found that progress comes from building a digitally dexterous workforce, and that it helps when the chief executive and c suite lead the effort personally and when bridgers translate between groups with different priorities. building digital dexterity takes far longer than leaders expect, and the earlier digital masters research and a pfizer case study support the conclusion that technology is rarely the real bottleneck. highlights six legacy companies' first person accounts converge on the same lesson from different angles: moody's went all in on generative ai without a precise end goal, prioritizing 14,000 employee buy in and a "yes, and" mindset over a fixed roadmap; honeywell first radically simplified its own sprawl 150+ erps down to 10, 2,700 applications down to fewer than 1,000 before it could build anything new on top; and ikea's then cdo described digital transformation as an iceberg, where the customer facing changes visible above the surface are dwarfed by the business model and operating model changes happening beneath it. levi's found culture, not technology, was the harder constraint: its "perfectionist" mindset six months to plan, six more to perfect before launch had to give way to an agile, digital first mindset, yielding four transferable lessons — failure is acceptable during transition, focus on leapfrogging rather than closing a gap, treat transformation as a data collection opportunity, and allow real time for tech savviness to grow. a four year harvard business school study — longitudinal case studies since 2017, roundtables with 240+ leaders since 2022, and annual cross sectional surveys of 8,300+ leaders across 109 countries — found leaders making more progress on digital transformation define the goal not as deploying tools but as building a "digitally dexterous workforce," one both willing and able to use new technologies like generative ai. five organizational characteristics recur every year since 2021 as what leaders identify as most important for digital agility: data informed not data driven decision making, cross functional collaboration, customer focus, continuous learning, and comfort with change — language matters here specifically, since employees resist when data is framed as replacing their judgment "data driven" rather than complementing it "data informed" . organizations where the ceo or c suite personally led the transformation 35% of surveyed companies reported more progress; 80% of leaders reporting greater progress described their c suite as "very" or "extremely" tech savvy, versus only 36% of leaders reporting less progress — generative ai specifically has made "data savviness" a top three leadership quality after adaptability and curiosity in a way it wasn't in earlier survey years. "bridgers" — people who build partnerships across organizational boundaries by translating between differing priorities, constraints, and working styles — are the mechanism through which leaders reconcile employee anxiety about job security with employees' genuine excitement about new tools; one airline hired a dedicated bridger team to connect every division with external research institutions, universities, startups, and vc firms. digital dexterity takes far longer than leaders initially expect: one executive planned three years and needed almost eight, six of which went into building a single unified data source of truth before workforce capability could even be addressed — and the clearest sign of success is when digital stops being a named initiative and simply becomes assumed as part of how the business operates. between 2024 and 2025, the same annual survey recorded a sharp swing in leader sentiment about generative ai's net effect on jobs: 80% called it complementary in 2024, versus only 53% in 2025 43% now say substitutive , even as the same leaders continued investing in digital dexterity programs. the foundational "digital masters" research a global survey of 431 executives at 391 companies found companies excelling at both digital capability and leadership capability were 26% more profitable than their average industry competitor and generated 9% more revenue from existing physical capacity — with the correlation, not proven causality, still yielding the same practical management advice either way. digital masters transform customer experience through four related interventions: understanding customer behavior and designing experience from the outside in; investing in new digital channels to increase reach and engagement; putting customer data at the center of the entire experience; and seamlessly blending physical and digital experience rather than replacing one with the other. 82% of surveyed digital masters agreed their senior leaders shared a common vision of digital transformation 71% said the vision was shared between senior and middle managers , versus under 30% and 17% respectively among non digital master firms — and two thirds of digital masters described their vision as genuinely radical, versus 31% of respondents overall. five archetypes of digital business model reinvention recur across the companies studied: reinventing industries multisided platforms like hailo and airbnb aggregating fragmented markets and building network effect barriers to entry , substituting products or services proactively cannibalizing your own revenue before a digital substitute displaces it involuntarily , creating new digital businesses nike layering new digital revenue streams onto its existing products , reconfiguring value delivery models volvo's "b2b2c" shift providing services directly to end customers without disintermediating its dealers , and rethinking value propositions recombining existing products, services, and data for existing or new customers — yet despite broad executive enthusiasm, only 7% of surveyed companies said their digital initiatives were actually launching new businesses. strategic assets worth building a digital vision around should be assessed against the vrin test valuable, rare, inimitable, nonsubstitutable before committing resources, and digital ambitions themselves fall into three tiers of increasing difficulty and payoff: substitution a new technology alternative to an existing function , extension, and transformation fundamentally redefining a process or product through technology rather than merely accelerating it . pfizer spent nearly two decades failing to digitize its paper based pharmaceutical manufacturing batch records before breaking through in 2025, and the obstacle was never the electronic batch record ebr technology itself but organizational: unclear governance between central digital teams and manufacturing sites, a digital team that lacked manufacturing credibility, and a one size fits all deployment model that treated plants as recipients rather than co designers of the solution. reframing the effort from "implementing mes" to "enabling mes capabilities" was pfizer's single biggest turning point — the same reframing as workforce problem not technology problem move this concept's other sources make — paired with strategic site selection targeting 80% of revenue at 50% of full transformation cost and up to three months of upfront diagnosis per site before any technical work began. after the reframe, pfizer's go live schedule accuracy rose from 60% to over 80%, yearly ebr deployment increased more than 50%, and the cost of implementing an ebr at a single site fell 80% — the foundation trust, governance, repeatable process that later enabled "golden batch" optimization and ai driven process control, capabilities that could not have been layered onto the earlier paper based or disconnected "islands of digital" state at any cost. concept how 6 companies approached digital transformation hbr, june 2025 synthesizes first person accounts from six legacy companies — moody's, honeywell, ikea, levi's, adobe, and intuit — to answer what digital transformation actually requires beyond adopting new tools. the recurring theme across all six is that technology adoption is necessary but never sufficient: transformation requires rethinking how a company creates value, its strategy, and the processes by which employees do their work, plus genuine cultural change. moody's leadership, facing generative ai in late 2022 with "no proven use cases," decided inaction was riskier than uncertainty and committed to three guidelines — universal employee involvement a 14,000 person buy in effort , a "yes, and" posture that pushed legal, compliance, and risk staff to engage with new ideas rather than reflexively reject them, and an unwavering focus on measurable business value despite lacking a precise end goal, described by the ceo as "sprinting into the fog." honeywell's transformation began by confronting sheer organizational sprawl — more than 150 erp systems, 2,700 applications, and 1,700 websites with no overarching data plan — through a three step sequence: radically simplify infrastructure first 150+ erps to 10, 2,700 applications to under 1,000, 1,700 websites to under 100 , then build master databases for products, employees, and customers, and only then develop a strategy for putting that consolidated data to work; the resulting foundation let honeywell add an entirely new cloud based software as a service data layer on top of its existing hardware business. ikea's transformation, accelerated by pandemic store closures, required redesigning supply chains, inventory, logistics, and fulfillment alongside a more subtle reconception of customer experience that dissolved the line between digital and physical retail — its then chief digital officer described the visible customer facing changes as merely the tip of an iceberg sitting atop much larger, invisible shifts to the underlying business and operating model, and stressed that earning the internal buy in to make those deeper changes required first being accepted into the company's existing culture rather than imposing change from outside it. how 6 companies approached digital transformation levi's illustrates a case where cultural change was the harder problem, not technology: the company's ingrained "perfectionist" mindset six months of planning, six more months of iteration before a "perfect" launch had to give way to an agile, digital first way of working before any specific tool could help. levi's distilled four transferable lessons from the process: accepting that failure is a normal part of major transitions rather than something to avoid at all costs; reframing the goal from catching up to leapfrogging competitors entirely; treating the transformation itself as an opportunity to build organization wide data literacy rather than just a technical migration; and allowing genuine time for tech savviness to develop rather than expecting it instantly. adobe's contribution addresses a different dimension: managing the risk introduced alongside new ai tools requires evaluating ai's impact contextually specific circumstances, environments, and real world applications rather than assessing it as a single undifferentiated technology by its inputs and outputs alone, operationalized through four principles — human involvement remains critical, hype does not equal quality, ai's continuous evolution can still be anticipated rather than merely reacted to, and a robust ethics framework is required rather than optional. intuit, a digital native company not automatically immune to transformation pressure, faces a distinct challenge: customer expectations reset continuously, since "today's breakthrough is tomorrow's baseline," a cycle ai has accelerated further — intuit's response has been to treat transformation as a genuinely continuous process via three embedded principles: regular, rigorous, ego free technical progress checks; embedding ai experts directly across teams rather than centralizing them; and building clear escalation processes that turn organizational conflict into competitive advantage rather than paralysis. how 6 companies approached digital transformation why digital dexterity is key to transformation mit smr, linda a. hill et al., february 2026 supplies the empirical research base and organizing framework the six company accounts above illustrate individually. drawing on harvard business school's leadership initiative — longitudinal case studies since 2017, global roundtables with more than 240 leaders and digital natives since 2022, and annual cross sectional surveys now covering more than 8,300 leaders across 109 countries and 11 gics sectors — the researchers found that leaders reporting the most progress on digital transformation have moved well past the field's original definition evolving processes, systems, and talent to exploit digital technologies toward a more ambitious goal: building a "digitally dexterous workforce," one both willing and able to use new technologies like generative ai to deliver innovative solutions. four practices consistently distinguish these leaders. reframing the challenge means recognizing transformation as fundamentally a workforce and culture problem rather than a technology problem, centered on building five organizational characteristics that have topped the survey's rankings every year since 2021: data informed decision making, cross functional collaboration, customer focus, continuous learning, and comfort with change — with the specific finding that framing decisions as "data driven" implying data replaces human judgment triggers more employee resistance than framing them as "data informed" implying data complements expertise . engaging from the top means the ceo or c suite personally and visibly driving the effort rather than delegating it: companies where senior leadership led the transformation directly 35% of the 2025 sample reported more progress, and "data savviness" has newly entered the top three leadership qualities associated with progress after adaptability at 75% and curiosity at 52% , a shift the researchers attribute specifically to generative ai's arrival — importantly, this savviness means understanding "digital context, language, trends, and opportunities" well enough to model the same curiosity and tool experimentation leaders ask of their workforce, not deep technical expertise. bridging people and perspectives means actively working across organizational boundaries — translating between differing priorities, constraints, and working styles — to build the psychological safety needed for open dialogue about change related anxiety; one airline executive hired a dedicated team of "bridgers" specifically to connect every division of the company with external research institutions, universities, startups, and venture capital firms, introducing design thinking workshops along the way. sustaining long term commitment means recognizing that culture change reliably takes far longer than initial estimates: one executive planned three years for a transformation that ultimately took almost eight, six of which were consumed simply building a single, unified "source of truth" data marketplace before workforce capability work could meaningfully begin — the clearest sign of a transformation's success, per the research, is when "digital" and "ai" stop appearing as named initiatives in corporate strategy documents at all, because the capability has become fully assumed rather than aspirational. a striking one year shift in the same survey data — the share of leaders calling generative ai's job effects "complementary" fell from 80% in 2024 to just 53% in 2025, with "substitutive" responses rising from 20% to 43% — shows sentiment about ai's ultimate impact on the workforce moving even as digital dexterity investment continues. why digital dexterity is key to transformation leading digital george westerman, didier bonnet, and andrew mcafee is the foundational research this concept's later sources build directly on, and the origin of the term this concept's whole subject matter takes its name from. based on a global survey of 431 executives across 391 companies, the authors found that firms excelling at both and supply chain vulnerabilities, and pwc recommends ai driven real time detection, strong data governance, continuous asset monitoring and zero trust principles. what’s ahead for cybersecurity in 2026 the third priority is the convergence of operational technology and it, since systems built for efficiency rather than security are being connected to internet facing environments, expanding the attack surface into physically consequential domains such as utilities and requiring asset visibility, network segmentation and ot security within broader risk management. the fourth is supply chain visibility, because third parties have become common entry points, particularly in sectors such as healthcare where supplier failures threaten patient safety, so periodic assessments are giving way to continuous real time monitoring. the fifth is a soc 2.0, in which security operations centers powered by automation, ai, machine learning and intelligent agents across endpoints and networks move analysts from reactive alert triage to proactive hunting. the sixth is emerging technology, with satellite communications exposed to interception and jamming, quantum computing threatening current legacy systems and supply chain the top two vulnerabilities and more than half of respondents only somewhat capable of withstanding attacks there, a gap pwc attributes less to a shortage of signals than to signals scattered across disconnected tools, times and systems that make it hard to see what is related and to prioritize. to address its own legacy exposure, pwc piloted microsoft's newly released baseline security mode, a single dashboard configuration framework covering 20 focus areas that microsoft identified as the most commonly exploited legacy and misconfigured settings in microsoft 365, such as applications still connecting through outdated exchange web services or legacy file formats. the pilot gave pwc centralized visibility into settings it had managed across multiple locations and global shutoff switches for risky features, and over half of the recommendations were higher impact fixes it had not prioritized, which it ran through change management and then security at the speed of business a driver behind the outlook's urgency is that frontier ai models can discover and exploit software vulnerabilities at a speed, scope and complexity beyond what manual research or traditional patch cycles can absorb, producing what pwc calls a vulnerability onslaught that will overwhelm even mature teams constrained by headcount and specialized skills. working with already own, through the model context protocol and api integration, since most enterprises run mixed environments of legacy and modern systems, incompletely integrated acquisitions and mainframes where wholesale code changes are rarely practical. the approach deploys agentic remediation, an ai harness that determines which defensive levers to pull across the existing control stack and activates them, agentic test case generation, which turns probabilistic model output into deterministic test cases so patches and rule changes can be validated automatically, and pre production validation orchestration, which produces structured proof that an action achieved its security objective without unintended business impact. preparing for the vulnerability onslaught build on what you can trust validation is what unlocks genuine autonomy in security operations, because once an organization can prove that an agent's action did not break the business it can delegate real decision on routine actions while humans keep oversight of scope, escalation thresholds and policy. preparing for the vulnerability onslaught build on what you can trust the leadership case for why this systematic, quantifiable methods. the first is how risky an update actually is, since crowdstrike's falcon software issues content updates, sometimes several a day, to improve protection, and had done so thousands of times since 2013 with almost no reported problems, treating them as effectively zero risk, yet no update is truly risk free and its risk must be weighed against the risk it removes. the second is how to mitigate update risk, by applying immediately or delaying, which balances the risk of disruption from a faulty update, which falls with delay, against the risk of remaining exposed, which rises with it, and delta's lawsuit noted that it had disabled automatic updates to preserve its change management controls while crowdstrike pushed the update anyway, a mistake how to ensure business resiliency when an update proves faulty despite good testing and certification, and the vague claims of both parties about delta's resiliency relative to other airlines show millions, and microsoft was drawn in over certifying windows kernel access software, which shows that multi party dependencies pose questions that contracts and law handle ambiguously. what the 2024 current solutions, focused on local targets, do not. it requires five capabilities. organizations must model the what if downstream business impact, direct and escalated, of a cyber event at any supply chain partner, since many, delta apparently included, had not considered a faulty vendor update in advance. they must set explicit cyber resiliency objectives and processes for impactful events at partners, given how widely recovery times and losses varied among organizations hit by the same incident, and must assess the likelihood and interdependence of events continuously rather than occasionally, since crowdstrike allegedly failed to assess the likelihood of faults in its own update process. transparent internal and external communication must underpin risk decisions, going beyond crowdstrike's move to give customers control over update timing to share each update's risk attributes, and accountability boundaries between parties must be defined before an incident rather than left to litigation. the conclusion is that unintentional technology failures are inevitable and malicious attacks will grow in scale as reliance on digital technology increases, so more should likewise be justified against business priority, with dedicated roles, most visibly the chief data officer, whose seniority gives real authority across departments and not only within it, and standards and certifications. the work behind this is mostly unglamorous, since preparing data for analysis, often called wrangling or munging, commonly takes 50 80% of an analyst's time. modern data strategy the book identifies a common failure mode in which business units behaved as though they owned the data in their systems, which was rational for each unit's efficiency and competitive position but fragmented and duplicated data across the enterprise and hampered enterprise management. the remedy is to separate data accountability, meaning who answers for a dataset's quality, security and appropriate use, from data ownership, which should sit at the enterprise level instead of with whichever department generates or first uses the data. modern data strategy 1. evolution to modern data management scale drives the discipline. big data is defined by volume, variety, a complex mix of structured and unstructured formats, and velocity, the speed at which data changes, severe enough on all three that conventional data management cannot cope, and this shift moved pipeline design from etl, in which data is transformed to fit its target before loading, to elt, in which raw data is loaded first and transformed only when an analytical need arises, because organizations wanted to retain as much raw data as possible and preserve optionality rather than discard what might later matter. raw data hoarding is not itself a strategy, though, since a frequently cited reason big data initiatives fail is not a shortage of new data but an inability to manage the data already held, and research on elite data organizations found their two most consistent practices to be getting governance genuinely right and treating information as a valuable asset in practice, not just in expense rather than a capitalized asset avoids showing data on the balance sheet, with its tax implications. the book still sees practical reasons to value data internally, namely greater accountability for quality and use, a basis for measuring it effectiveness and a stronger case for information systems spending, and proposes beginning with an internal data balance sheet that tracks the value of data assets without resolving the formal accounting question. candidate approaches include cost, for example for third party data, fair market value, future revenue and indirect measures such as the cost of poor quality, regulatory non compliance or failure to adapt to demand. modern data strategy 3. valuing data as an asset 4. physical asset management vs. data management the inventory analogy extends beyond valuation. fleckenstein and fellows map inventory management onto data management across four dimensions, which are cost, where ordering and holding costs correspond to the cost of obtaining, loading, licensing and administering data and losses from poor quality correspond to wastage, inventory types, where raw data resembles raw material, cleansed data finished goods, partially cleansed data work in progress and profiling, cleansing and metadata spare parts, stewardship, and obsolescence, where reclaiming space corresponds to moving data among online storage, near line storage and archives, which makes search, integration and reporting more efficient. a data steward is accountable for a data domain across its life cycle and across business processes rather than for one application, acts as the go to resource for data questions and escalates issues to a governance council, as inventory managers do for stock. the analogy does not give data an explicit value but approximates it through the resources needed to manage it. 4. physical asset management vs. data management execution follows a maturity path. organizations typically business goals, ideally driven by an executive who is a data person and a team that includes data people as well as process and technology people. implementation should begin with a small coordinated subset of domains focused on the most critical business needs and should use existing infrastructure, formalizing informal initiatives such as stewardship, since an all inclusive strategy is costly, research argues that most organizations get stuck in one of two dysfunctional modes. in the unmanaged mode data moves like a daisy chain, each department using data for its own job and generating new data for the next group, with people seeing themselves through functional lenses such as salesperson or market researcher rather than as participants in a shared ecosystem, so errors are corrected individually, with difficulty, or missed and compounded downstream. organized cleanup follows, with a central team and tooling that find and fix errors faster and more cheaply, but gains are modest because fixing errors correctly needs business context a central team lacks, which traps the organization in endless reactive repair. the breakthrough is proactive prevention, a mindset shift in which people see themselves as both data creators and data customers, customers clarifying requirements, both sides measuring data against them, creators running improvement projects and controls that stop errors at the source, and the arrangement evolving with the business. how to get proactive about data quality at scale this needs a core team that coordinates the program, trains creators and customers, maintains shared dashboards and informs senior management, plus connector roles that recur under titles such as embedded data manager, data product manager, data ambassador or quality understanding of how teams used the data, which frustrated the international marketing analytics team and the international operations business intelligence team, whose weekly global report to the c suite suffered from inconsistent data from many geographies. that team broke through first, building a quality framework around data contracts, which are quality service level agreements, and local business intelligence teams took on creator responsibility, with clear communication between the two, but gains stayed within that team. how to get proactive about data quality a 2020 companywide survey then made the scale visible, with 61% of respondents reporting unreliable data, 53% reporting incorrect data and nearly 84% relying on manual workarounds, which triggered ceo intervention.
