enterprise-negotiation-tactics: summary skilled negotiators can create leverage even when they have no complete alternative to a deal, by using partial alternatives that cover only part of the need, by taking actions that do not require the other side's agreement and by presenting a possible walk away as a warning instead of a threat. dependence between buyer and supplier is also usually more balanced than it feels, since a sole source supplier typically needs the customer's revenue too. large company negotiations tend to underperform for structural reasons, because frontline negotiators are rewarded for closing any deal and because the people who negotiate are not aligned with those who decide. the recommended fixes are to give negotiators no authority to commit, so that they act as problem solvers who bring recommendations to decision makers, and to replace deal review boards with proactive deal value boards that give teams a view across related deals. highlights when a complete alternative to a deal doesn't exist, partial alternatives that only cover a fraction of the need can still shift negotiating dynamics: a tech company facing an intransigent sole electronics supplier found two smaller suppliers that together covered just 30% of its volume, and used that partial coverage to force better pricing from the incumbent rather than accepting an unaffordable increase. negotiating when there is no plan b dependence between negotiating parties is usually more balanced than it feels: a company that relies heavily on a sole source supplier is often just as important to that supplier's revenue and fixed cost coverage, meaning even a party that seems to have "no alternative" often retains real leverage — genuine walk away brinkmanship is rare the authors saw it only once in 25 years of dealmaking . negotiating when there is no plan b beyond a formal batna, negotiators can pursue "procedural alternatives" — unilateral actions that don't require the other side's agreement, such as paying invoices based on the lowest price a supplier charges anywhere globally with a note explaining the "correction" rather than formally demanding renegotiation, using inertia and tacit rather than active consent to shift the relationship without a confrontation. negotiating when there is no plan b reframing a walk away possibility as a warning "we can't afford this, so we'll be forced to find someone else" rather than a threat "agree or we cut you off" avoids the coercion counterthreat spiral, since warnings signal self protection rather than an intent to harm the other side — and appealing to fairness "why are you demanding this?" can extract concessions that raw power plays cannot, since people will sometimes concede rather than be shown to be acting unfairly. negotiating when there is no plan b enterprise negotiations underperform not from negotiator skill gaps but from two structural problems: the agency problem frontline negotiators are incentivized toward closing any deal — commission, time pressure — rather than the enterprise's actual interests, so organizations restrict their authority, turning them into "couriers" who must repeatedly seek approval and the alignment problem in complex, multi stakeholder deals, forcing early pre negotiation consensus on the most conservative acceptable terms leaves negotiators no room to explore creative trade offs . why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals the counterintuitive fix for the agency problem is to give negotiators no commitment authority at all, reframing them as problem solvers who explore options and bring a recommended business plan back to decision makers, rather than agents defending preapproved minimums — removing the incentive to make self interested concessions just to close, while letting them engage counterparties creatively without triggering internal vetoes. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals organizations should first decide which deals and issues are actually worth negotiating hard, since most contract terms can be resolved at reasonable "market standard" levels without real loss of value — the operative question is not how large an issue is but how much of that value is genuinely at stake in negotiating it versus accepting a market norm, and companies increasingly use generative ai agents to close standardized, low variance deals automatically. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals traditional deal review boards drbs , which evolved from capital project approval processes, should be reimagined as proactive "deal value boards" dvbs that give negotiating teams an enterprise wide view of related deals and current/future leverage, and that broker internal "side deals" compensating business units that would otherwise block a proposal that benefits the company overall — evolving from expectation setting early in a deal, to problem solving support during negotiation, to a final go/no go decision made by a small group once options are fully understood. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals concept two complementary pieces of negotiation research address the same underlying challenge — how organizations extract more value from high stakes deals — from opposite ends: one focuses on individual negotiator tactics when a walk away alternative seems unavailable, the other on the organizational structures that prevent even skilled negotiators from creating value at scale. on the individual tactics side, the starting premise is that the absence of a clear batna best alternative to a negotiated agreement, the term roger fisher and william ury introduced in getting to yes doesn't actually mean a negotiator is powerless — it usually means they haven't expanded their search enough. the first lever is the power of partial alternatives: when negotiators search for a batna, they typically look for one complete substitute that addresses every problem, but a breakthrough often comes instead from an option that only partially replaces the deal on the table. a high tech company entirely dependent on one supplier for critical electronic components, facing repeated price increases and degrading service, identified two smaller, qualified suppliers that together could cover only 30 percent of its total volume — but that partial coverage was enough to credibly reduce its dependence on the incumbent and extract better pricing in exchange for a modest volume commitment, rather than accepting an unaffordable increase under the illusion that its only alternative was catastrophic supply disruption. negotiating when there is no plan b a second lever is recognizing that dependence between negotiating parties is almost always more balanced than it feels from inside the weaker seeming position: if a company relies heavily on a sole source supplier, that supplier typically also depends heavily on the company's revenue, and the higher the switching costs for the customer, the more painful losing that customer usually is for the supplier too — meaning genuine walk away brinkmanship is exceedingly rare in practice the authors, who have advised on hundreds of negotiations across three decades, saw a deal actually blow up under firm but reasonable pressure only once . a global manufacturer facing a coatings supplier demanding a 10 percent price increase during contract renewal discovered that, although its business represented "only" 10 percent of the supplier's revenue, that revenue came from one of the supplier's most profitable and specialized product lines, meaning losing it would force costly retooling and strain the supplier's cash flow far more than the raw percentage suggested — illustrating that even a seemingly weak negotiating position can rest on hidden supplier vulnerabilities worth actively researching rather than assuming away. a third lever, for situations where a genuine batna search keeps coming up empty, is pursuing procedural alternatives: unilateral actions a negotiator can take without needing the other side's formal agreement, distinguishing between active consent an explicit "yes" and tacit consent proceeding as long as the counterpart doesn't actively object . a global microprocessor company discovered a supplier was charging wildly inconsistent prices for identical components shipped to different sites; rather than opening a formal negotiation it couldn't easily win given it had no qualified alternative supplier , it simply began paying every invoice at the lowest price the supplier charged anywhere, with a note explaining the "correction" — and continued receiving shipments uninterrupted for nearly a year, saving significant money each month, until the supplier finally escalated in a notably non aggressive tone once market conditions had shifted back toward better balance. related to this is the principal agent distinction: negotiators facing a large counterparty organization should distinguish the company from the specific individuals at the table, since a client's business may be small relative to the counterparty's total revenue but critical to a specific negotiating unit's targets or a specific negotiator's personal quota — leverage that headline revenue comparisons obscure entirely. finally, communicating a walk away possibility is a delicate art: framing it as a threat "agree or we cut off shipments" triggers a coercive, defensive spiral, while framing the identical substance as a warning "we can't afford this, so we'll be forced to look elsewhere" signals self protection rather than an intent to harm, which is far less likely to provoke a counterthreat — and when power plays alone don't move a counterparty, appealing to fairness "why are you demanding this?" can succeed where raw leverage cannot, since people sometimes concede simply because they can't justify their position once asked to explain it. negotiating when there is no plan b the second, complementary piece of research addresses why large organizations underperform at negotiation systematically, even when individual negotiators are skilled. two structural problems drive this: the agency problem, where negotiators act on the organization's behalf but their personal incentives commission on closing a sale, time pressure to move on to the next of dozens of supplier relationships don't perfectly match the enterprise's actual interests, leading organizations to restrict negotiator authority so tightly that dealmakers become, in effect, couriers who must repeatedly return to superiors for approval on every concession — a dynamic that slows deals, damages credibility, and strips away the room to solve problems creatively at the table. and the alignment problem, which compounds as deals grow more complex: in multiproduct, multiregion, or cross functional negotiations, each internal stakeholder sales wants pricing and revenue, engineering wants realistic deadlines, legal wants minimized risk needs to be satisfied, and forcing early pre negotiation consensus typically means agreeing on the most conservative minimums acceptable to everyone — after which negotiators have essentially no room left to explore genuine trade offs, and if a counterparty won't accept those preapproved terms, the negotiator must reopen the internal debate from scratch, repeatedly, prolonging the process and eroding trust on both sides of the table. common organizational fixes often make this worse rather than better: "guardrails" that preapprove specific concessions in advance tend to grow so long and restrictive that they almost never match the realities of a live negotiation one lead negotiator described winning a deal within tight guardrails as something that "never happens" , and traditional deal review boards drbs — which evolved out of capital project approval, where a project can be approved or rejected on the basis of projected risk and return alone — simply replicate the authority parceling problem with more senior people involved, since a negotiation additionally requires guesswork about what an external counterparty will actually accept. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals the prescribed fix works by attacking both problems simultaneously rather than separately. first, organizations should decide upfront which deals and issues are genuinely worth a full negotiation effort at all — not every deal merits it, and within any single complex deal, not every issue does either. the operative test isn't how large an issue is in absolute terms but how much of that value is actually at stake in negotiating it versus simply accepting a reasonable, market standard term: in mature markets like eurobonds, most terms already proceed on standardized forms with only a small number of genuinely negotiated adjustments, and companies increasingly use generative ai agents to close standardized, low variance deals automatically within set parameters, freeing skilled human negotiators for the comparatively few issues where negotiation can genuinely change the outcome. second, and most counterintuitively, the fix for the agency problem is not giving negotiators more authority but giving them essentially none: reframing them as problem solvers tasked with exploring the counterparty's actual needs and constraints and bringing back a recommended business plan, rather than agents empowered to make binding commitments within a narrow, preapproved band. removing commitment authority removes the incentive to make self interested concessions purely to close a deal directly addressing agency , and because the negotiator's job becomes exploration rather than defending fixed minimums, they can engage in genuinely creative problem solving with a counterparty without triggering internal vetoes at every turn addressing alignment . a midsize technology company renewing a critical $180 million partnership deal used exactly this approach — requesting authority to explore innovative structures with the incumbent partner and to open unauthorized, no commitment talks with a disliked rival, which the board initially resisted but ultimately allowed; the rival partner turned out to be a genuinely viable option, and the resulting leverage helped the company close nearly $1 billion in improved terms with its original incumbent partner. third, this requires replacing early, locked in stakeholder sign off with ongoing, two way consultation throughout the negotiation — testing volume and delivery trade offs with business unit leaders, payment term trade offs with finance, service capacity trade offs with operations, as new information emerges from the actual talks — rather than freezing every internal position before external negotiation even begins, since forcing people to commit early to minimum acceptable terms predictably leads them to inflate those minimums defensively, hiding the organization's true fallback position even from its own negotiators. finally, the traditional drb should evolve into a "deal value board" dvb : a proactive, cross silo body whose job is not merely to approve deals but to give negotiators visibility into related deals and future opportunities elsewhere in the organization that could strengthen current leverage, and to broker internal "side deals" that compensate business units who would otherwise block a proposal that benefits the enterprise as a whole — evolving from managing stakeholder expectations early in a deal's life, to active problem solving support as talks progress, to a final, well informed go/no go decision made by a small group only once every viable option has actually been surfaced and understood. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals related algorithmic auditing and ai failures — the stakeholder mapping discipline of the ethical matrix parallels this concept's principal agent distinction between a counterparty organization and the specific individuals negotiating on its behalf. pyramid principle — minto's structured approach to organizing an argument is a complementary communication discipline for the "business plan" recommendations this concept's empowered but uncommitted negotiators bring back to decision makers. open questions neither source addresses how the "no commitment authority" negotiator model should handle genuinely time critical negotiations, where the delay inherent in bringing recommendations back to decision makers could itself cost the deal. sources negotiating when there is no plan b — hbr's tactics for creating negotiating leverage without a clear batna: partial alternatives, procedural moves, warnings versus threats, and fairness appeals. why big companies struggle to negotiate great deals — danny ertel hbr on the agency and alignment problems in enterprise negotiation, and the shift from deal review boards to deal value boards.
executive-ai-digital-twins: summary a small but growing number of executives are creating ai replicas trained on their own writing, speeches and communication style to handle routine tasks, public appearances and employee questions. linkedin co founder reid hoffman's twin, trained on 22 years of his material, has delivered more than 75 presentations, and companies are also using twins for internal coaching and mentoring. early adopters report substantial time savings, but the practice raises open questions about accuracy, since twins can invent answers or misjudge tone, about whether employees will accept them and about who owns a twin's accumulated knowledge when an employee leaves. the clearest governance principle so far is that digital twins should support human decisions without replacing human accountability. highlights an executive ai digital twin is built by training a system on an individual's own emails, speeches, podcasts, articles, and interviews so it can answer questions, draft communications, or appear at events in that person's communication style. linkedin co founder reid hoffman's "reid ai," trained on 22 years of his own material, has delivered more than 75 addresses and presentations since its 2024 launch, speaks 74 languages, and saves hoffman an estimated 50% of his time in weeks it's deployed. digital twins are being used for internal coaching and mentorship, not just external appearances: greif's "balabot" has interacted with nearly 3,300 employees since december, and quantium health's "virtual brian" helped one executive manager recognize she had underrated her own accomplishments in a self evaluation. a december report from the institute for corporate productivity concluded digital work twins could become the most significant productivity multiplier since the personal computer, with reid hoffman predicting most companies over 50 employees will have executive ai twins within a decade, and rank and file employee twins following within two. digital twins have real failure modes requiring human oversight: hallucination reid ai has invented answers to opinion questions , tonal misfires failing to sound appropriately serious or light , and outright technical glitches one executive's twin visibly malfunctioned, repeating the same line, in front of a live conference audience . employee acceptance is not automatic — early resistance is common staff at one firm objected to having their emails used to train a twin but is often resolved through opt out mechanisms for sensitive personal or work content and scoped access to only explicitly authorized material. ownership of a digital twin's accumulated knowledge when an employee departs is an unresolved legal and organizational question; one company's policy lets a departing employee take their twin's likeness and personal expertise while the employer retains proprietary business knowledge the twin accumulated. the clearest governance principle articulated so far is that digital twins should support human decision making rather than substitute for human accountability, particularly in supervisory or legal adjacent contexts where a misstatement could create real liability. concept too much work to do? have your digital twin handle it wsj, may 2026 documents an emerging executive practice: creating an ai driven replica of oneself, trained on one's own writing, speeches, and communication patterns, to absorb routine work that would otherwise consume an executive's time directly. reid hoffman's "reid ai" is the most developed example — trained on 22 years of his books, speeches, podcasts, and articles, it has delivered more than 75 addresses and presentations since 2024 with human preparation involved , speaks 74 languages, and by hoffman's own estimate saves him roughly half his time in the weeks it is deployed. other examples extend the pattern to internal, one on one coaching contexts rather than only public facing appearances: greif's chief human resources officer built "balabot," which has interacted with nearly 3,300 employees seeking guidance since its december launch, while quantium health ceo brian hartzer's "virtual brian" has been used by direct reports to prepare for performance reviews, in one case helping an executive manager recognize she had underrated her own contributions in a self assessment. adoption is not without friction. advocates frame the trend in ambitious terms — a december report from the institute for corporate productivity's chief strategy officer concludes digital work twins could be "the most significant productivity multiplier since the personal computer," and hoffman predicts within a decade most companies with more than 50 employees will assign trained virtual counterparts to senior roles, with rank and file employee twins following within a similar timeframe. but the article documents concrete, present day failure modes: reid ai has hallucinated answers to simple opinion questions and occasionally misjudges tone failing to look serious after a joke , while one executive's public facing digital twin visibly malfunctioned mid event, stuttering and repeating the same line in front of roughly 200 conference attendees, prompting the executive to shut it down live and acknowledge "ai isn't ready for the main stage." workforce acceptance is also not automatic: employees at one firm initially resisted having their own emails and work documents used to train a colleague's digital twin, a concern addressed through explicit opt out provisions for sensitive personal or work content. a senior intellectual property counsel quoted in the piece frames the emerging governance principle as one where digital twins with any supervisory role must "support human decision making, not replace legal review or human accountability" — reflecting the real risk that an ai double could misstate employment policy or other legally consequential information without a human catching the error. the article closes on the practice's most unresolved dimension: ownership of the accumulated knowledge inside a digital twin once the underlying employee leaves the company. one organization studied, upwork, had already confronted this directly and established a policy — departing employees may take their digital twin's likeness and personal expertise with them, while the company retains any proprietary business knowledge the twin accumulated while the employee was there. more broadly, the article raises the possibility that departing employees could eventually be compensated specifically for leaving a digital twin and its associated knowledge behind — treating what the twin has learned as a distinct, potentially severable company asset from the human who trained it. related ai work and organization redesign — that concept provides a broader account of ai redistributing organizational work and hierarchy, of which the executive digital twin pattern is one specific, high profile instance. strategy in an era of abundant expertise — that concept covers the economic logic collapsing cost of accessing expertise that helps explain why replicating a single executive's judgment at scale is now commercially attractive. open questions the source does not report any independent verification of the productivity gains claimed by digital twin users e.g. hoffman's 50% time savings estimate , which are self reported by the executives themselves rather than measured by a third party. no source addresses how digital twins interact with existing data privacy or employment law outside the single example of upwork's departure policy; the broader legal landscape for ai replicas trained on an employee's communications remains unaddressed. sources too much work to do? have your digital twin handle it — wsj, joann s. lublin, 2026 05 21; covers reid hoffman's "reid ai," greif's "balabot," quantium health's "virtual brian," and upwork's digital twin departure policy.
federated-machine-learning: summary federated learning lets several organizations train a shared ai model on their combined data without any of them handing over raw data, because the training algorithm travels to each organization's data instead of the data traveling to a central location. combined with encryption, it has allowed zurich insurance to improve a prediction model using orange's data and has let competing hospitals and banks cooperate without revealing their records. the sources classify an organization's data into four types, poor, horizontal, vertical and rich, according to how many samples and how many features per sample it holds. the type of data an organization holds shows what kind of partner would improve its own ai systems, and organizations with rich data can still gain by contributing it to train other organizations' systems while keeping full ownership. highlights federated learning, combined with specialized encryption, lets an ai model or algorithm be trained using data from multiple decentralized servers controlled by different organizations while preserving the privacy of the individuals or organizations whose data is used — in effect, sending the algorithm to the data rather than sending the data to the algorithm. zurich insurance group used a commercial federated learning platform to improve a predictive algorithm with data from telecom company orange, without orange ever releasing any data — the collaboration delivered a 30% improvement in zurich's ai predictions and a significant revenue increase, while giving orange a privacy preserving way to monetize its data. federated learning enables cooperation even between direct competitors: pathology departments at competing private hospitals train a shared diagnostic algorithm on their combined tissue image data sets, with each hospital benefiting from a higher performing algorithm than its own smaller data set could produce alone, and ownership shares of the resulting algorithm allocated based on each hospital's data contribution. an organization's data falls into one of four types based on two dimensions — sample count and feature count per sample: "poor" data few samples, few features , "horizontal" data many features per sample, but too few samples — needs more samples via horizontal learning , "vertical" data many samples, but too few features per sample — needs more features via vertical learning , and "rich" data sufficient on both dimensions . the right federated learning partner depends on an organization's own data type: organizations with vertical data many samples, thin per sample detail should seek partners in different industries who observe different things about the same population a telecom and an insurer both serve overlapping customers but record entirely different variables about them ; organizations with horizontal data rich per sample detail, too few samples should seek partners within their own industry, even direct competitors, since more samples of the same variable set is what's needed. organizations already sitting on rich data still have a reason to pursue federated learning: they can monetize that data by contributing it to train other organizations' ai systems while retaining full ownership and never releasing the underlying data itself — the mayo clinic's solutions studio program offers exactly this kind of access to global, federated, de identified data. banks use federated learning with multiparty homomorphic encryption to check whether a prospective client has been flagged by a competing bank as unreliable, without either bank disclosing its actual client list to the other — reducing the cost of "know your customer" compliance, which otherwise runs to roughly 3% of banks' operational costs globally. federated learning also has an underused internal application: within a single organization, data sharing barriers between legal entities, jurisdictions, or business units often imposed for compliance or ethics reasons can block one group from data another group already owns, and federated learning lets the organization use that data across such internal barriers while remaining compliant with the restrictions that created them in the first place. six factors determine which organizations to pursue as federated learning partners: the state of one's own data poor/horizontal/vertical/rich ; the resulting structure of what to seek cross industry for vertical data, same industry for horizontal data ; a logical starting point one algorithm, one trusted partner, before scaling ; the potential for data monetization; likely technical challenges unstructured data needing conversion to machine readable form, disparate labeling conventions across organizations requiring catalog synchronization ; and employee buy in, since resistance to collaborating with external organizations — especially competitors — is identified as the single most critical obstacle to federated learning success. concept know your data to harness federated machine learning mit smr, josé parra moyano and karl schmedders, october 2024 opens from a competitive strategy observation: deploying ai no longer guarantees an edge on its own, since what actually differentiates companies is access to diverse, extensive, high quality data that improves their ai system's performance relative to competitors — but privacy concerns routinely limit how much unique, relevant data an organization can actually put to use. privacy preserving federated learning addresses this directly: combined with specialized encryption techniques, it lets an ai model or algorithm be trained using data held on multiple decentralized servers controlled by different organizations, all while respecting the privacy of the individuals or organizations whose data is involved — the technique is best summarized as sending the algorithm to the data, rather than sending the data to the algorithm. zurich insurance group's collaboration with british telecom company orange illustrates the mechanism concretely: using a commercial federated learning platform, zurich's predictive algorithm was trained and its predictions improved using orange's data, without orange ever having to release that data to zurich — the resulting 30% improvement in zurich's ai predictions translated into a significant revenue increase for zurich, while orange gained a new, privacy preserving way to monetize its data asset. a large bank's credit unit achieved a comparable result, improving its loan default prediction accuracy by roughly 10% using data owned by one of the largest global telecommunications companies. know your data to harness federated machine learning real world applications span both cross industry and, counterintuitively, within industry collaboration — including between direct competitors. pathology departments at competing private hospitals, each struggling to compile a sufficiently robust data set alone, train a shared diagnostic algorithm on their combined tissue image data; every participating hospital ends up with a higher performing, potentially lifesaving diagnostic tool than its own in house data set could have produced, with ownership shares of the resulting collectively developed algorithm allocated based on each hospital's proportional data contribution — a genuinely new, data driven business model, since the shared algorithm can also be commercialized and rented to third party hospitals, with resulting revenue split by ownership share. the financial sector applies a related but distinct pattern using multiparty homomorphic encryption: participating banks can check whether a prospective client has been flagged by a competing bank as unreliable or otherwise problematic, without either bank disclosing its actual client list to the other, reducing the cost of "know your customer" compliance processes that otherwise account for roughly 3% of banks' global operational costs while improving the customer's experience. hospitals use the same encrypted computing pattern for dermatology diagnostics trained across multiple countries' data sets, and for simpler distributed analytics producing personalized reference intervals for healthy versus sick patients, letting doctors diagnose against a personalized threshold rather than a one size fits all population reference. know your data to harness federated machine learning the article's central practical contribution is a framework for identifying which external partner an organization should actually pursue, built on two dimensions of its own data: the number of samples clients, patients, policies — whatever the ai system aims to understand and the number of features recorded per sample. crossing these dimensions yields four data types. "poor" data has both too few samples and too few features per sample to be useful as is. "vertical" data has many samples but too few features recorded about each — a large customer base, thinly described — and requires "vertical learning" adding more features per sample to become genuinely useful; the fix here is partnering with organizations in different industries, since companies serving different purposes for overlapping populations tend to record entirely different variables about the same people the orange zurich case is the given example: the telecom records communications and mobility data, the insurer records risk aversion, consumption, and major life events, about what can be a substantially overlapping customer base . "horizontal" data has many features recorded per sample but too few samples — deep description, thin population — and requires "horizontal learning" adding more samples with the same feature set to become useful; the fix here is partnering within one's own industry, even with direct competitors, since same industry organizations tend to already record comparable features and what's genuinely missing is simply more observations. and "rich" data has sufficient volume on both dimensions already; an organization in this position doesn't need external data to improve its own ai, but federated learning still offers a monetization opportunity — contributing that rich data to train other organizations' ai systems while retaining full ownership and never releasing the underlying data itself, the model the mayo clinic uses through its solutions studio program, which offers global, federated, de identified data access. a less obvious but genuinely valuable federated learning use case operates entirely within a single organization: data sharing barriers between legal entities, jurisdictions, or business units — often erected deliberately for compliance or ethics reasons — can prevent one internal group from accessing data another group within the same company already owns, and federated learning lets the organization use that data across its own internal barriers while remaining fully compliant with whatever restriction created them in the first place. know your data to harness federated machine learning beyond identifying the right partner, the article names practical obstacles that recur regardless of which data type an organization is starting from. unstructured data faxes, pdfs, handwritten or scanned reports needs to be converted into a usable, machine readable format before it can enter a federated learning pipeline, and business leaders should estimate this structuring cost in collaboration with the technical team that will actually train the resulting ai system. disparate labeling conventions across collaborating organizations — different terms for the same underlying feature — commonly require the participating organizations' data catalogs to be synchronized before training can proceed, extending expected project timelines. but the most critical obstacle, per the article, is people rather than technology: resistance to collaborating with an external organization, particularly a direct competitor, can stall or derail federated learning exploration entirely, which is why the authors stress that individuals across all collaborating organizations need to actively engage with one another throughout implementation rather than treating federated learning as a purely technical integration project. the article distills six factors business leaders should weigh when deciding which organizations to approach: their own data's current state poor, horizontal, vertical, or rich ; the resulting partner search logic that state implies cross industry for vertical data, same industry — including competitors — for horizontal data ; starting with one specific algorithm and one trusted partner rather than attempting a sweeping multi partner rollout immediately; the potential to monetize already rich data by supplying it to others' training processes; anticipated technical challenges around data structuring and label harmonization; and genuine employee buy in, since federated learning is ultimately a transformational, cross organizational undertaking that requires widespread support and clearly assigned roles and resources to succeed, not simply a technology deployment. know your data to harness federated machine learning related enterprise data strategy and governance — the broader enterprise data strategy discipline this concept's four type data assessment framework operates within, specifically for the cross organizational collaboration use case. genai supply chain and procurement — a parallel account of ai driven cross organizational collaboration, though built around supply chain data sharing rather than model training collaboration specifically. data mining fundamentals — the general data mining vocabulary and process this concept's federated training specific techniques extend into a privacy preserving, multi organizational setting. open questions the article doesn't address what happens when collaborating organizations' data quality or labeling practices are fundamentally incompatible even after harmonization efforts — it treats the technical challenges unstructured data, disparate labels as solvable friction rather than potential dealbreakers. it's not established how an organization should value its own data contribution when negotiating an ownership share or revenue share arrangement with a federated learning partner, beyond the general principle that shares should reflect each party's contribution to the resulting model's accuracy. sources know your data to harness federated machine learning — mit smr, josé parra moyano and karl schmedders, 2024 10 16; the mechanics of privacy preserving federated learning, a four type poor/horizontal/vertical/rich data assessment framework for identifying partners, and six factors for choosing among them.

attention and even adopting the assistant's specific terminology on unrelated topics — even when the ai's input was unhelpful and the team explicitly said they didn't trust it; and a separate study found ai generated feedback, while helping individuals learn, caused population level intellectual homogenization "algorithmic monoculture" as people receiving feedback from the same centralized ai system tended to specialize in increasingly similar ways, while also disproportionately benefiting already highly skilled and motivated employees. how to use ai to build your company’s collective concept mit sloan management review's research on organizational learning argues generative ai represents a genuinely new category of organizational capability rather than merely another automation technology — a distinction the authors illustrate through two companies that treated it accordingly. blue cross blue shield of michigan, a $35 billion health insurer, built a cross functional genai/ai genai-creativity-and-human-capability: summary generative ai can strengthen idea generation when people treat it as a collaborator and not a faster search box, but its effects on human capability are mixed. research on prompting, and on how language models imitate human persistence and flexibility, shows how to obtain ideas that are both original and appropriate. product development cases show that the right level of trust and human oversight differs by stage. studies of creative work find that ai raises individual quality but narrows the diversity of ideas across a group. experiments also show that ai can close skill gaps for conceptual work, yet it stops helping where domain expertise is needed to judge and refine its output, a limit the researchers call the ai wall. managers should therefore sequence human and ai contributions deliberately, allow time for original thinking and protect the diversity that innovation depends on. highlights most people prompt ai like a search engine, asking a direct question for one best answer, which reproduces linear, predictable thinking, so a mindshift to treating ai as a creative collaborator is needed, supported by twelve exercises such as exploratory prompting, what if framing, persona role play and a journal of breakthrough prompts. train your brain to work creatively with gen ai llms emulate two pathways of human creativity, persistence through tireless volume, since originality of a pool rises with the number of ideas up to a plateau, and flexibility through the semantic breadth of their training data. when used correctly, llms can unlock more creative ideas because models predict the most likely continuation, default output gravitates to the familiar, so persona modifiers, hybrid prompting, chain of thought and higher temperature increase originality, while fine tuning, few shot examples and retrieval improve appropriateness. when used correctly, llms can unlock more creative ideas an llm can act as lead genai-supply-chain-and-procurement: summary generative ai and large language models are automating two connected supply chain functions, which are planning and analytics, and supplier contracting and negotiation. in planning, microsoft uses a language model to let planners ask plain language questions about server supply across more than 300 data centers, with the model translating each question into a change to the existing mathematical optimization model. in negotiation, companies move through three stages, from ai that flags risks and drafts terms while a human sends everything, to ai that can accept pre approved clauses, to fully autonomous negotiation on low margin routine items, as walmart does. both functions depend on the same disciplines, namely precise language so that the ai reads ambiguous terms correctly, ways to catch and recover from errors, and guardrails, and both shift human time from routine work to strategic work. highlights microsoft deployed an llm based system to manage server supply across more than 300 data centers, letting planners ask plain language questions "what is the cheapest option for shipping items from factory f to retailer r?" and get answers translated automatically into database queries, cutting analysis tasks that took a week down to minutes. llms complement rather than replace the mathematical optimization models underlying supply chain tools — a plain language what if question gets translated into a small modification of the existing mathematical model, which is then re solved and the result translated back into natural language. one automotive oem fed an llm data from thousands of supplier contracts and discovered volume threshold price reductions its procurement team had overlooked due to contract complexity, worth millions of dollars in savings. companies are adopting ai driven supplier negotiation through a deliberate three stage maturity curve: assisted ai flags risks and drafts terms, but a human sends nothing , semi autonomous ai can accept pre approved clauses or adjust prices within set limits, with humans approving critical decisions , and fully autonomous ai closes routine, low margin deals end to end within guardrails , rather than jumping straight to full automation. walmart progressed from experimenting with ai negotiation tools in specific product categories to using them for fully autonomous negotiation of replenishment terms on frequently purchased, low margin items — illustrating the full maturity arc within a single company. vodafone and deutsche telekom used semi autonomous ai systems to negotiate maintenance and operations contracts, with vodafone 300+ million customers achieving significant savings while a human expert still approved each final agreement. successful ai adoption in both planning and negotiation contexts depends on the same underlying disciplines: precise language/training so the ai interprets ambiguous terms correctly, mechanisms to catch and recover from ai errors verification, accountability frameworks , and regulatory compliance data privacy, required human oversight for high stakes decisions . in both domains, ai adoption is expected to shift the affected workforce's time from routine, repeatable tasks contract drafting, demand drift analysis, reviewing routine negotiations toward higher value strategic work — cross functional collaboration in supply chain, and complex high stakes negotiations in procurement — rather than eliminating the roles outright. concept how generative ai improves supply chain management mit smr/hbr, january 2025 documents how large language models are being used to automate supply chain planning and analytics, drawing primarily on microsoft's deployment of an llm based system to manage server supply across more than 300 global data centers, piloted from march to october 2023 and fully deployed by november 2023. the core capability is translating plain language questions from planners into database queries and, for more complex requests, into small modifications of the mathematical optimization models that actually generate supply chain recommendations — the llm complements rather than replaces these models. concrete applications include data discovery and insight generation answering "how much raw material does supplier s have today?" in seconds rather than requiring a data science team , what if analysis modeling the cost impact of a 15 percent demand increase or a factory shutdown , and interactive re planning in response to real time disruptions automatically generating an updated plan when a manufacturing facility goes down . a directly procurement relevant example is that one automotive oem fed an llm data from thousands of supplier contracts and discovered volume threshold price reductions its own procurement team had overlooked due to sheer contract complexity, worth millions of dollars. the article identifies three adoption barriers — the need for precise, trained language use since ambiguous terms like "better" can be interpreted multiple ways; verification challenges, since llm output can be wrong and must be kept "inside the rails" with fallback mechanisms; and workforce role changes, as planners and procurement staff shift from routine task execution toward strategic, cross functional work. how ai is reshaping supplier negotiations hbr, july 2025 picks up precisely the procurement contracting thread the supply chain article touches only briefly, and examines it as a distinct discipline in its own right. drawing on more than six years of research into human ai collaboration and autonomous negotiation across retailing, pharmaceuticals, consumer packaged goods, logistics, and it, the article documents a deliberate three stage adoption path companies follow rather than jumping directly from manual negotiation to full automation. in the assisted stage, ai tools act as copilots — flagging risks, drafting contracts, simulating tariff scenarios — without directly contacting suppliers; luminance's legal grade ai system, used by a multinational utilities company, exemplifies this. in the semi autonomous stage, systems can accept pre approved clauses or adjust prices within set limits while critical decisions remain under human control — maersk's negotiation ai improved its price results over successive rounds with a given supplier while a human still approved the final agreement, and vodafone and deutsche telekom used semi autonomous systems to negotiate maintenance and operations contracts, with vodafone over 300 million customers achieving significant savings this way. in the fully autonomous stage, systems close deals end to end within guardrails — walmart, having progressed through the earlier stages in specific product categories, now uses ai to negotiate replenishment terms for frequently purchased, low margin items without human approval. the article specifies five practices for making this transition responsibly: ensuring high data quality, protecting data privacy, establishing clear accountability frameworks since legal responsibility for an ai's mistake falls on the company, not the software , staying compliant with regulations requiring human oversight for sensitive decisions gdpr, the eu ai act , and building trust through explainability rather than deploying black box systems for high stakes decisions. read together, the two sources describe complementary halves of ai's advance into supply chain and procurement functions: one covers the planning and analytics side understanding and optimizing the supply chain itself , the other covers the contracting and negotiation side structuring and managing the relationships and agreements that supply chain depends on — scale and fast analysis of open ended answers. a blind validation study by ey found that synthetic personas reproduced its real brand survey results closely, and other work shows that digital twins variation, and that it becomes cheap to produce credible looking but low quality research. researchers therefore still need human oversight, and insights reach decisions only where culture, data standards and ownership of the work are settled. highlights traditional marketing research costs tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars and takes weeks to months; generative ai compresses this by handling the labor intensive middle stages data collection, analysis while humans remain in charge of problem definition, research design, and final judgment. consumer "digital twins" — synthetic, llm generated personas built from demographic, psychographic, and behavioral data — let researchers simulate concept tests, pricing moves, and campaign reactions before committing budget to a live study; a university of wisconsin study found llm generated qualitative responses matched or exceeded human responses in depth and insightfulness, and a b2b cybersecurity study using the startup evidenza's synthetic decision makers found 0.75 0.88 correlations against a real human survey. in a rigorous double blind validation study, ey withheld its actual annual brand survey results from evidenza, which geopolitical-fragmentation-and-global-ex: summary the global digital economy is splitting into diverging national and regional paths, shaped as much by us china rivalry, regulation and access to ai computing capacity as by markets and technology. the 2026 digital evolution index covers 125 countries. it finds that the united states and china together account for just over half of digital gdp and pursue structurally different ai strategies, that global digital momentum has slowed since the pandemic and that digital regulation is diverging by region. chinese companies facing trade tensions and tighter foreign investment scrutiny are responding by targeting microregions, meaning provinces, cities and economic zones, instead of entire countries. their approach, which often favors singapore for its talent, trade infrastructure and neutrality, offers a company level playbook for expanding globally despite fragmentation. highlights the 2026 digital evolution index sorts 125 countries into four quadrants by digital development level and momentum: "stand outs" high development, fast momentum — us, china, singapore, south korea , "stall outs" high development, slowing momentum — finland, germany, japan, uk , "break outs" lower development, fast momentum — india, vietnam, brazil , and "watch outs" low development, weak momentum — pakistan, nigeria, ethiopia . the us and china alone account for just over half of the aggregate digital gdp of all 125 countries studied, with the two pursuing structurally different ai strategies: the us emphasizes private sector investment and an estimated 39.7 million petaflops of ai compute about half the world's total , while china emphasizes government industry coordination, algorithmic efficiency under compute constraints, and open source ai leadership — a gap stanford hai reports has "effectively closed" on model performance despite the compute disparity. global digital momentum has slowed sharply since the pandemic ended, from 4.3% annual growth pre pandemic to 2.4% post pandemic, with lower income countries experiencing the greatest deceleration — even as ai investment surges, reinforcing a "winner takes most" dynamic where countries already strong in digital infrastructure pull further ahead. digital regulation is diverging by cluster rather than converging: the us minimizes federal ai regulatory hurdles, china follows a "move fast but obey the rules" model set centrally, the eu concentrated among "stall out" countries is imposing extensive ai and data protection rules, and break out economies are assembling hybrid frameworks borrowing from all three — a fragmentation serious enough that classifying markets by regulatory logic permissive, precautionary, state directed, hybrid may become as strategically important as classifying them by growth potential. facing a slow domestic recovery, chinese companies have adopted "chu hai" going overseas as a rallying strategy, but confront a threefold challenge: rising us china trade tensions and export controls, tightening foreign investment regulatory scrutiny in north america and europe, and infrastructure/cultural unfamiliarity in emerging markets they might otherwise target. rather than targeting entire countries, chinese executives increasingly target "microregions" — subnational units like provinces, cities, or economic zones mckinsey identified more than 40,000 globally in 2019, each averaging $3 billion in gdp and 180,000 residents — a mental model that comes naturally given china's own historically decentralized, place based development pattern, in which 1.1 billion of the roughly 2 billion people worldwide who reached high living standards in the past 20 years were chinese. three place based strategies recur across chinese companies' international expansion: finding new routes to existing markets by relocating supply chain nodes or entire headquarters to strategically advantageous microregions shein relocating its headquarters to singapore for its talent access, trade infrastructure, and geopolitical neutrality ; building hubs in specific cities to reach entire emerging market regions chinese firms clustering in dubai as a middle east/north africa gateway, or addis ababa/accra/nairobi for africa ; and going virtual through digital talent hubs that connect distributed teams without requiring heavy in country investment shenzhen's electronics brands, hangzhou's alibaba trained e commerce talent pool . singapore recurs as the single most attractive microregion for chinese companies preserving western market access, for three specific reasons: access to talent, trade infrastructure, and geopolitical neutrality — the same three attributes any company assessing a fragmentation resilient hub location should weigh regardless of its country of origin. concept what a fragmenting digital economy means for global competition hbr, bhaskar chakravorti et al., june 2026 , reporting on the 2026 digital evolution index a collaboration between tufts university's digital planet research center and via science, tracking 185 indicators across 125 countries , argues that 25 years of digitalization connecting countries, supply chains, and markets through common standards and platforms is giving way to a fragmenting "erosion of a singular global digital economy." the index sorts countries into four quadrants by digital evolution state current development level and momentum compound annual growth rate from 2008 2025 : "stand outs" combine high development with fast momentum the us, china, singapore, south korea ; "stall outs" have high development but slowing momentum finland, denmark, germany, japan, the uk ; "break outs" have lower development but fast momentum india, vietnam, brazil, thailand ; and "watch outs" have both low development and weak momentum pakistan, nigeria, venezuela, ethiopia . the us and china's combined digital gdp alone represents just over half of the aggregate digital gdp across all 125 countries studied, and their ai rivalry dominates the pace of digital investment globally: the us leans on private sector investment, foundation model development, and an estimated computational lead of 39.7 million petaflops roughly half the world's total ai compute driven by advanced semiconductor design, while china leans on coordinated government industry investment, algorithmic efficiency engineered around compute constraints, vast domestic data pools, rapid large scale data center construction, and open source ai leadership — a strategic divergence that, according to stanford hai, has nonetheless resulted in the us china ai model performance gap "effectively closing" despite china's estimated compute disadvantage roughly 400,000 petaflops . what a fragmenting digital economy means for global competition beyond the two superpowers, "stand out" status also includes smaller open economies succeeding through non scale strategies: singapore executing on private sector strength and government directed digital transformation while explicitly leveraging ties to both the us and chinese ecosystems; the uae pursuing state led investment toward an autonomous governance ai hub, though regional war has introduced real economic uncertainty; estonia pioneering e government infrastructure its x road secure data exchange layer and e residency program ; and ireland positioning itself as a global tech export and innovation commercialization hub via eu membership and cultural proximity to the us. "stall out" countries, concentrated in europe, have built exceptional digital infrastructure and strong institutions but see innovation speed dampened by their own regulatory investment data privacy, security, transparency policies — a "neighborhood effect" that nonetheless lowered the cost of cross border scaling enough to help smaller central/eastern european and baltic economies become surging stand out and break out performers in their own right. "break out" economies combine lower digital evolution scores with the fastest momentum of any cluster, frequently leapfrogging pc based development entirely via mobile first infrastructure paired with digital public payment systems india's upi hit 22.64 billion transactions in march 2026 alone; global mobile money transactions surpassed $2 trillion in 2025, doubling in four years, with most growth in africa . "watch out" economies lag on both development and momentum, concentrated in sub saharan africa and fragile middle eastern and central/south asian states, but paradoxically report the highest trust in ai of any cluster per un survey data — a trust based adoption mindset that could jumpstart future momentum but currently operates with the fewest institutional guardrails. several cross cutting patterns compound the fragmentation: ai is reinforcing a "winner takes most" dynamic as already advanced digital economies pull further ahead; global digital momentum has slowed markedly since the pandemic from 4.3% annual growth pre pandemic to 2.4% post pandemic, with lower income countries decelerating fastest ; and digital regulation is diverging by cluster rather than converging toward a single global standard — the us minimizing federal ai rules, china's centrally set "move fast but obey the rules" approach, extensive eu ai and data protection regulation concentrated among stall out countries, and break out economies assembling hybrid frameworks that borrow from all three, with the 2026 ai impact summit's new delhi declaration signaling an emerging "global south bloc" aspiring to co author its own global ai governance norms. the article's practical implication for business leaders is that classifying markets by regulatory logic — permissive, precautionary, state directed, or hybrid — may soon matter as much as classifying them by growth potential, and that ai strategies premised on a single harmonized global technology stack will increasingly misread the actual operating environment. what a fragmenting digital economy means for global competition how chinese companies expand globally despite headwinds mit smr, shameen prashantham and lola woetzel, february 2025 supplies a concrete company level playbook for exactly the kind of fragmented environment the digital evolution index describes, drawn from 40 interviews with chinese business leaders conducted from early 2023 through early 2024. facing a slow post pandemic recovery in china's domestic consumer market, chinese companies have adopted "chu hai" "going overseas" as a rallying strategy, but confront a threefold set of headwinds that mirror this concept's macro fragmentation thesis directly: rising us china trade tensions and export controls the october 2022 us restriction on ai chip exports to china hit not only chinese semiconductor firms but also nvidia's and broadcom's stock prices ; tightening foreign investment regulatory scrutiny in north america and western europe chinese owned seed producer syngenta was ordered to divest 160 acres of arkansas farmland under a 2023 foreign land ownership law ; and genuine infrastructure deficits, bureaucratic inefficiency, and cultural unfamiliarity in the emerging markets that otherwise offer fewer trade barriers. the authors' central finding is that chinese executives are navigating these headwinds by reconceiving their unit of international strategy: rather than targeting entire countries, they target "microregions" — subnational units such as provinces, cities, or defined economic zones a 2019 mckinsey study identified more than 40,000 globally, each averaging 3,000 square kilometers, $3 billion in gdp, and 180,000 residents . this mental model comes naturally to chinese business leaders given china's own historically decentralized, place based development pattern predating even the 1980s economic reforms: of the roughly 2 billion people worldwide who achieved high living standards over the past 20 years, 1.1 billion did so within chinese microregions specifically. how chinese companies expand globally despite headwinds three place based strategies recur across the companies studied. finding new routes to existing markets means relocating supply chain nodes or entire company headquarters to strategically advantageous microregions rather than tactically dodging trade barriers through loopholes — power drill maker chervon established a wholly owned vietnamese manufacturing facility to diversify its supply chain while still serving western customers, while fast fashion retailer shein relocated its entire headquarters to singapore specifically to preserve its ability to forge western partnerships that have become increasingly difficult from within mainland china. building hubs to reach emerging markets clusters chinese investment in specific gateway cities — singapore again for southeast asia shanghai based leyan used a singapore headquarters to market its ai chatbot to southeast asian e commerce platforms like shopee and lazada , dubai for the middle east and north africa, and addis ababa, accra, and nairobi as african beachheads, despite those cities lagging singapore on trade infrastructure and bureaucratic efficiency and therefore requiring more reliance on local partners to compensate. going virtual through digital talent hubs uses distributed digital talent to connect resources and opportunities without the heavier commitment of physical market entry — shenzhen has produced internationally recognized consumer electronics brands anker innovations, govee that sell through western retail channels under their own brand identity rather than as generic marketplace listings, while hangzhou, home to alibaba's global digital talent training program, has generated a local entrepreneurial talent pool capable of building direct to consumer brands for western markets — in at least one case studied, a chinese founded company launched successfully in the us within a couple of years without disclosing its chinese origin anywhere on its website, on the reasoning per one founder that "because the product works so well, where we come from is irrelevant." singapore recurs across all three strategies as the single most valuable microregion specifically because it combines talent access, trade infrastructure, and geopolitical neutrality — the same three attributes the authors argue any company, regardless of national origin, should weigh when selecting a hub location resilient to the kind of geopolitical fragmentation this concept's other source documents at the macro level. the authors close by noting the strategy generalizes beyond chinese companies specifically: as protectionist policies spread, any company facing restricted access to a given national market may find a microregion based, place first approach — rather than a country first one — the more durable response. how chinese companies expand globally despite headwinds related deepseek and chinas ai ecosystem — that concept provides a deeper account of china's ai specific competitive strategy, complementary to this concept's broader digital economy and internationalization framing. telecom regulatory economics — sector specific regulatory divergence that instantiates this concept's broader thesis about diverging national digital regulatory logics. sovereign ai ecosystems — national ai self sufficiency strategies that are a direct driver of the digital economy fragmentation this concept documents at the country level. open questions neither source explains how a western non chinese company should adapt the microregion strategy given it may lack the "returnee" talent pool chinese professionals who lived and worked abroad before returning home the second source identifies as helping chinese companies execute multicultural, multilocational teams. the digital evolution index source doesn't address how the four quadrant country classification should be revisited if a "break out" or "watch out" country experiences a geopolitical shock as it notes happened to iran, sliding from break out toward watch out — it's unclear how frequently the underlying index itself is expected to be recalculated as conditions change quickly. sources what a fragmenting digital economy means for global competition — hbr, bhaskar chakravorti,
