high-performing-team-practices: summary research on roughly 6,000 people in teams rated as high performing or average found that the strongest predictor of team success is a culture of experimentation, not a concentration of talent. teams that keep improving share five habits that reinforce one another, namely trying new approaches routinely, valuing curiosity over ego, surfacing problems early, staying close to the actual work and investing deliberately in people's growth. surfacing problems early separates high performers most clearly from average teams, since problems caught early are cheap to fix and those caught late compound. frequent, specific feedback, as in adobe's overhaul of its performance reviews and spotify's confidence platform, supports the growth habit. highlights psychologist and workplace researcher ron friedman studied roughly 6,000 people across teams identified by their organizations as either high performing or average performing, isolating the habits that most reliably distinguished the two groups — talent concentration was not the strongest predictor; a culture of experimentation was. high performing teams treat trying new approaches as routine rather than exceptional, running small low stakes experiments constantly instead of waiting for a formal initiative or crisis to justify change; the oklahoma city thunder's analytics driven, defense first roster construction approach built years before it became a "smallball" adjacent trend across the nba illustrates a team culture willing to test unconventional approaches ahead of consensus. curiosity and humility outperform defensiveness and ego on high performing teams: members treat being wrong as useful information rather than a threat to status, which measurably increases how often problems and disagreements are voiced rather than suppressed. the habit of surfacing problems early separates high performers most sharply from average teams, since problems caught early are cheap to fix and problems caught late compound; teams with psychological safety to raise a concern before it becomes a crisis systematically outperform teams where concerns wait for a formal review. staying close to the actual work — leaders and senior members maintaining direct, hands on contact with front line execution rather than managing purely through reports and dashboards — correlates with faster detection of both problems and opportunities that would otherwise surface only after significant lag. growth oriented feedback, delivered frequently and specifically rather than saved for formal review cycles, is illustrated by adobe's overhaul of its performance review process and by spotify's "confidence" platform, both aimed at replacing infrequent, high stakes evaluation with continuous, lower stakes feedback loops. investing in people's growth beyond their current role — treating skill development as a team level investment rather than an individual's private responsibility — reinforces all four other habits, since teams confident their members are growing take more experimental risks, surface more problems, and sustain curiosity over ego for longer. concept how to build a superteam that keeps getting better draws on psychologist and workplace researcher ron friedman's study of roughly 6,000 people distributed across teams that their own organizations had independently classified as either high performing or average performing. rather than starting from a theory of what should distinguish elite teams, friedman's approach worked backward from the classification, isolating which concrete, observable habits most reliably separated the two groups. the headline finding runs against a common assumption in team building: talent concentration — stacking a team with the most individually skilled people available — was not the strongest predictor of sustained high performance. a culture of experimentation was. high performing teams treat running small, low stakes trials of new approaches as a routine, ongoing habit rather than an exceptional response to a mandate or crisis, which lets them discover better methods continuously instead of only when forced to. how to build a superteam that keeps getting better the article illustrates this experimental culture with the oklahoma city thunder's roster construction philosophy, built on data driven, defense first evaluation years before comparable approaches became mainstream across the nba — a team willing to act on unconventional internal analysis ahead of external consensus validating the approach. beyond the willingness to experiment, high performing teams share a related but distinct trait: curiosity and humility take priority over ego and self protection. members of these teams treat being shown wrong as useful information about the world rather than a threat to their status, and this orientation has a direct downstream effect — it measurably increases how often problems, disagreements, and uncomfortable observations actually get voiced in the room rather than quietly suppressed to avoid conflict or embarrassment. this connects directly to the habit the article identifies as most sharply distinguishing high performers from average teams: surfacing problems early. problems caught while still small and cheap to fix stay small; problems caught late, after they've compounded, become expensive and sometimes irreversible. teams with enough psychological safety that a member will raise a concern before it becomes an emergency systematically outperform teams where concerns only surface once they can no longer be avoided, typically in a formal review that arrives too late to prevent the damage. how to build a superteam that keeps getting better a further habit — staying close to the actual work — describes leaders and senior team members who maintain direct, hands on contact with front line execution rather than managing exclusively through secondhand reports, dashboards, and summaries. this proximity correlates with faster detection of both emerging problems and emerging opportunities that would otherwise surface only after a meaningful reporting lag, since problems and opportunities are often visible in the texture of the work itself well before they show up in aggregated metrics. the article's fifth habit, growth oriented feedback, calls for feedback that is frequent and specific rather than concentrated into infrequent, high stakes formal review cycles; it points to adobe's well documented overhaul of its performance review process and to spotify's "confidence" feedback platform as two concrete examples of organizations deliberately re engineering feedback delivery around continuous, lower stakes loops instead of periodic, high stakes evaluation events. the final habit, investing in people's growth beyond their current role, functions as reinforcement for the other four: when team members trust that the organization is investing in their long term development rather than treating them as fixed capacity for the current task, they take more experimental risks, surface more problems rather than hiding them to protect their standing, and sustain curiosity over defensive ego for longer, since their sense of security doesn't depend on always being right in the moment. how to build a superteam that keeps getting better related organizational bottleneck management — a complementary framework for diagnosing and clearing what actually limits team and organizational throughput, relevant to why some teams sustain the experimentation habit this concept describes and others don't. organizational readiness for ai collaboration — that concept discusses psychological safety as a precondition for ai adoption experimentation, the same underlying mechanism this concept identifies behind the curiosity over ego and early problem surfacing habits. open questions the article doesn't specify how friedman's research controlled for confounding factors like resourcing, leadership tenure, or industry — it's unclear whether the five habits are causal drivers of high performance or correlates that themselves depend on some prior organizational advantage. the oklahoma city thunder example illustrates the experimentation habit but isn't drawn from friedman's underlying research sample; the article doesn't clarify whether it's an independently sourced case study or an author added illustration. sources how to build a superteam that keeps getting better — a synthesis of ron friedman's roughly 6,000 person research comparing high and average performing teams, covering five reinforcing habits experimentation, curiosity over ego, early problem surfacing, staying close to the work, growth oriented feedback and investment illustrated via the oklahoma city thunder, spotify's "confidence" platform, and adobe's feedback process overhaul.
how-people-actually-use-genai: summary research that mined online discussions over three years shows that the most common uses of generative ai shifted from technical assistance in 2024 to emotional and self actualization needs in 2025, with therapy and companionship becoming the top use and organizing one's life and finding purpose entering the top ranks. usage data from openai and anthropic broadly corroborate this, and all three sources show that usage is highly concentrated in a few categories, although they disagree on how much ai is used for coding. a separate meta analysis of 106 experiments by mit researchers found that human ai combinations on average beat humans working alone but did not beat the better of human only or ai only performance. combinations succeed mainly when each party is given the subtasks it does better, and content creation is one area where they produced a real gain. highlights the 2024 study mined tens of thousands of reddit and quora posts to identify 100 real world gen ai use cases across six themes — content creation & editing 23% , technical assistance & troubleshooting 21% , personal & professional support 17% , learning & education 16% , creativity & recreation 13% , and research/analysis/decision making 10% — finding idea generation, not content output, was the single most common use case. how people are really using genai by 2025, using the identical methodology scaled to more data, the top use case flipped entirely: therapy/companionship became 1, with two more self actualization entries "organizing my life" and "finding purpose" newly in the top 5 — personal & professional support grew to 31% of all use cases from 17% the year before , stealing share mainly from technical assistance & troubleshooting, which fell from 21% to 15%. how people are really using genai in 2025 reddit users reported ai delivered therapy filling genuine mental healthcare access gaps one south african user cited a ratio of one psychologist per 100,000 people locally and cited three consistent advantages: 24/7 availability, low or no cost, and freedom from human judgment — while ey was independently deploying sector specific agentic systems including 150 tax specific ai agents to nearly 400,000 staff around the same period. how people are really using genai in 2025 the 2025 meta research piece triangulated three independent studies of the same underlying question openai's usage log report, anthropic's economic index, and the author's own social listening research , each with distinct strengths and weaknesses — usage logs capture real behavior but only on one platform and without context; surveys allow any detail but suffer self selection bias; social listening captures the truth people feel strongly enough to write publicly, with lower volume and demographic blindness. making sense of research on how people use ai all three 2025 era studies agreed on a power law concentration of usage: openai found 78% of messages fall into just its top three categories; anthropic found 20% of task categories account for 87% of usage; the author's own top 20 use case buckets of 100+ accounted for more than half of total use — a signal the author reads as meaning leaders should focus ai investment on a small handful of high impact use cases rather than trying to cover everything. making sense of research on how people use ai the three studies also genuinely disagreed in informative ways: anthropic reported 36% of its sample using gen ai for coding versus just 8% in the author's own research and 4.2% in openai's — a gap the author attributes partly to anthropic's broader category definition including math and partly to anthropic's early reputation specifically as a coding assistant, while still flagging the discrepancy as warranting further investigation rather than dismissal. making sense of research on how people use ai mit center for collective intelligence researchers, reviewing 370 effect sizes across 106 experiments published between january 2020 and july 2023, found human ai combinations on average outperformed humans working alone but did not outperform ai working alone — and scored below the single best performing human only or ai only system in the comparison, a finding the study's lead author called "our most surprising finding." when humans and ai work best together — and when each is better alone the mit researchers distinguish "human ai augmentation" the combination beats humans alone from the much rarer "human ai synergy" the combination beats both humans alone and ai alone — synergy specifically emerged in tasks where humans already outperformed ai on their own, such as classifying bird images by species humans 81% accurate, ai 73% accurate, combination 90% accurate , because in those cases humans were also good at correctly judging when to trust their own judgment versus the ai's. when humans and ai work best together — and when each is better alone generative ai specifically showed a positive synergy effect where most human ai research dominated by decision making tasks showed a negative one: content creation tasks — still only 10% of the studies reviewed — produced significantly better combined results than decision making tasks did, which the researchers attribute to generative ai's uniquely iterative, feedback adapting collaboration loop draft, edit, rework, repeat compared to earlier single shot ai systems. when humans and ai work best together — and when each is better alone concept marc zao sanders' original 2024 hbr study set out to answer a question he found conspicuously under addressed a year into the chatgpt era: despite hundreds of millions of weekly users and multi trillion dollar economic projections, were people actually finding gen ai useful in concrete, specific ways, or was the discourse mostly generic feature list phrases "text summarization," "code review" that did little to persuade the skeptical majority — a group that, even among the world's billion knowledge workers, represented 90% of people who still weren't using chatgpt regularly at the time. to find out, zao sanders' team at filtered technologies mined tens of thousands of posts from reddit and quora specifically for concrete, first person accounts of gen ai delivering real value, filtering out the substantial noise inanity, repetition, abuse endemic to anonymous online forums to surface authentic use cases, eventually cataloging more than 100 distinct categories ranked by frequency and expert assessment. these 100 categories organized into six broader themes: content creation & editing 23% , technical assistance & troubleshooting 21% , personal & professional support 17% , learning & education 16% , creativity & recreation 13% , and research, analysis & decision making 10% — a spread the study reads as evidence of gen ai's genuinely broad utility across both work and leisure, creative and technical domains. notably, the single most common use case wasn't a content generation task at all but idea generation — brainstorming — a finding the study treats as significant precisely because it positions gen ai as augmenting an existing human process a person still has to select, refine, and act on the ideas rather than fully automating a task end to end, a pattern the study found held true for the vast majority of the 100 identified use cases, with a human somewhere in the loop to check, approve, or apply the ai's output in nearly every case. the study also identified a striking access democratization pattern: 13 of the 100 use cases concerned law, coding, or medicine — domains where expert human services are traditionally expensive, hard to access on demand, and often unavailable to many people at all — with users increasingly treating gen ai as filling that gap directly, drafting legal documents, reviewing code, or seeking preliminary medical guidance without engaging a paid professional, while the study is careful to note the models don't always grasp the nuanced, context specific, or ethical considerations a genuine expert would, meaning oversimplified or outright incorrect outputs remained a real risk in these higher stakes categories. how people are really using genai exactly one year later, zao sanders and hbr's editors repeated the identical social listening methodology at greater scale, scouring more data and adding article sourced examples alongside the original reddit/quora forums, and found the resulting 2025 top 100 list had shifted dramatically: 38 of the 100 entries were entirely new compared to 2024, and — most strikingly — the single most common use case flipped from a technical, work oriented category to an explicitly emotional one. therapy/companionship became the new 1 use case, joined in the top five by two other newly prominent, self actualization oriented categories: "organizing my life" helping people become more aware of and act on their own intentions, habits, and goals and "finding purpose" determining personal values, working through roadblocks, and taking concrete self development steps . at the theme level, personal & professional support grew from 17% of use cases in 2024 to 31% in 2025 — becoming by far the largest single theme — pulling share mainly from technical assistance & troubleshooting, which fell from 21% to just 15% over the same period. reddit users describing ai delivered therapy consistently cited three converging advantages: round the clock availability, low or no cost, and freedom from the fear of human judgment — with one south african user specifically framing this as filling a genuine structural access gap, noting their country has roughly one psychologist per 100,000 people and one psychiatrist per 300,000, making an always available llm a meaningful, if imperfect, substitute where professional mental healthcare is simply scarce; the study notes recent research finding ai delivered therapeutic responses can already be indistinguishable from human written ones in blind comparisons, even as broader debate about computerized therapy's full potential and risks continues the phenomenon has also been separately observed emerging in china . this shift toward emotionally weighted use cases wasn't confined to individuals experimenting privately — ey was independently training employees across its roughly 400,000 person workforce to work alongside sector specific agentic systems, including 150 ai agents deployed specifically for tax related tasks, illustrating that the same underlying capability shift was simultaneously reshaping formal enterprise deployment. the study closes on a genuinely contested note about gen ai's effect on human cognition itself: some reddit users candidly described having "grown too dependent" on the tools, worried about atrophying their own capacity for complex thought, while others framed active, deliberate use of ai as essential to avoiding career stagnation — a tension the research surfaces without resolving, since both experiences appeared to be authentic in the underlying forum data. how people are really using genai in 2025 a third installment in the same research program, published roughly seven months later in late 2025, shifts from single study reporting to explicit methodological synthesis, motivated by a practical concern for business leaders: companies are investing billions in ai tools while struggling to demonstrate meaningful returns, and understanding how people actually use ai — as distinct from how vendors claim they use it — is a genuine input into avoiding costly missteps and identifying real opportunities. the piece triangulates three major 2025 studies of human ai usage behavior, each built on a fundamentally different method with its own tradeoffs: usage logs what users actually do, as captured directly by the llm provider itself — openai's and anthropic's own reports rely on this method offer real behavioral data at large volume but are limited to a single platform, exclude logged out or opted out users, and lack rich context due to privacy constraints openai states explicitly that "no member of the research team ever saw the content of user messages" ; surveys what users say, when asked allow researchers to probe any specific detail including demographics, but carry real self selection bias and typically yield lower data volume; and social listening what users say, unasked — zao sanders' own method captures unusually candid truth, since forum anonymity creates the psychological safety for people to discuss therapeutic, intimate, or controversial use cases they wouldn't disclose to a survey or reveal in privacy sanitized corporate logs, at the cost of lower volume, source bias, and no demographic data at all. the piece is explicit that none of these three methods alone captures the full picture, and that all research — including studies published by ai companies themselves — should be read with awareness of the publisher's own vested interest, since usage reports in particular tend to emphasize growth and impressive examples while downplaying failure modes or limitations; the strongest signal, in the author's framing, comes specifically from convergence across genuinely independent methods. where the three 2025 studies agreed, the agreement was substantial and consistent: chatgpt had reached roughly 800 million weekly active users sending about 20 billion messages weekly; anthropic found 40% of employees now report using ai at work, double the share from two years earlier; and all three studies independently found usage highly concentrated in a power law distribution — openai found 78% of all messages fall into just its top three categories practical guidance, writing, and information seeking , anthropic found 20% of task categories account for 87% of usage, and zao sanders' own top 20 use case buckets out of 100+ identified accounted for more than half of total observed use — a convergent finding the piece reads as a clear signal that organizations should concentrate ai investment on a small number of genuinely high impact use cases rather than attempting comprehensive coverage from the outset. writing similarly dominated across all three studies openai found it accounts for about 40% of work related messages; at least 20 of zao sanders' top 100 use cases are squarely writing related , and education/learning use grew consistently across the same period anthropic's education related usage grew from 9.3% to 12.4%; roughly 10% of all chatgpt messages are tutoring or teaching requests; 20% of zao sanders' catalogued use cases fall in the learning/education bucket — as did automation oriented, "doing rather than asking" usage anthropic found directive, automation style conversations rose from 27% to 39% of usage within eight months, reaching 77% of enterprise api transcripts specifically; openai found 56% of work tasks are "doing" rather than "expressing or asking" . where the three studies genuinely diverged, the piece treats the divergence itself as informative rather than as noise to be smoothed over: anthropic reported 36% of its sample using gen ai for coding, versus just 8% in zao sanders' own research and 4.2% in openai's data — a gap the piece attributes partly to anthropic's broader category definition which folds in math and partly to anthropic's distinct early reputation specifically as a coding focused model provider, while explicitly flagging that "there's some further explanatory work to do" rather than treating the discrepancy as fully resolved. a second, smaller apparent disagreement — openai finding only 1.9% of messages fall into "relationships and personal reflection" versus zao sanders' own finding that therapy/companionship was the 1 single use case in his 2025 report — turns out to be less dramatic than it first appears once the underlying percentages are compared directly: therapy/companionship, despite ranking 1 among 100 plus categories in zao sanders' data, still only accounted for roughly 4% of his total observed use, meaning the "disagreement" largely reflects differing methodology and categorization rather than a genuine substantive conflict about how much therapeutic ai use is actually occurring. the piece closes with seven concrete practices for business leaders reading ai research critically: deliberately following ai optimists, skeptics, and neutrals to avoid a filter bubble view of the technology; mapping any given study's findings against one's own direct organizational experience rather than accepting them at face value; using ai itself to summarize and synthesize ai research a genuinely meta but practical technique ; periodically reading one full scientific paper closely rather than only registering headline level takeaways, since headlines are optimized to surprise rather than to convey essential truth; tracking an organization's own internal usage metrics rather than relying purely on external studies, since external research can suggest what and how to measure but a specific organization's actual context is what ultimately matters for decision making; treating cross study disagreement like the coding usage discrepancy documented here as a signal worth investigating rather than dismissing, since it may reveal either an unresolved measurement problem or a genuine untapped business opportunity; and, finally, simply experimenting with social listening as a research method directly, since — unlike usage log access — it remains available to essentially anyone willing to do the reading. making sense of research on how people use ai running alongside this three part usage pattern research program, a distinct and more rigorously experimental line of research from mit's center for collective intelligence addresses a related but methodologically separate question: not what people are using gen ai for, but whether combining human and ai effort actually improves task performance compared to either working alone — and its central finding runs directly counter to a common industry assumption. reviewing 370 unique effect sizes drawn from 106 separate experiments published between january 2020 and july 2023, comparing human only, ai only, and combined human ai performance directly, the mit researchers found that human ai combinations on average did outperform the baseline of humans working entirely alone — but did not, on average, outperform ai working entirely alone, and scored below whichever single approach human only or ai only happened to be the strongest performer in a given study; the study's lead author called this "our most surprising finding," directly contradicting an assumption that many people would hold going in. the mechanism the researchers propose is a calibration problem: in tasks where ai substantially outperforms humans their example is detecting fake hotel reviews — ai alone achieved 73% accuracy, versus 69% for the human ai combination and just 55% for humans alone , the humans involved tend to also be poor judges of exactly when to trust the ai's output versus overriding it with their own weaker judgment, which drags the combined performance below what the ai alone would have achieved unassisted. the inverse pattern held in tasks where humans already outperformed ai on their own — classifying bird images by species being the researchers' example, where humans alone scored 81% accuracy, ai alone scored 73%, but the human ai combination reached 90%, exceeding both individual baselines — because in these cases, the humans involved were also comparatively skilled at correctly judging when their own judgment should override the ai's suggestion, rather than deferring to it indiscriminately. this distinction leads the researchers to separate two genuinely different forms of human ai collaboration: "human ai augmentation," where the combined system merely beats humans working alone a comparatively low and, per this research, commonly achieved bar , and the much rarer "human ai synergy," where the combination beats both humans alone and ai alone simultaneously — the outcome most organizations implicitly assume they're getting when they deploy ai collaboratively, but one this research suggests is achieved far less consistently than commonly believed. achieving genuine synergy, per the researchers, depends on correctly diagnosing in advance which of the three configurations human alone, ai alone, or combined will actually perform best for a specific task — a diagnosis many organizations get wrong because they tend to systematically overestimate the effectiveness of whatever collaborative system they've already built, a bias the researchers suggest can be corrected through randomized, a/b style experiments comparing outcomes across all three configurations directly — and then, critically, redesigning the entire underlying work process around that diagnosis rather than simply reassigning individual subtasks between human and ai within an unchanged process; the researchers' guiding heuristic is that humans tend to excel specifically at subtasks requiring contextual understanding and emotional intelligence, while ai systems excel at subtasks that are repetitive, high volume, or heavily data driven, and that after an initial redesign, organizations should adopt a continuous improvement loop — start with a basic workflow, monitor its actual performance, and refine it iteratively based on outcomes and user feedback, rather than treating the initial design as final. generative ai specifically stood out within the broader dataset as a genuinely promising exception to the discouraging headline finding: across the reviewed studies, human ai combinations performed worse than best alone baselines specifically on decision making tasks which made up the bulk of the research reviewed and tended to show negative combined effects , but performed measurably better on content creation tasks — a category still comparatively underexplored, representing only about 10% of the papers reviewed, but showing a significantly more positive average effect size for human ai synergy than decision making tasks did. the researchers attribute this specifically to generative ai's fundamentally more iterative and interactive collaboration model compared to earlier, single shot ai systems designed to complete one discrete task and stop: humans can now engage gen ai in an ongoing cycle of drafting, editing, and reworking text, images, music, or video, with the ai adapting to human feedback in real time — a dynamic, back and forth refinement loop that echoes, from a controlled experiment angle, exactly the kind of "human somewhere in the loop" pattern the zao sanders usage research separately observed emerging organically across the vast majority of real world use cases people described in their own words. the researchers are careful to frame their headline finding as a call for more sophistication rather than a reason to retreat from human ai collaboration altogether: the lesson isn't that combining humans and ai doesn't work, but that organizations need to become considerably more deliberate and evidence based about specifically when and how to combine them, rather than assuming collaboration is automatically beneficial by default. when humans and ai work best together — and when each is better alone related gen ai organizational learning and knowledge — the "verification evaluation learning capture" flywheel covered there is a direct organizational answer to the calibration problem this concept's mit research identifies knowing when to trust ai output versus override it . gen ai value creation frameworks — the risk slope and value creation pyramid frameworks covered there for staging enterprise gen ai adoption are complementary to this concept's finding that usage itself concentrates heavily in a small number of high impact categories. genai creativity and human capability — the "ai wall" and creativity tax findings covered there connect directly to this concept's own unresolved tension over whether gen ai use strengthens or erodes users' independent thinking capacity. open questions none of the four sources reconciles why usage pattern research zao sanders' three part series finds gen ai succeeding across an enormously broad range of use cases including many decision adjacent ones, while the mit performance research specifically finds human ai combinations underperforming on decision making tasks — it's unclear whether real world users are self selecting into task types where combination genuinely helps, or whether usage volume and actual performance improvement are simply different, only loosely correlated measures. the shift toward therapy/companionship as gen ai's top documented use case between 2024 and 2025 raises questions about mental health safety and regulation that none of the three usage research pieces address in depth — the vault would benefit from a dedicated source on ai therapy risk/regulation to pair with this concept's account of ai therapy's documented growth. sources how people are really using genai — hbr's 2024 social listening study identifying 100 real world gen ai use cases across six themes. how people are really using genai in 2025 — hbr's 2025 follow up using the same methodology, documenting the shift toward therapy, life organization, and self actualization use cases. making sense of research on how people use ai — hbr's 2025 synthesis triangulating openai's, anthropic's, and the author's own usage research. when humans and ai work best together — and when each is better alone — mit smr on the center for collective intelligence's 106 study meta analysis of human ai combined task performance.
information-goods-economics: summary carl shapiro and hal varian analyze information goods, which are expensive to create the first time but almost free to reproduce, so pricing based on cost fails and sellers price by the value to different customers instead, charging different segments different prices. because people cannot judge information before consuming it, it behaves as an experience good every time it is bought, and sellers must find ways to let buyers sample it. the same cost structure has strategic consequences. network effects make growth a strategic imperative, and an information market can sustain only two long run structures, a market dominated by one firm with a durable scale advantage or a market of many firms offering differentiated varieties of similar information. lock in and standards competition also shape how companies compete, and an incumbent threatened by copycats can price low enough to make entry unattractive or build a reputation for retaliating against new entrants. highlights information goods have an unusual cost structure — high fixed "first copy" costs to create the good in the first place, but near zero marginal cost to reproduce and distribute additional copies — which means cost based pricing a fixed markup on unit cost is economically meaningless, and pricing must instead be based on the value a specific consumer places on the information. information rules because different consumers value the same piece of information very differently, value based pricing leads naturally to differential pricing — charging different prices to different customer segments for functionally the same underlying good. information rules information is an "experience good" every single time it's consumed, not just on first purchase, since a consumer generally cannot judge the value of a specific piece of information without first experiencing it — a problem information businesses address through browsing/previews, branding, and reputation, and more recently through free distribution online. information rules a product exhibits network externalities network effects when the value a given user gets from it depends on how many other users there are — which makes growth a strategic imperative for reasons beyond ordinary production side economies of scale, since network effects generate an additional, demand side form of scale economy. information rules there are only two economically sustainable long run structures for an information market: a dominant firm market one firm achieves a durable cost advantage through scale economies, as with microsoft's desktop operating system dominance or a differentiated product market many firms coexist by each offering a distinct variety of essentially the same kind of information, as in publishing, film, and television . information rules switching costs and lock in are commonplace in information/network markets because so many information systems are built from complementary components supplied by different companies; a firm's optimal competitive posture is often to encourage multiple competing suppliers for its partners' components while working to prevent a strong rival from emerging for its own component. information rules a go it alone strategy competes to become the standard itself high stakes, winner take all, and only advisable if a firm can be genuinely aggressive on timing, pricing, and complementary product relationships , while participating in a formal standard setting process or allying with other firms around a shared technology competes within an already agreed standard instead — a materially lower risk posture. information rules an incumbent information provider facing the threat of commoditization by copycat entrants has two available pricing strategies: limit pricing deliberately sacrificing some short term margin by pricing low enough that entry becomes unattractive to a would be competitor or building a credible reputation for aggressive retaliatory pricing against any new entrant, which — even though costly if it triggers an actual price war — pays for itself over time by discouraging future entry. information rules concept information rules carl shapiro and hal varian builds its entire strategic framework from one foundational economic observation: information goods have a highly unusual cost structure, combining high fixed "first copy" costs the cost of creating the information good in the first place — writing the software, producing the film, researching the report with near zero marginal cost to reproduce and distribute each additional copy once the first exists. this structure has a direct and non obvious pricing implication that the book states plainly: cost based pricing — applying a fixed percentage markup to unit production cost, the default pricing heuristic in most physical goods industries — simply does not work for information goods, because unit cost approaches zero regardless of how much value a given copy delivers to its buyer. instead, information goods must be priced according to the value a specific consumer places on them, and because different consumers value the same underlying information very differently a stock quote is worth far more to an active trader than to a casual investor , value based pricing leads naturally and directly to differential pricing — charging different amounts to different customer segments for functionally the same good, a strategy explicitly less available in commodity physical goods markets where the marginal cost floor constrains how far prices can differentiate. information rules a related structural feature is that information functions as an "experience good" on every single instance of consumption, not merely on a buyer's first exposure to a new brand as in most physical goods markets — a consumer generally cannot judge whether a specific piece of information is valuable without first experiencing it, since experiencing it is precisely what would reveal that value, creating a fundamental tension between a seller's need to demonstrate what they're offering and their need to be paid for it. the book catalogs the range of strategies information industries have historically used to resolve this tension — newsstand browsing, radio previews of songs, movie trailers, and more durably, branding and reputation, which let a consumer form value expectations about new information from a producer's established track record rather than needing to fully experience each new piece of content first; the rise of free online distribution of samples and even full content is presented as a natural extension of this same underlying logic rather than a novel phenomenon unique to the internet. information rules the book identifies network externalities or network effects — where a product's value to any individual user depends on how many other users the product already has — as a second, independent economic force shaping information industry strategy, distinct from but often compounding the first copy cost dynamic. because network effects generate a demand side form of economies of scale on top of ordinary production side scale economies, growth itself becomes a strategic imperative in network markets in a way it typically isn't in markets without network effects, since acquiring users doesn't just spread fixed costs the standard scale economy logic but also directly increases the product's value to every existing user. given these combined cost and network dynamics, the book argues there are only two economically sustainable long run market structures for information goods: a dominant firm structure, in which one firm achieves and sustains a durable cost advantage through scale economies the book's example is microsoft's historical dominance of desktop operating systems , or a differentiated product structure, in which many firms coexist by each offering their own distinct variety of a broadly similar underlying kind of information the book's examples are publishing, film, television, and much of the software industry — implying that a firm's core strategic choice is essentially binary: pursue cost leadership through scale in a dominant firm type market, or pursue genuine differentiation in a fragmented, variety driven market, since strategies that fall between these two poles tend to be unstable. information rules because information systems are typically assembled from complementary components supplied by different companies rather than produced end to end by any single firm, switching costs and lock in are described as commonplace in these markets, and a sophisticated competitive posture requires attending as much to a firm's collaborators as to its direct competitors — the book's specific strategic recommendation is that a firm should generally try to encourage multiple competing suppliers for whatever complementary component its partners provide keeping that side of the ecosystem competitive and low cost while simultaneously working to prevent a strong rival from emerging for its own specific component protecting its own position within the broader system . this logic extends directly to standards competition: a "go it alone" strategy that tries to make a firm's own proprietary technology become the market standard is a high stakes, winner take all bet that the book cautions against attempting unless a firm can be genuinely aggressive on pricing, timing, and its relationships with complementary product makers, whereas participating in a formal, cooperative standard setting process or building an alliance around a shared technology instead competes within an already established standard — a materially lower risk posture that sacrifices the potential for outright standard ownership in exchange for reduced downside risk. finally, on defending an information market position against commoditizing entrants, the book identifies two available pricing responses: limit pricing, deliberately sacrificing some near term margin by pricing low enough that market entry becomes financially unattractive to a prospective competitor in the first place, and building a credible reputation for aggressive retaliatory pricing against any entrant that does appear — a strategy that can be costly if it actually triggers a price war, but which the book argues pays for itself over time by deterring future entrants who correctly anticipate that retaliation. information rules related platform business models — network externalities are the same underlying economic force examined there through the lens of platform design and the four way network effect taxonomy; this concept supplies the classical economic vocabulary network externalities, dominant firm vs. differentiated product markets that platform strategy literature builds on. api and digital value chain strategy — the complementary component and standards competition logic here encouraging competition among partners' components while protecting one's own directly parallels api providers' decisions about how open to make their own platform. corporate value creation — that concept shares an interest in pricing and competitive positioning strategy, though applied to information goods specifically rather than corporate portfolios generally. open questions the book's chapters on specific antitrust case law the microsoft antitrust case is referenced but not detailed and on rights management/versioning strategy were only partially captured in the highlights available for this ingest. sources information rules — carl shapiro and hal varian's economic analysis of information goods cost structure, pricing strategy, network externalities, lock in, and standards competition.
intelligent-choice-architectures: summary intelligent choice architectures use predictive and generative ai to produce and refine sets of decision options for people, instead of a single best answer, and extend the behavioral economics idea of choice architecture, which means deliberately organizing the context in which people decide. the research finds that organizations using ai to generate sets of options achieve better outcomes than those relying on a single recommendation, and it identifies five design categories, including nudges and personalized decision environments. as these systems grow from decision support into semi autonomous agents, they create a dilemma in which their demonstrated ability exceeds the formal decision rights they hold, so organizations must redesign decision rights and accountability. the leadership question then shifts from who should decide to who designs and governs the systems that generate choices, and mit cisr's ai decision matrix and an ai enabled version of the raci chart offer practical guidance on who or what should decide. highlights intelligent choice architectures icas extend richard thaler and cass sunstein's behavioral economics concept of "choice architecture" — intentionally organizing the context in which people decide — into an ai driven system that generates, refines, prioritizes, and presents choice sets, learning from outcomes through feedback loops rather than remaining static. the research's central finding is that organizations using ai to generate sophisticated sets of options, rather than a single "optimal" recommendation, achieve superior outcomes across sectors — the deliverable of good ai assisted decision making is better choices, not just better decisions. five categories of ica design were identified: nudge algorithms that guide toward better decisions while preserving perceived autonomy, personalized decision environments tailored to an individual's role and history, predictive choice modeling that surfaces likely outcomes and trade offs, complexity management that distills large data volumes into actionable insight, and embedded ethical decision making guardrails. a large international bank's ai pilot that fed meeting transcripts and agendas into an llm for automatic summarization and next step generation produced dramatically higher meeting satisfaction scores than the bank's prior survey baseline, and improved follow up coordination on subsequent meetings — illustrating ica principles applied to a mundane, universal organizational pain point. the raci responsible, accountable, consulted, informed project management framework is itself a form of choice architecture for decision rights; combining it with ai "intelligent raci" could predict optimal responsibility allocations from real time data, adjust decision rights fluidly as project contexts shift, and proactively flag decision bottlenecks. as icas mature from decision support tools into semi autonomous decision making agents, they create a "learning authority dilemma": when an ica's demonstrated decision making ability exceeds the formal decision rights it has been granted, organizations need dynamic governance frameworks that can deliberately expand its authority while maintaining oversight, rather than freezing the ica's authority at its original design point. at a pharmaceutical company, an ica used for revenue forecasting evolved through three stages — a decision support tool, then a collaborator whose joint output with finance managers produced the most accurate forecasts, then an increasingly autonomous forecaster that improved without further human intervention — illustrating in miniature how decision rights can shift toward an ai system as its demonstrated competence grows. the research identifies "meta decision rights" as the emerging center of organizational power: not who gets to make a given decision, but who has the authority to design and govern the choice generating systems themselves — meaning leadership accountability increasingly attaches to the quality of the decision environments leaders build, not just the individual decisions made within them. mit cisr's ai decision matrix, built from interviews with 30 executives, sorts decisions by ambiguity and risk into routine, consequential, exploratory and strategic types and assigns humans and ai different roles across framing, acting and learning, always with human oversight. a framework for determining when ai can make decisions one new zealand, running over 50 ai agents, illustrates the matrix: an audience segmentation agent cut segmentation time 60% under marketer review, pricing decisions stay human in the loop as a non negotiable constraint, and network resilience decisions remain human led although 15 task agents and orchestration agents supply analysis. a framework for determining when ai can make decisions best practice includes business units owning the framing of each ai use case, an ai centre of excellence owning data, orchestration and responsible ai policy, a named human owner for every agent, and managing ai as a portfolio of business decisions rather than use cases. a framework for determining when ai can make decisions hbr identifies four mistakes that make raci type decision rights tools fail, based on work with more than 100 companies: assigning roles before clarifying goals, treating rights as a static list from one senior leader, misunderstanding what each role means half of 30 consultancy partners thought the "responsible" person had the final say , and letting hierarchy override roles. what companies get wrong about decision rights concept intelligent choices reshape decision making and productivity mit smr, october 2024 , the first installment in a research collaboration between mit smr and tata consultancy services, introduces the core concept: an intelligent choice architecture ica is an ai system, combining generative and predictive capabilities, that produces and refines sophisticated sets of decision options rather than a single recommended answer. the article grounds this in richard thaler and cass sunstein's nobel prize winning behavioral economics work on "choice architecture" — deliberately organizing the context in which people make decisions — arguing that ai strengthens the connection between the design of a decision environment and the decisions that emerge from it, because ai systems can learn and improve their choice sets through outcome feedback in a way static choice architectures cannot. the article identifies five categories of ica design nudge algorithms, personalized decision environments, predictive choice modeling, complexity management, and embedded ethical guardrails and illustrates practical impact through a large international bank's pilot: feeding meeting transcripts and agendas into an llm for automatic summarization produced substantially higher meeting satisfaction scores than the bank's prior survey baseline, and the resulting summaries also improved follow up coordination on subsequent meetings. the article closes by identifying decision rights as the central organizational design question icas raise — proposing "intelligent raci" combining the classic responsible/accountable/consulted/informed framework with ai that predicts optimal responsibility allocation and adapts it as project contexts shift as an early example — and explicitly previews a follow up article and long form report to come. the great power shift: how intelligent choice architectures rewrite decision rights mit smr, january 2025 is that promised second installment, drawing on interviews with senior leaders across six major industry groups to examine how icas concretely reshape decision rights once deployed at scale. the article's central argument is that as compound ai systems combining predictive and generative ai become more sophisticated choice architects, organizational focus shifts from decision execution to decision design — executives become accountable for the decision environments their staff operate within, not just for individual decisions. it documents three structural shifts already occurring: power flowing to whoever designs the best decision environments, whether human or machine illustrated by sanofi's use of icas to systematically counteract sunk cost bias in r&d portfolio decisions ; network effects that make icas more valuable the more they're used, since each transaction or decision improves future accuracy illustrated by mastercard's fraud detection icas, which improve for the entire payments ecosystem with every transaction processed ; and real time optimization contexts — like algorithmic trading, programmatic advertising, and a pharmaceutical company's revenue forecasting ica, which evolved from decision support tool to human ai collaborator to increasingly autonomous forecaster — where ceding real time authority to the ica outperforms retaining it exclusively with human managers. this maturation creates what the article terms the "learning authority dilemma": when an ica's demonstrated decision making capability exceeds its formally granted authority, organizations need dynamic governance frameworks capable of deliberately expanding that authority rather than either freezing it prematurely or ceding it without appropriate oversight. the article's culminating concept is "meta decision rights" — as icas mature, the most consequential organizational power shifts from the right to make a given decision to the right to design and govern the systems that generate decision options in the first place, reframing the central leadership question from "who should decide?" to "how do we architect better ways to decide?" read together as a deliberate two part research series, the articles build from foundational concept to organizational consequence: the first establishes what an intelligent choice architecture is and demonstrates its value through concrete pilots, while the second traces what happens as icas mature and gain real organizational traction — a fundamental redistribution of decision rights toward whoever, human or machine, is positioned to design the best decision environment, with a wholly new category of "meta accountability" emerging for the leaders responsible for those designs. a framework for determining when ai can make decisions mit smr, september 2026 gives the concrete allocation rule this concept's decision rights thesis lacks. the matrix pairs ambiguity how clearly data determines the answer and whether people agree with risk consequences and reversibility , and each of the four resulting decision types implies a different split. routine decisions can have framing codified and action and learning automated with humans close by until confidence builds; consequential decisions keep humans monitoring execution and managing exceptions; exploratory decisions let framing evolve through human ai interaction under strong governance; strategic decisions keep humans leading framing and learning while ai facilitates action. a framework for determining when ai can make decisions what companies get wrong about decision rights hbr, july 2026 addresses the human side of the same question and why decision rights documents often fail. in a medical technology company, 12 executives crowded a meeting that a raci had assigned to four, ending 90 minutes later without a decision. the authors recommend setting measurable goals and subgoals first, co creating roles with those affected raci sessions are conversation starters, with one accountable person and two to four responsible people , defining behavioural descriptions for each role, tailoring roles to the topic so the best informed person is accountable, challenging senior leaders to name just four decisions a year only they should make, and embedding roles in meeting agendas and performance guides. the lessons carry over to human agent teams, where agent ownership and role clarity face the same hierarchy and ambiguity problems. what companies get wrong about decision rights related philosophical frameworks for ai — by the same author pair michael schrage and david kiron , published in the same window; draws on the same thaler sunstein choice architecture theory to argue agentic ai needs deliberate philosophical training, a complementary but distinct argument from this concept's decision rights focus. matching ai type to decision type — that concept provides a complementary framework for calibrating analytical ai and generative ai to specific decisions, addressing a related but distinct question from this concept's focus on how ai reshapes decision rights and organizational power once deployed. ai work and organization redesign — that concept covers the general thesis of ai pressuring organizations to redesign structures and processes, of which this concept's decision rights redistribution is one specific mechanism. ai in strategy and decision making — the strategy process and decision agent material there applies this concept's decision rights logic to the executive committee. open questions neither article specifies concrete criteria or thresholds for resolving the "learning authority dilemma" — how an organization should decide when an ica's demonstrated capability warrants an expansion of its formal decision rights, beyond citing the pharmaceutical revenue forecasting example as an illustration after the fact. the promised "long form report" mentioned at the end of the october 2024 article is not itself in the vault, so it's unclear whether further empirical detail beyond these two articles exists to substantiate the six industry group interview research cited in the january 2025 piece. the ai decision matrix draws on 30 interviews and one detailed telecom case, and does not say how decision types should be reclassified as an agent's track record improves. sources intelligent choices reshape decision making and productivity — mit smr, michael schrage and david kiron, 2024 10 29; architectures rewrite decision rights — mit smr, michael schrage, 2025 01 28; the explicit second installment, examining how icas redistribute decision rights and create "meta decision rights" as they mature a framework for determining when ai can make decisions — mit smr, beth stackpole reporting on mit cisr research, 2026 09 22; the ai decision matrix of ambiguity and risk. what companies get kpi-design-in-the-ai-era: summary organizations that search for a single perfect performance indicator fall into goodhart's law, which holds that when a measure becomes a target it is gamed until it stops reflecting the goal, as in wells fargo's cross selling scandal. machine learning offers four techniques for avoiding overfitting that translate into kpi design, which are reassessing metrics against the true objective, adding unpredictability such as random audits, matching a metric's complexity to the organization's ability to oversee it and adding constraints that make gaming more costly than performing well. agoda's long search for one comprehensive metric shows why ai is often needed to build a robust one, since its supply equity points metric, which assigns a machine learned expected margin to each business action, took five years to develop and is still unfinished. the search for one kpi usually ends with several. highlights wells fargo's 2016 cross selling scandal employees opened millions of unauthorized accounts to hit an "eight products per customer" sales target is the canonical illustration of goodhart's law — "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" — and mit smr argues machine learning's own long studied fight against a structurally identical problem, overfitting, offers organizations four concrete, adaptable techniques traditional balanced scorecards and kpis lack. what ai can teach us about designing better kpis early stopping halting ml model optimization once validation performance peaks, even if training performance could still improve maps to periodically reassessing metrics against true objectives — amazon shifted its primary metric from profit margin to free cash flow per share in 2004, and intel shifted from pure clock speed optimization to a balanced set including energy efficiency after discovering pure speed optimization was causing overheating and diminishing real world performance gains.
