random audits and unpredictable evaluation timing — the irs's random audit program generates up to $6 in additional revenue per dollar invested through pure deterrence effects, with compliance gains persisting at least five years post audit, and the fda's unannounced pharmaceutical manufacturer inspections consistently surface problems planned inspections miss. what ai can teach us about designing better kpis capacity alignment matching ml model complexity to available training data and monitoring capability maps to matching kpi complexity to an organization's actual oversight capacity — wework's opaque "community adjusted ebitda" metric which excluded even basic operating expenses helped attract billions in investment specifically because it was too complex for most investors to properly dissect, while jpmorgan chase's 2012 "london whale" incident involved a sophisticated but flawed value at risk model whose complexity let traders game it within technically acceptable ranges, understating risk by 50% and costing over $6 billion. what ai can teach us about designing better kpis regularization penalizing excessive model complexity to prevent overfitting to idiosyncratic training data quirks maps to organizational constraints that make gaming a metric more costly than simply performing well — netflix shifted from raw hours viewed to a "views" metric hours viewed divided by runtime specifically to avoid incentivizing attention capturing but unsatisfying content, and amazon's seller rating algorithm actively detects and penalizes suspicious review solicitation patterns to keep star ratings aligned with genuine seller quality. what ai can teach us about designing better kpis agoda's business development team needed a kpi to guide decisions across a genuinely enormous permutation space — a typical business developer managing 100 hotels, each with roughly 125 availability/price permutations per date, faces more than a million total permutations across the next 90 check in days alone, making some form of ai assisted prediction essentially mandatory rather than optional for the kpi to be usable at all. building one kpi to rule them all agoda's five desired kpi attributes — highly measurable and not too "noisy," aligned with overall business value, understandable, expressed in a comparable currency across teams, and minimizing communication costs — map onto a fundamental input kpi versus output kpi tradeoff: output kpis revenue, bookings align tightly with p&l but are heavily distorted by uncontrollable externalities an unpredictable taylor swift concert announcement spiked singapore travel interest in a way no analyst could have forecast , while input kpis like program adoption rate are directly actionable and controllable but don't reliably indicate whether the underlying action actually created value. building one kpi to rule them all agoda's resulting "supply equity points" sep metric — assigning a machine learning modeled expected margin value to every possible business developer action, refreshed daily — took five years to develop and still isn't finished: it struggles with predictability frequent gaps between predicted and realized value , misses genuinely valuable but hard to quantify actions like relationship building meetings , and can discourage long term entrepreneurial bets in favor of short term optimization, forcing agoda to add two supplementary kpis a price competitiveness score and locally defined "innovation kpis" rather than ever achieving the originally hoped for single metric. building one kpi to rule them all agoda's own closing lesson directly echoes the ml derived framework: "the greater one's analytical capabilities, the more control one has over kpi fluctuations" — without machine learning and ai to strip out external noise, the company's multi year search for a workable kpi would likely have failed outright, and the team explicitly frames ai as actively "rewriting much of the kpi playbook" going forward, not as a one time fix. building one kpi to rule them all concept mit smr's research on organizational metric design starts from goodhart's law — "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" — and its most vivid recent illustration, wells fargo's 2016 scandal, in which employees, incentivized to sell eight financial products per customer, opened millions of unauthorized accounts to hit that target, harming customers and the bank alike. the article's core argument is that traditional solutions to this problem — balanced scorecards, conventional kpis — routinely fail precisely because they remain vulnerable to narrow optimization and gaming absent careful, ongoing oversight, and that a more sophisticated approach is needed. that more sophisticated approach, the piece argues, already exists — inside machine learning research, which has spent decades studying a structurally identical problem under a different name: overfitting, where a model performs flawlessly on its training data but fails on real world data because it learned incidental patterns in that training set a background detail correlated with the label, say rather than the genuine underlying signal. ai researcher jascha sohl dickstein's observation that "increased efficiency can sometimes, counterintuitively, lead to worse outcomes" — true "almost everywhere," in his words, whether in machine learning or organizational settings — frames the article's central translation project: taking four established anti overfitting techniques from ml research and mapping each onto a concrete organizational metric design strategy. the first, early stopping, addresses overoptimization directly: ml researchers monitor a model's performance on data separate from its training set and halt training the moment validation performance peaks, even though training performance alone might still be improving — a warning sign of overfitting in progress. organizationally, this maps to periodically reassessing metrics against true objectives rather than pursuing a fixed metric indefinitely: amazon shifted its primary internal metric from profit margin to free cash flow per share in 2004 specifically to prevent any single metric from being over optimized past its useful point; intel, having long emphasized processor clock speed as its central performance metric, discovered continued speed optimization was producing excessive power consumption, overheating, and diminishing real computing performance returns, prompting a shift toward a more balanced set of metrics including energy efficiency; and microsoft under satya nadella moved from rigid annual targets to quarterly business reviews specifically so metrics and goals could be adjusted as market conditions and understanding evolved, rather than being pursued past the point of usefulness. a related early stopping variant is setting minimum rather than maximization targets — unlike wells fargo's aggressive "eight products per customer" ceiling chasing target, a genuine minimum target a customer service department resolving at least 85% of inquiries within 24 hours, for instance establishes an acceptable performance threshold without rewarding indefinite over optimization once that threshold is met. the second technique, noise injection, addresses a related overfitting mechanism: when ml models rely too heavily on specific, predictable patterns in training data, they can memorize incidental quirks rather than learning genuine underlying relationships, so researchers deliberately introduce controlled randomness randomly disabling some model connections during training, rotating or perturbing training examples to force the model toward more robust, generalizable learning. organizations can apply the same logic through random audits, rotated team compositions, and unpredictable evaluation timing, preventing people from learning and exploiting predictable assessment patterns: jpmorgan chase uses random compliance audits specifically to discourage employees from developing gaming workarounds calibrated to predictable review schedules; the irs's random audit program is empirically documented to generate up to $6 in additional revenue for every dollar invested, purely through deterrence, with compliance gains among randomly audited taxpayers persisting for at least five years post audit; the fda's unannounced pharmaceutical manufacturer inspection program expanded further in 2025 specifically because of its effectiveness consistently surfaces compliance problems that scheduled, predictable inspections would have missed as facilities temporarily optimized for evaluation day; and the tsa rotates screening personnel across checkpoints and functions specifically to prevent bad actors from studying and exploiting predictable individual screener patterns. the third technique, capacity alignment, addresses the mismatch between model sophistication and available training/validation resources: ml researchers deploy complex, many parameter models only when they have enough training data and strong validation methods to support that complexity safely, defaulting to simpler models when data or oversight capacity is limited, since overly complex models trained on insufficient data collapse quickly, especially when the same small validation set gets reused repeatedly. organizationally, this means matching metric complexity to an organization's actual analytical and oversight capabilities — a company with genuinely advanced analytics infrastructure and skilled data scientists can safely implement complex, multidimensional metrics, while an organization with limited oversight capacity should favor simpler, more robust metrics even at the cost of some lost nuance, since the real danger zone is metric complexity that outpaces the organization's actual capacity to validate and monitor it. wework's notorious "community adjusted ebitda" — a metric so complex it excluded not just standard ebitda adjustments but even basic operating expenses like marketing and administrative costs — illustrates the danger directly: the metric was sophisticated enough to obscure the company's real financial position from investors who lacked the expertise to properly dissect it, yet it wasn't a genuinely sophisticated measure of real business performance, and it helped attract billions in investment before the sec intervened and the company's underlying business model ultimately collapsed into bankruptcy. jpmorgan chase's 2012 "london whale" trading incident shows the same dynamic inside a highly analytically sophisticated organization: a value at risk model fatally undermined by spreadsheet errors that understated risk by 50%, complex enough that traders could manipulate price inputs within technically acceptable ranges while risk managers lacked the analytical infrastructure to detect either the underlying errors or the deliberate gaming — a combination that produced over $6 billion in losses. startups, by contrast, tend to naturally practice good capacity alignment by focusing on simple, stage appropriate metrics customer acquisition cost, monthly recurring revenue, retention directly tied to product market fit and cash flow, only expanding toward more sophisticated unit economics and predictive analytics as their own analytical maturity genuinely grows. the fourth technique, regularization, addresses the core mechanism behind gaming most directly: in ml, regularization penalizes excessive model complexity to prevent a model from becoming so finely tuned to its training data's idiosyncrasies that it performs poorly on new data — forcing the model toward simpler, more generalizable patterns instead. organizationally, regularization means adding deliberate constraints that make gaming a metric more complex and costly than simply performing well genuinely: amazon's seller rating algorithm actively detects suspicious review patterns sudden five star review spikes from low purchase history accounts, clusters of generic reviews posted in tight time windows that indicate solicited reviews, penalizing the practice specifically to keep star ratings aligned with real seller quality rather than gaming activity; netflix, recognizing that optimizing purely for hours viewed risked incentivizing attention capturing but ultimately unsatisfying content, shifted in 2023 to a "views" metric hours viewed divided by content runtime that the company explicitly called "our best measure of member satisfaction," using multiple complementary metrics that balance each other in a way analogous to ml regularization; unilever's sustainable living plan added explicit sustainability constraints on pure profit seeking after discovering unconstrained profit maximization was producing environmental costs the company hadn't been measuring; and whole foods pre amazon acquisition tied executive compensation caps to average worker pay specifically as a structural constraint against optimizing purely for leadership enrichment. the article's closing framing treats these four techniques as most powerful when applied together rather than in isolation, and stresses that successful implementation typically involves the people who will actually be measured directly in designing the measurement system — producing both better calibrated metrics and greater genuine buy in than a top down metric design process tends to achieve. what ai can teach us about designing better kpis agoda's own multiyear account of its search for a single comprehensive kpi illustrates several of these same dynamics playing out in a real, high stakes operational context, while adding a distinct complication the abstract framework doesn't fully address: sheer combinatorial complexity that makes ai assisted prediction close to mandatory rather than merely helpful. agoda's business development team supports hotel, airline, and attraction partners in maximizing their sales on the platform, and the underlying decision space each business developer must navigate is genuinely enormous — a typical portfolio of 100 hotels, each with a conservative estimate of 125 availability/price permutations room type, room features, pricing segment per future check in date, works out to 12,500 permutations per date and more than a million permutations across just the next 90 check in days for a single business developer. without some form of comprehensive kpi capable of guiding decisions across that space, agoda argues the job would be genuinely impossible to perform well. the company's search, chronicled as a continuation of an earlier 2022 mit smr piece on the same quest, converged on five desired attributes for a workable kpi: high measurability with low "noise" natural fluctuation should be much smaller than the effect of deliberate actions, described as "controlling your own destiny" ; alignment with overall business value tying to p&l, though closer p&l alignment tends to increase noise, requiring a deliberate balance ; understandability the easier the underlying logic is to explain, the easier adoption and organizational buy in become ; a comparable currency across individuals and teams enabling fair comparison and compensation ; and minimized communication costs clarity reduces time spent debating the metric itself rather than acting on it . these attributes map directly onto a fundamental tension between output kpis and input kpis that agoda found itself repeatedly navigating. output kpis bookings, revenue correlate tightly with actual business value and support genuine roi measurement and cross team comparison, but are heavily distorted by externalities entirely outside a business developer's control — an unpredictable taylor swift concert announcement, for instance, spiked travel interest in singapore in a way no analyst could have forecast, meaning a business developer whose portfolio happened to include affected hotels would be credited with strong performance driven by pure luck rather than skill. input kpis like the percentage of a portfolio's hotels enrolled in a specific promotional program are directly actionable, controllable, and quick to execute, requiring little upfront analysis — but don't reliably indicate whether the underlying action actually generated real value, and tend to apply unevenly across different market contexts a black friday promotion works well as an input kpi for hotels serving european and us customers, for whom black friday drives impulse purchases, but is a poor indicator for hotels serving predominantly southeast asian customers . beyond this core tradeoff, agoda's kpi search had to account for a wide range of genuine externalities entirely beyond the business development team's control — market growth, new flight routes, geopolitical and macroeconomic shifts, competitor and partner activity, and idiosyncratic events like covid 19 recovery patterns varying sharply by market, or japan's 2015 visa requirement relaxation producing a travel boom that flattered the japan team's output kpis for reasons having nothing to do with the team's own decision making — plus internal confounds like company run a/b experiments that could distort a subset of business developers' metrics for reasons entirely outside their control. after considering and rejecting several simpler candidate metrics raw revenue, too noisy and externally driven; pricing competitiveness, too fragmented across millions of individual price points and complicated by the gap between public and member rates; single program adoption rate, too uneven in value across different programs and hotel tiers , agoda eventually developed what it calls supply equity points sep : a machine learning modeled expected margin value assigned to every possible business developer action activating a promotional program, negotiating a price, securing room availability for a given date , refreshed daily, expressed in a common unit that makes global comparison across business developers finally possible. building sep required substantial machine learning investment specifically to model millions of scenario permutations, accounting for the depth of potential value a given action might unlock, how that action interacts with a hotel's existing live products, how long the resulting value is expected to persist, and what behavioral changes increased occupancy leading to higher prices, for instance might follow a given action going live — work agoda explicitly states "would likely have failed without the benefit of reliable prediction models," since the noise reduction and confound removal sep performs is precisely the kind of computational problem machine learning is well suited to and traditional manual analysis isn't. even after roughly five years of continued development, sep remains imperfect in three specific, ongoing ways: predictability continues to lag accuracy, since internal and external factors that shift quickly create real gaps between predicted and realized sep values, frustrating business developers who feel disempowered when outcomes diverge from projections; sep structurally misses some genuinely valuable but hard to quantify actions, such as relationship building, face to face meetings with hotel partners, whose incremental value the underlying machine learning model simply can't isolate, forcing agoda to encourage such activity through separate, non kpi based means; and sep, like most kpis, can discourage longer term entrepreneurial bets in favor of short term optimization, illustrated by agoda's japan team pursuing acquisition of ryokans traditional japanese inns that scored poorly under sep due to insufficient historical data, requiring the team to add ryokan onboarding as a separate input kpi entirely outside the sep framework to protect the strategic bet from being starved by short term metric pressure. to manage these gaps, agoda ultimately settled not on the single comprehensive kpi it originally set out to build, but on three complementary measures: sep itself as the primary, machine learning derived input kpi; a supply health score shs , a noisier but genuinely output oriented price competitiveness metric that captures value sep structurally misses and preserves business developers' sense of entrepreneurial ownership over their portfolio; and locally defined "innovation kpis" that let regional management teams pursue strategic, longer horizon bets like ryokan acquisition that wouldn't survive evaluation under sep alone. agoda's own distilled lessons for other organizations pursuing a similar kpi search echo the ml derived framework directly: the greater the influence of uncontrollable external factors on a given output goal, the more an organization needs to lean on input kpis to reduce noise and evaluate performance fairly a real estate agent's commission, largely insulated from major external confounds, needs far less of this correction than agoda's booking dependent business developers do ; the greater an organization's own analytical capability, the more control it gains over kpi fluctuation — machine learning and ai, in agoda's own words, "helped us remove fluctuations that might affect performance evaluation," and without that capability the company's kpi search would likely have failed outright; and complexity itself carries a real, ongoing cost, since a kpi too complex to be understood, or one perceived as an opaque black box, consumes organizational time defending and explaining the metric rather than acting on the business performance it's meant to represent. agoda's closing reflection frames its multiyear search not as a solved problem but as an ongoing one specifically because ai capability keeps advancing: the team explicitly expects ai to keep "rewriting much of the kpi playbook" by enabling ever more accurate predictions and more flexible, real time adjustment to what actually matters in a genuinely dynamic operating environment — meaning, in the company's own assessment, this won't be its last search for a better kpi. building one kpi to rule them all related measuring ai project value and quality — eric siegel's argument there that business metrics not technical ones should drive ai project evaluation is the mirror image of this concept's argument that ai derived techniques should drive better organizational kpi design; both concern the gap between what's easy to measure and what actually reflects value. gen ai organizational learning and knowledge — the "measure the cycle, not just the output" discipline covered there for organizational gen ai learning shares the same underlying insight as this concept's early stopping and regularization techniques: consumption/output metrics alone invite exactly the kind of gaming goodhart's law predicts. open questions neither source addresses how an organization should decide, in advance, which of the four ml derived techniques early stopping, noise injection, capacity alignment, regularization is most urgently needed for a given metric design problem — the article presents all four as generally applicable but doesn't offer a diagnostic framework for prioritizing among them under real resource constraints. agoda's account doesn't fully reconcile its own sep metric's five year, still unfinished development timeline with the "capacity alignment" principle from the companion research — it's unclear whether agoda's continued investment in an imperfect, complex metric reflects appropriately matched analytical capacity, or the kind of complexity outpacing oversight risk the wework and jpmorgan chase examples warn against, since the piece reports ongoing predictability problems without fully assessing whether sep's complexity has in fact outpaced agoda's ability to validate it. sources what ai can teach us about designing better kpis — mit smr's "metric intelligence framework" mapping four ml anti overfitting techniques early stopping, noise injection, capacity alignment, regularization onto organizational kpi design. building one kpi to rule them all — agoda's five year account of developing supply equity points, its machine learning modeled comprehensive kpi for business developers.
lean-startup-customer-development: summary customer development and the lean startup reframe a startup as a temporary organization searching for a repeatable, scalable business model, not as a smaller version of an established company executing a known plan. the method proceeds through customer discovery, customer validation, customer creation and company building, where the first two are the search for a model and the last two the execution of it. the concept covers the business model canvas, the pivot as a substantive change to one of its nine boxes, early adopters called earlyvangelists as the target of a minimum viable product, and the build measure learn loop, in which each product version is an experiment that turns a hypothesis into validated fact. it also describes startup metrics that track hypotheses turning into facts and growth hacking as a cross functional responsibility. highlights a startup is defined not as a smaller version of a company but as a temporary organization designed to search for a repeatable and scalable business model; this "search" mode requires a different organizational structure a founder led customer development team than the functional structure needed once a validated model moves into "execution" mode. the startup owner's manual customer development runs through four stop and assess steps — customer discovery, customer validation, customer creation, and company building — where the first two constitute the "search" for a business model and the last two constitute "execution" of a model once validated. the startup owner's manual a pivot is a substantive change to one of the nine boxes of the business model canvas driven by customer feedback, distinct from a minor iteration e.g. changing a price point ; pivots are treated as a normal, expected part of the search process rather than a failure. the startup owner's manual "earlyvangelists" — customers who already recognize they have a painful problem, have cobbled together an interim workaround, and have or can acquire budget — are the correct target for a minimum viable product, not mainstream customers who expect a finished, fully featured product. the startup owner's manual startup appropriate metrics track progress converting hypotheses into facts e.g. whether the problem and product features have been validated rather than execution against a static plan; the only financial metric that always matters at this stage is cash burn rate and months of runway remaining. the startup owner's manual the build measure learn loop treats a minimum viable product as an experiment designed to generate validated learning as fast as possible, not as a shrunken version of the final product; the goal of each loop is to test a specific hypothesis and decide, with evidence, whether to persevere or pivot. the lean startup "growth hacking" reframes growth as an organization wide, cross functional responsibility spanning product, engineering, and support as well as marketing, driven by rigorous analytics and a deep understanding of customer behavior rather than treated as marketing's job alone — a shift the source frames as an evolution of marketing rather than an alternative to it. startup growth engines concept both customer development steve blank and bob dorf and the lean startup eric ries, building directly on blank's work begin from the same reframing: a startup is not a smaller version of an established company but a temporary organization whose sole purpose is to search for a repeatable, scalable, and profitable business model, as distinct from an established company's purpose of executing a known model. on day one, a startup's understanding of its customer, problem, and business model is treated as a set of unproven hypotheses rather than facts, and the entire discipline exists to convert those hypotheses into evidence as quickly and cheaply as possible before committing to scale. the startup owner's manual the customer development process organizes this search into four sequential steps, each with an explicit stop and assess checkpoint before proceeding. customer discovery translates the founder's vision into a set of business model hypotheses recorded on a nine box business model canvas covering value proposition, customer segments, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partners, and cost structure and then runs face to face tests, first of the customer's perceived problem and then of the proposed solution, targeting "earlyvangelist" customers rather than the mainstream market — earlyvangelists are recognizable by already having an acute, recognized problem, an improvised interim workaround, a search already under way for a solution, and either existing or readily acquirable budget. customer validation repeats these tests at greater scale and rigor to confirm the model is genuinely repeatable and scalable, not just anecdotally promising. only once discovery and validation succeed — described as reaching "escape velocity" — does the company move into customer creation aggressively spending to build end user demand and company building transitioning from a founder led search organization into a functionally structured execution organization . the startup owner's manual a central working distinction is between a pivot and an iteration: an iteration is a minor adjustment to a business model component e.g. changing a price from $99 to $79 , while a pivot is a substantive change to one or more of the nine business model canvas boxes, driven directly by evidence from customer testing. far from signaling failure, frequent pivoting is presented as the expected mechanism by which a startup converges on a working model — the canvas is redrawn after each pivot, and the accumulated stack of past canvases documents the company's actual learning trajectory. because startups face a hard cash constraint that established companies don't, the methodology insists on startup specific metrics rather than the metrics used to run an existing business: rather than tracking progress against a revenue plan or launch date, teams should track whether the customer problem and minimum feature set have actually been validated through direct customer contact, alongside the one financial number that always matters regardless of stage — cash burn rate and the number of months of runway remaining. the startup owner's manual the lean startup formalizes the same underlying loop — most explicitly credited by ries to blank's customer development work — as build measure learn: a minimum viable product is built not as a stripped down version of the eventual finished product but as a deliberately minimal experiment designed to generate the maximum validated learning for the minimum effort, after which the results are measured against a specific hypothesis and used to decide, with evidence rather than opinion, whether to persevere with the current approach or pivot to a different one. this closes the loop back to customer development's core discipline of treating every product decision as a testable hypothesis rather than an assumption to build around. the lean startup a complementary account of what happens once a startup has validated its business model and moved into scaling is offered under the "growth hacking" label: sustained growth is described as coming from a shared organizational commitment that treats growth as everyone's responsibility — product, engineering, and support, not marketing alone — built on a genuinely must have product and a rigorous, data driven, deeply customer informed approach to acquisition, retention, and monetization, reframing "growth hacking" as an evolution of marketing practice rather than a replacement for or opponent of it. startup growth engines related platform business models — platform launch strategies share the same chicken or egg, evidence before scale logic that customer development applies to single sided products. scrum methodology — agile/scrum is the engineering side discipline that customer development is explicitly meant to be paired with, so that validated learning from customers can be converted into working product increments quickly. cloud and saas business economics — that concept describes how, once a company moves past validation into execution, ongoing usage data continues to drive the same build measure learn cycle inside an already scaled product. open questions the lean startup file in this vault contains only a single highlight on build measure learn; the book's fuller treatment of the pivot/persevere decision, innovation accounting, and the "five whys" root cause technique is not yet captured here. sources the startup owner's manual — steve blank and bob dorf's fourteen rules of customer development, the four step process, and the business model canvas. the lean startup — eric ries's build measure learn loop and minimum viable product discipline. startup growth engines — sean ellis and morgan brown's account of cross functional "growth hacking" as an organization wide discipline.
llm-mechanics-limitations-and-scaling: summary large language models generate text by repeatedly predicting the next token, which makes hallucination an inherent consequence of the design and produces limits in reasoning, knowledge, understanding and planning that no prompt or retrieval technique removes entirely. practical use therefore depends on human review, ai judges, retrieval and complementary technologies, as the finding that consultants using gpt 4 erred more often on a reasoning task shows. scaling laws reliably predict better next word prediction but not new capabilities, and data limits, the possibility of sudden plateaus, the narrow role of synthetic data and a market shift toward smaller, longer trained models suggest that capability gains from scale alone may slow. highlights an llm predicts one token at a time in a loop run by external software, which decides when to stop through the model's learned end of sequence token, a maximum length or a user defined stop sequence. how llms work — top 10 executive level questions a model does not learn from a single correction, and apparent memory comes from a separate feature that re injects stored facts into new prompts, while any improvement from corrections appears only in a later training run. how llms work — top 10 executive level questions parameters, training data volume and context window size shape what a model can do, as with gpt 3's 175 billion parameters, roughly half a trillion training tokens and 2,000 token context window. the working limitations of large language models what are llms and generative ai retrieval augmented generation stays useful with million token context windows because irrelevant material degrades output, models attend less to the middle of long prompts and longer prompts cost more and respond more slowly. how llms work — top 10 executive level questions hallucination cannot be eliminated because it arises from probabilistic token prediction rather than fact verification, and mitigations such as prompt engineering, retrieval, fine tuning and rule based checks reduce it but cannot guarantee its absence, including in citations. how llms work — top 10 executive level questions four limitation categories are reasoning, knowledge and expertise, understanding of prompt structure and planning and execution, and in a field experiment with over 750 bcg consultants, gpt 4 users got a reasoning task wrong 23% more often than a no ai control group because of its confident rationale. the working limitations of large language models practical workarounds are human review with sampling or risk based triage, a second ai judge that can itself hallucinate, and complementary technologies such as knowledge graphs, reasoning engines and domain specific fine tuned models. the working limitations of large language models mckinsey's explainer separates predictive machine learning from generative ai, notes gpt 3's roughly 45 terabytes of training text and recommends careful data selection, smaller specialized models, proprietary customization, human review and avoiding generative ai for critical decisions. what is generative ai scaling laws predict lower perplexity reliably but say nothing reliable about emergent abilities, which are what users value, and on benchmarks testing extrapolation to unseen tasks llms tend to perform poorly. ai scaling myths high quality data is a near term constraint, since transcribing all of youtube would add less usable data than llama 3's roughly 15 trillion tokens, exponential trends such as cpu clock speeds can plateau abruptly, and synthetic data mainly fills targeted gaps. ai scaling myths labs are shifting toward smaller, cheaper, more capable models trained for longer, as gpt 4o, claude 3.5 sonnet and gemini 1.5 pro show, trading higher training compute for lower inference cost. ai scaling myths concept at the mechanical level an llm does one thing repeatedly, predicting the most likely next token, a word or sub word unit, given everything before it, appending that token and repeating. external software, not the model, runs the loop and decides when to stop, based on the model's own predictions, since it learns in training to emit a special end of sequence token where an example's answer was complete, and on external rules such as a maximum token limit or a user defined stop sequence. the appearance of a model deciding that it is done is therefore an interaction between statistical prediction and configurable software logic, which a team building an application can and should tune deliberately. how llms work — top 10 executive level questions three technical factors shape what a model can do. parameters are the trainable weights that encode relationships extracted from training data, and more of them generally means more nuanced, knowledgeable output, as gpt 3's 175 billion do, training data volume, measured in tokens, matters because a larger and more diverse corpus generally improves generalization, as gpt 3's roughly half a trillion tokens did, and context window size sets how much prompt text the model considers at once, 2,000 tokens for gpt 3, with a larger, more detailed context generally improving accuracy for the task at hand. a model does not learn from a correction in real time, since a user's correction might inform a training run weeks or months later but the running model does not update, and apparent memory of earlier conversations is a separate feature that stores facts such as a name, preferences and recurring topics and silently re injects them into a new prompt, so the model receives reminders as input rather than recalling a past interaction. how llms work — top 10 executive level questions what are llms and generative ai the working limitations of large language models the same mechanism explains why retrieval augmented generation remains valuable even with context windows in the million token range. overloading a prompt with excess or irrelevant material degrades output, models do not weigh all parts of a long prompt equally and attend more to the beginning and end, missing details buried in the middle, and longer prompts cost more and run slower in production, all of which argue for retrieving and including only the most relevant material instead of stuffing everything into a larger window. how llms work — top 10 executive level questions hallucination, confident and plausible output that is fabricated or wrong, is a structural consequence of token prediction rather than a bug that engineering will eliminate, because the model generates statistically likely sequences rather than verifying claims against a ground truth source. prompt engineering, retrieval, domain specific fine tuning and rule based post processing checks can each reduce hallucination for a use case but none can guarantee its absence, and this extends to the citations a model provides, which can be as readily fabricated or misapplied as any other content, so a citation should never be trusted without independent verification that the source exists and supports the claim. how llms work — top 10 executive level questions four broader limitations follow from the same mechanism. reasoning limits mean llms simulate individual logical rules convincingly but do not reliably chain them into valid multi step conclusions, as a cabbage classification puzzle that a model confidently answers wrongly shows, each step carries a nonzero chance of error, and the model often cannot explain the chain that produced its answer, so reviewers struggle to catch errors. knowledge and expertise limits mean the model is bounded by, and can reproduce errors in, its training data, producing fabrication such as invented citations and case law and inconsistency, since the same question can receive materially different answers depending on phrasing or timing. understanding limits mean it can misread the logical structure of a prompt, as in a nested boxes puzzle it gets backwards, which is hardest to catch when the user does not know the domain well enough to notice or to write a better prompt. planning limits mean plans that look step by step can be practically naive, since the model does not question whether a stated goal is realistic or interrogate the user's assumptions as a competent advisor would. the working limitations of large language models the stakes appeared in a field experiment with more than 750 boston consulting group consultants, in which participants using gpt 4 on a business reasoning task got the answer wrong 23% more often than a no ai control group, not mainly because the model erred more often alone but because its confident, persuasive rationale led users to accept the wrong answer without independent verification. the working limitations of large language models since the limitations cannot be engineered away entirely, applications should be designed around them. human review remains the most reliable safeguard for open ended tasks, with sampling or risk based triage used to manage the cost of reviewing at scale. for structured or high volume tasks a second ai judge, typically another llm that evaluates the first model's output, scales better, but the judge can also hallucinate or fail to match human judgment on complex cases, so its feedback should be combined with retrieval based fact checking or escalation of low confidence outputs to a person. complementary technologies address specific limits, namely knowledge graphs and dedicated reasoning engines for multi step inference and domain specific fine tuned models, such as models trained on clinical literature to medical licensing exam caliber, for expertise beyond a general model's broad training. the working limitations of large language models mckinsey's introductory explainer places these limits in a business risk frame, noting the reputational and legal exposure from publishing biased, offensive or copyrighted output and estimating that generative ai could add up to usd 4.4 trillion a year to the global economy. it distinguishes predictive machine learning, which classifies patterns, from generative ai, which creates content, describes supervised and self supervised training and cites gpt 3's roughly 45 terabytes of training text to explain why only well resourced firms build such models. its mitigations are careful selection of training data, smaller specialized models, customization on proprietary data, keeping a human in the loop and avoiding generative ai for critical decisions about significant resources or human welfare, and its examples of counting errors, basic algebra and jailbreak style manipulation reflect early models. what is generative ai scaling laws describe a highly predictable relationship, since as model size, training compute and dataset size rise together, language models reliably achieve lower perplexity, meaning better accuracy at predicting the next word. this predictability underlies the popular expectation that scaling will continue for many more orders of magnitude and eventually yield artificial general intelligence, but the expectation misreads the laws. perplexity is largely irrelevant to end users, who care about emergent abilities, the new capabilities that appear with scale, and although emergence has accompanied scaling so far, it follows no comparably law like regularity, so past emergence guarantees nothing about further scaling. on benchmarks designed to test extrapolation to genuinely unseen task types, llms tend to perform poorly, which suggests, without proving, that their gains come more from interpolating within patterns in training data than from a general capacity to extrapolate, and if so capability gains should plateau once the space of tasks represented in available data is effectively exhausted. ai scaling myths data availability is a more immediate constraint. developers already draw on essentially all readily available high quality text, and proposed new sources are smaller than they appear, since transcribing all of youtube's roughly 150 billion minutes of video would, after removing music and non speech content and applying deduplication and quality filtering, likely add substantially less usable data than llama 3's training set of about 15 trillion tokens. acquiring more is also getting costlier, as copyright holders increasingly expect compensation and reputational and regulatory pushback against large scale collection grows. precedent, in cpu clock speeds through the 2000s and civil aircraft speeds since the 1970s, shows that exponential trends can plateau suddenly and that a trendline alone gives no warning, so it is impossible to know how many further orders of magnitude of useful scaling remain. ai scaling myths synthetic data is often proposed to get around the ceiling, but the evidence suggests it works mainly for closing specific capability gaps, in math, code, low resource languages and alignment, rather than for increasing overall training volume. the clearest successes, such as alphago's self play, depend on a fully self contained, simulatable environment in which a model can generate unlimited high quality training signal by playing itself, a system 2 to system 1 distillation pattern expected to extend to bounded domains such as code generation but not to open ended tasks such as translation, where no equivalent self play loop exists. ai scaling myths industry behavior is shifting from maximizing model size to maximizing capability per dollar. dataset size, model size and training compute once scaled together as the jointly optimal strategy, but with high quality data a growing bottleneck developers push toward smaller models trained for longer. using api pricing as a rough size proxy, gpt 4o costs about 25% of gpt 4 while matching or exceeding its capability, claude 3.5 sonnet is about five times cheaper than claude 3 opus yet more capable, and gemini 1.5 pro is cheaper and more capable than gemini 1.0 ultra, so in each family the largest model is no longer the most capable. smaller models need proportionally more training compute to reach a given level, so the shift trades training cost for lower inference cost, a deliberate rebalancing because inference cost over a model's lifetime is thought to dominate total cost, and earlier models such as gpt 3.5 and gpt 4 are considered under trained on this measure, with llama 3's 8 billion parameter model using roughly 20 times the training compute of the original similarly sized llama. ai scaling myths narayanan frames the trend as a ladder of generality, a long running progression in which computers need less effort to be directed at a new task, from special purpose machines through turing machines to today's instruction tuned llms, and expects that the current step is unlikely to be the last, but notes that the ai research community has been poor at predicting how many steps remain, what triggers the next or when, a difficulty expected to persist however the scaling debate resolves. ai scaling controlled settings github reports copilot users up to 55% more productive; mckinsey finds developers completing tasks up to twice as fast with ai assistance , carries a major caveat: those studies were conducted on isolated tasks in controlled environments, not on software built atop complex, real world existing systems. when ai generated code is scaled rapidly or applied to brownfield legacy environments, technical debt compounds far faster and becomes much harder to manage. technical debt itself functions like financial debt: the "principal" is the work needed to modernize and refactor code, and the "interest" is the ongoing complexity tax that slows maintenance, complicates scaling, and raises failure risk — while some debt is unavoidable, deploying ai generated code without care brownfield environment — the researchers suggest it may be best to avoid deploying ai generated code entirely. the consequences of letting this kind of debt compound unmanaged are not abstract: newark liberty international airport. to manage rather than eliminate this ai accelerated debt, the researchers recommend three concrete moves: developing clear, specific guidelines for when and how ai assisted coding tools should be used going beyond the high level responsible ai principles — fairness, privacy, inclusiveness — that companies like microsoft, google, meta, and salesforce have cost; and investing specifically in training junior developers to use ai tools without letting debt snowball, which requires evolving traditional code review so senior developers coach junior costs of coding with generative ai an earlier, broader mit smr piece on the same underlying problem — co authored with accenture and grounded in a study of 1,500 global companies across 10 countries and 19 industries, plus in depth c level interviews — establishes the strategic framework this more ai coding specific research builds on. technical debt, in this account, isn't just an it problem: with over $2.4 trillion in annual us costs, it's a business liability requiring ceo level attention, and as ai is poised to penetrate every business function, "all technical debt is becoming ai technical debt" — outdated infrastructure and applications directly block organizations from deploying the ai solutions that could otherwise reshape how they compete. companies best positioned for ai driven change share a "reinvention ready digital core" — cloud infrastructure, data, and ai components that can be easily updated — and typically dedicate around 15% of their it budget to tech debt remediation. snack company mondelez international illustrates this pattern concretely: facing a fragmented it landscape of more than 1,000 applications, many redundant and costly to maintain, mondelez later launch a generative ai powered marketing platform with accenture and publicis groupe. the research's core strategic reframe is that the goal of tech debt management is not eliminating debt entirely, but managing it deliberately, using categories borrowed from lending — principal cost of updating outmoded technology , interest the ongoing cost of working around it , liabilities issues that arise from leaving it unaddressed , and opportunity cost value the company cannot realize because of it — with remediation prioritized at the level of principal first, since managing it well minimizes the accrual of interest, liabilities, and lost opportunity downstream. not all technical debt is bad: some is a deliberate, worthwhile investment, illustrated by a company deploying a custom generative ai chatbot for internal knowledge management that will inevitably encounter bugs and a learning curve due to knowledge gaps — if leaders let fear of that debt kill the project outright, the company loses the team, talent, and head start it would otherwise have once more mature ai solutions emerge, ceding the opportunity to a competitor willing to tolerate the same short term cost. to prioritize among many candidate remediation projects, the researchers developed the paid framework, which scores debt along two axes — the level of technical debt present and its effect on business value — yielding four action categories: prioritize high debt, high business value impact, needing immediate remediation — e.g., a healthcare provider's patient data scattered across silos, directly affecting care quality ; address high debt, low business value impact currently, but scheduled for remediation before that impact grows — e.g., a bank's outdated but functional crm that limits personalization ; investigate low debt, high business value impact, where neglect is nonetheless risky — e.g., an outmoded inventory system quietly complicating long term financial planning ; and document low debt, low business value impact, warranting monitoring but low remediation priority — e.g., obsolete software used by a team about to be merged into another business unit . the paid matching-ai-type-to-decision-type: summary analytical ai and generative ai do different jobs, and organizations should match each to the kind of decision at hand. narrow decisions have clear objectives, usable data and fast feedback, such as where to open a store or which customers will leave, and they suit analytical ai, with generative ai acting as an accelerator that structures unstructured data and explains results. wide decisions have contested goals, incomplete information and political stakes, such as a brand repositioning, and generative ai helps there by surfacing assumptions, framing scenarios and making trade offs clear, while causal machine learning answers what if questions that plain prediction cannot. the main risk in wide decisions is mistaking ai's fluent writing for understanding. mckinsey's 2025 state of ai report found that 88 percent of companies use ai but only about 40 percent see a positive bottom line impact, which the sources attribute to treating all ai as interchangeable. highlights mckinsey's 2025 state of ai report found 88% of companies use ai in at least one function, but only around 40% see a positive bottom line impact — a gap attributed to organizations applying generic ai enthusiasm to decisions without matching the specific ai capability to the decision's actual characteristics. decisions can be diagnosed as narrow clear objectives, usable data, fast feedback loops — e.g., where to open the next store, churn prediction or wide contested goals, incomplete information, political stakes — e.g., a brand repositioning, an organizational redesign using a six question scorecard: objective clarity, data readiness, causal stability, boundary transparency, feedback loop speed, and reversibility. wide, strategic decisions routinely contain narrow subdecisions that can still be modeled and optimized — a brand pivot wide may include message testing, media mix optimization, and demand forecasting all narrow — so the diagnostic should be applied at the subdecision level, not just to the decision as a whole. for narrow decisions, generative ai's most reliable role is as an accelerator around an analytical core rather than a replacement for it: labeling unstructured data into structured inputs a predictive model can use, and translating technical model outputs like shap variable importance results into plain language explanations business stakeholders can act on. llms can also accelerate the development of prescriptive optimization models by conversationally interviewing a decision maker to identify decision variables, objective functions, and constraints, producing a first draft mathematical formulation that a modeling expert still must review — and by explaining infeasibility or trade off results like shadow prices back to non technical stakeholders in plain language. a european retail bank's churn prevention project illustrates the narrow decision pattern working correctly: a predictive model drove the actual targeting decision, while generative ai translated unstructured complaint center transcripts into structured model inputs and drafted context aware outreach scripts — analytics led, generative ai supported. for wide decisions, generative and agentic ai's role shifts to synthesis and legibility: surfacing assumptions, framing scenarios, and articulating trade offs to help people reason together, illustrated by a multinational insurer using generative tools to synthesize internal strategic history alongside external organizational design research ahead of a product to customer segment restructuring. the central risk in wide decisions is mistaking ai's fluency for understanding or judgment — a system can produce a persuasive, well formatted narrative while missing context or embedding unexamined assumptions, so ai should be treated as an amplifier of human perspective rather than an authority that can substitute for organizational commitment and alignment. even before deciding how to use ai on a specific decision, organizations must first identify which ai projects to pursue at all — a task complicated by generative ai's high profile overshadowing analytical ai, even though mckinsey research suggests generative ai use cases add only 15% to 40% on top of the economic benefits already available from analytical ai use cases. a customized generative ai "companion tool," fed a company's strategic reports, financial records, and data inventory, can improve ai project ideation workshops across six steps split into a divergent stage idea generation, idea structuring, data exploration and a convergent stage identifying ai solutions, pitch design, and impact quantification — though the tool should not be trusted to do the actual financial quantification math itself. a holding company spanning telecommunications, retail, banking, and real estate used a generative ai companion tool across its ideation workshops and identified roughly 100 possible ai projects — twice what the company expected based on the number of participants — with the tool proving especially valuable for surfacing cross subsidiary data assets e.g., banking spending data informing a retail promotion strategy that no single business unit knew existed elsewhere in the company. the same generative ai companion tool that surfaces ai project ideas also counteracts predictable human biases in ideation — rank and file workers tend to over index on efficiency opportunities while senior leaders over index on growth opportunities, and a well customized llm prompts groups toward the full range of options either group alone would tend to miss. a complementary technical level framework classifies ai problems along two axes instead of narrow vs wide: is the problem a prediction problem or a generation problem, and is the input data tabular/structured or unstructured text, images, audio ? generation problems any task where the desired output is itself unstructured — text, images, video, music have only one real answer: generative ai. prediction problems with tabular input data should favor traditional machine learning regression, gradient boosting over deep learning, since ml models are faster to build, easier to interpret, and often just as accurate for structured data. for prediction problems with unstructured input data — the case where "the right answer has changed most in recent years" — the recommendation is to try an llm first when both the inputs and the output labels are "everyday" natural language e.g., classifying product reviews as mentioning a defect , since llms can often solve this class of problem with zero specialized training; only fall back to deep learning ideally a pretrained model fine tuned on a modest amount of problem specific data if the llm proves unacceptable on accuracy, cost, latency, or data privacy grounds. llms can also reduce deep learning's traditional data hunger indirectly: instead of manually labeling thousands of training examples, an llm can perform the labeling itself "llm as a judge" , or — if even unlabeled examples are scarce — generate synthetic training examples seeded from the available real ones. traditional ml answers "what will happen" using correlations; causal ml answers "what would happen if" — the genuinely distinct counterfactual question a manager needs answered before committing to an r&d budget, a discount, or a staffing level, since a strong correlation e.g. r&d spend and revenue both rising in a growing economy can mislead if acted on as if it were causal. a decision suits causal ml when it is repeated often enough to generate dozens to thousands of historical examples, can be expressed as a number or binary choice, and has enough data on the decision itself, its outcome, and likely confounders — one off decisions or those requiring intuition and creativity remain outside causal ml's reach, just as they remain outside prediction and generation's reach in this concept's other frameworks. building a causal ml model requires an interdisciplinary team data scientists with causal the decision actually made, never the counterfactual — companies use either a "human in the loop" approach a model recommends, a human still decides, e.g. a newsroom's promoted article recommendations actual usage and to catch degradation when underlying llm vendors update their models. the genai app step you’re skimping on evaluations concept eric siegel's analysis of predictive machine learning project failure, adapted from his book the ai playbook , identifies a specific and remarkably consistent structural cause behind why so many ml projects never reach deployment or fail to deliver value once they do: a near total substitution of technical metrics for business metrics throughout the project lifecycle. machine learning generates predictive models with genuine potential to improve targeted marketing, fraud mitigation, financial risk management, logistics, and countless other large scale operational processes — work sometimes distinguished from generative ai by the label "predictive ai" — and one would reasonably expect the resulting business value to be front and center in how these projects get evaluated. in practice, siegel argues, the opposite happens: data scientists overwhelmingly report on technical metrics like precision, recall, and lift a measure of how many times better than random guessing a model performs , rather than on business metrics like revenue, profit, cost savings, or customers acquired that would directly convey the model's actual value to business stakeholders. this isn't a matter of data scientists not knowing better — the 2023 rexer analytics data science survey found data scientists themselves rank business kpis like roi and revenue as the most important metrics, even while reporting technical metrics as what they most commonly and consistently measure in practice — a gap siegel attributes largely to the fact that most ml software tooling is built to surface technical metrics by default, with business metric translation requiring deliberate additional work most teams skip. even the most commonly cited technical metric, accuracy, is "a blunt instrument" precisely because it treats every kind of prediction error as equally costly, when in the overwhelming majority of real business contexts it isn't: a false positive the model wrongly flags something as positive and a false negative the model wrongly flags something as negative typically carry very different real world costs, and accuracy simply can't distinguish between them. siegel's credit card fraud detection example makes this concrete: when a bank's model wrongly blocks a legitimate transaction a false positive , the customer is inconvenienced and might shift future spending to another card — a cost siegel estimates at roughly $100 on average; when the model wrongly approves a fraudulent transaction a false negative , the bank is typically liable for the full loss, and siegel estimates this cost at roughly $500 on average — a fivefold difference that a single "accuracy" number completely obscures. working through a realistic worked example — a mid sized regional bank with 100,000 issued cards, 100 million annual transactions, and a 0.1% fraud rate — siegel shows the bank faces roughly $50 million in annual fraud losses with no detection model deployed at all, but that a properly cost calibrated model one explicitly built around the asymmetric $100 versus $500 misclassification costs, rather than optimized for raw accuracy can capture roughly $16 million of that loss as savings. counterintuitively, the model that achieves this savings is actually slightly less accurate 99.8% than a "dumb" baseline model that simply assumes every transaction is legitimate and takes no action at all 99.9% accurate, since fraud is rare — demonstrating directly that pursuing accuracy and pursuing business value can point in genuinely different directions, and that a model sacrificing a small amount of accuracy specifically to reduce costlier false negatives is the better business outcome even though it looks "worse" on the naive technical metric. siegel's broader argument is that this technical metrics fixation sabotages ml projects in two compounding ways: during development, data scientists benchmarking against metrics that don't directly measure business value are, by construction, not optimizing for that value even if the underlying model architecture is sound; and at the deployment decision point, business stakeholders lacking visibility into a model's actual business value are forced to either authorize deployment on faith or cancel the project outright — and siegel's data suggests cancellation dominates, consistent with the ibm institute for business value finding that average enterprise wide ai initiative roi sat at just 5.9% as of late 2021, below the prevailing cost of capital, meaning the same capital would have performed better simply invested passively in the market. what leaders should know about measuring ai project value where siegel's research addresses predictive ml specifically, rama ramakrishnan's companion research addresses the parallel and increasingly urgent measurement problem facing generative ai application development: the systematic underinvestment in rigorous, iterative "evaluations" evals that most genai teams exhibit, and the concrete cost of that underinvestment in canceled projects and applications that fail to reach their intended business goal even when they do ship. building an llm based application typically proceeds through three adaptation techniques of escalating complexity and effort, generally applied in sequence as simpler approaches prove insufficient: prompt engineering — directly instructing the llm to perform a task, sufficient when the task is one an ordinary untrained human could reasonably accomplish, though small wording changes can still produce large output changes, requiring iterative tuning; retrieval augmented generation rag , needed when the application must draw on proprietary company data not present in the base model's training, by extracting the most relevant facts and content for a given query and injecting them into the prompt before sending it to the llm; and instruction fine tuning, needed when the task involves specialized jargon or domain knowledge medical notes, legal briefs that prompt engineering and rag alone can't reliably capture, achieved by training the model further on curated input output examples drawn directly from the task domain. once a team has built an application using some combination of these techniques, ramakrishnan argues a rigorous evaluation process becomes the only reliable way to answer the questions that determine whether the project actually succeeds: how does the team know it's making genuine progress as it iterates? how does it decide prompt engineering alone isn't enough and fine tuning is warranted? how does it decide the application is actually good enough to ship? after deployment, how does it keep the application aligned with evolving real world user behavior, and how does it verify the application still performs well as underlying llm vendors release new model versions? a robust evaluation process, per ramakrishnan, has three interlocking components. first is gathering the questions: assembling a representative suite of inputs — ideally a few hundred well chosen examples spanning both typical requests and deliberately included corner cases incomplete, incorrect, or irrelevant input — using synthetic data techniques prompting an llm to generate realistic test inputs, using tools like llamaindex or ragas when real end user data isn't yet available, with synthesized inputs requiring their own quality and relevance checks before being trusted as a test set. second is conducting error analysis: running every question in the suite through the application, manually examining each output for correctness and for softer criteria like tone, style, and bias, and identifying and correcting every error found — genuinely time consuming, labor intensive work performed in the spirit of "data centric ai" practices common in machine learning but comparatively rare in traditional software engineering, and consequently the step teams most often skip, despite ramakrishnan calling it indispensable, since it's the only reliable way to build genuine understanding of what's actually going wrong and why. third is automating that error analysis, since repeating painstaking manual review after every development change simply isn't practical at iteration speed: for structured or rule governed outputs checking whether a response contains a url or email address it shouldn't, for instance , straightforward code based checks suffice; for open ended qualitative questions is this llm generated summary actually faithful to the source article? does this response avoid slang? , the "llm as a judge" technique comes into play — feeding the original input, the llm's output, and a verified ground truth answer to a second, separate llm and prompting it to judge whether the first llm's output matches and satisfies stated criteria, with the judge llm's own outputs periodically checked against human evaluation and iterated until the two are mostly in agreement, since a judge model can itself hallucinate or err just like any other llm. once this evaluation foundation exists, teams gain the ability to "push the button" after every application change and immediately see which quality metrics improved, which regressed due to unintended side effects elsewhere in the system, and which specific components most need further attention — but ramakrishnan is explicit that the work doesn't end at launch: the team must instrument the live application to log every real user interaction, then regularly examine those logs, since actual end user inputs reliably prove more varied than any pre launch synthetic test suite, requiring the team to continually feed new inputs, new discovered error types, and updated error checking code back into the evaluation suite to keep pace with real usage patterns and to catch quality degradation whenever an underlying llm vendor ships a model update. as a secondary benefit, the same evaluation infrastructure that supports iterative development quality checking also directly supports instruction fine tuning efforts, since a mature evals process efficiently generates both realistic inputs via synthetic data generation and captured real usage and high quality corresponding outputs via automatic filtering of incorrect outputs , which together constitute exactly the input output training data fine tuning requires. the over technical metrics argument here connects directly to that concept's account of goodhart's law and metric gaming, since both concern the gap between what's easy to measure and what actually reflects genuine value. agentic ai enterprise transformation — pwc's finding there that few companies have concrete workload tiering plans for agentic ai parallels this concept's finding that few ml/genai teams have rigorous plans for measuring what their models or applications are actually worth. open questions neither source directly addresses how the two measurement disciplines business metric driven predictive ml evaluation, and evals driven genai app quality assurance should be combined for ai systems that blend both predictive and generative components, which is an increasingly common architecture — it's unclear whether a single unified measurement framework would apply, or whether the two disciplines genuinely need to stay separate given their different underlying model types. ramakrishnan's evals process assumes the availability of specialized tooling promptfoo, humanloop, deepeval, llamaindex, ragas and organizational capacity to build and maintain the evaluation objective-c-programming-basics: summary objective c extends the c language with objects and messaging, and its core concepts are memory management, the class, object and method model, and the system of frameworks and header files. in the introductory text by aaron hillegass and mikey ward, a program runs through functions whose local variables live on the stack and disappear when the function returns, so data that must outlive a function is placed on the heap. automatic reference counting tracks how many references point to each heap object and destroys it when the count reaches zero, which removes the manual bookkeeping of earlier versions. a class acts both as a blueprint for objects and as an object itself, sending a message to nil is legal and does nothing, and a framework such as apple's foundation bundles related classes and functions. highlights a program executes via functions, each with its own frame of local variables stored on the stack; when a function returns, its frame is discarded, which is why a buffer that needs to survive beyond the function that created it must instead be allocated on the heap. objective c programming an object is analogous to a c struct extended with its own functions methods : a class defines both the instance variables and methods an object of that type will have, acting simultaneously as a blueprint describing the type and a factory producing instances of it . objective c programming automatic reference counting arc tracks how many references point to each heap allocated object and automatically destroys the object once that count reaches zero, removing the need for the manual reference count bookkeeping earlier objective c developers had to perform themselves. objective c programming sending a message to nil objective c's null object pointer is explicitly legal and simply does nothing, returning a value that should be treated as meaningless — a deliberate language design choice distinct from languages where messaging a null reference raises an error. objective c programming a framework bundles a set of related classes, functions, constants, and types e.g. apple's foundation framework ; import differs from the c include directive by first checking whether a file has already been imported elsewhere, avoiding the duplicate inclusion errors a plain include can cause. objective c programming concept this source is an introductory programming text covering c and objective c fundamentals: variable declaration and typing, control flow, functions and the stack based frame model that stores their local variables, pointers and heap allocated memory used when data must outlive the function that created it , and the transition from c's struct based data modeling into objective c's object model, where a class combines a struct's grouped instance variables with its own methods, and where the class itself acts as both a blueprint describing a type and a factory producing new instances of it via its alloc / init pattern. memory management on the heap is handled through automatic reference counting arc , which tracks how many active references point to each object and automatically deallocates it once that count reaches zero, removing the need for the fully manual reference count management earlier objective c code required; a related language design detail is that sending a message to nil objective c's null object pointer, distinguished by convention from c's null is explicitly legal and simply does nothing, rather than raising an error as it would in many other object oriented languages. above the level of individual objects, a framework such as apple's foundation framework, prefixed ns for its nextstep origins bundles a related set of classes, functions, constants, and types, and objective c's import directive improves on c's plain include by tracking which files have already been imported and skipping duplicate inclusion automatically. objective c programming related data mining fundamentals — no direct topical connection, but both are foundational technical reference sources in this vault's readwise/books collection. open questions this source is a general programming language reference with no clear thematic connection to this vault's predominant focus on ai, telecom, cloud, and business strategy; later material on foundation classes, collections, and ios specific apis is not reflected here. sources objective c programming — aaron hillegass and mikey ward's introductory text on c and objective c programming fundamentals.
organizational-bottleneck-management: summary organizational bottlenecks come in two kinds. a task bottleneck arises when a task waits on the output of another task, and it depends on how centralized and how complex the work system is. a resource bottleneck arises when the needed resource is not available, and it depends on how flexibly resources can be reused, called fungibility, and on how much spare capacity, or slack, exists. a study of 28 large us airlines from 2002 to 2020 found that performance is best when each pair of factors is aligned, not when any one factor is minimized, and that task and resource bottlenecks interact. southwest airlines' storm meltdown in december 2022 and jetblue's valentine's day failure in 2007 show what happens when factors are misaligned or slack is too research finds that outsiders, who are unburdened by a field's norms, are well placed to connect distant ideas, but they gain traction only if they learn insiders' language and win at least one ally inside. creative success tends to belong to people who straddle boundaries, and organizations such as pixar and the national science foundation deliberately create that position. a study of 300 firms
