the roughly 20x that data center and cloud providers command, a gap bcg attributes to investor doubt that operators can capture ai value without fundamental change. conventional efficiency programs show diminishing returns and arpu growth has proved elusive, so ai is positioned as the lever that could change both the cost base and the growth narrative. bcg's value creator research places ai among seven ingredients that successful telcos combine, alongside defending the core, growing outside the core, maximizing asset leverage, radically optimizing costs, core to cloud transformation and next generation network architecture. a new formula for success turning ai disruption into telcos’ growth engine the core of the ai first agenda is the reinvention of two domains. in customer care, agents authenticate customers and detect intent to power an always on omnichannel concierge, calls that need a human are supported by real time scripts and coaching modeled on the best performers, and root cause analysis of customer issues feeds insight across the company, which bcg estimates can raise productivity by 45 60%, far beyond what call deflection chatbots achieve. in network operations, reusable agents span the technology stack, from sensor agents monitoring telemetry to agents that schedule field engineers and advise on site, coordinated by an agent orchestrator that runs diagnostic, root cause and preventive agents, for an estimated 40 50% productivity gain. smaller gains are available in it and corporate functions, and the overall estimate is a 30 40% productivity improvement. beyond productivity, hyper personalized customer value management, dynamic pricing and network as a service, which lets enterprises consume bandwidth as software, are expected to lift revenue by 2 3%, together with reduced revenue leakage from more completely billing enterprise value added services, and growth levers account for roughly 30% of the projected ebitda gain. because running ai raises recurring costs, the net picture is that the operator keeps 70 90% of the benefit and earns a projected 20 35% five year internal rate of return, provided the transformation is a coherent redesign. the productivity gains are open to any operator that executes well, but the revenue opportunities will be captured disproportionately by first movers in each market. the ai first telco a new formula for success bcg's central instruction is to reshape rather than deploy. value comes from connecting ai initiatives so that agents and assets are reused across the enterprise and an observe plan act cycle links key processes end to end, with an orchestrating role coordinating specialized agents on cross functional tasks, whereas disconnected pilots remain isolated and capture little. the recommended starting point is a readiness check covering c level and business alignment, a three year investment horizon and clear profit and loss accountability for each major solution. the 10 20 70 rule expresses the same lesson quantitatively, directing only 10% of effort to algorithms and 20% to technology and data while 70% goes to people and operational transformation, and the data must be ready first because consistent agent performance depends on it. some capability must also be built internally, since off the shelf products cannot always supply the business context, reusability and architectural fit an operator's workflows require. an operator's perspective from singtel's chief ai, data and analytics officer reinforces this, arguing that the strongest opportunities combine material business value, proprietary data or context, and a workflow ai can meaningfully change, so that a great model in a weak process creates a demo while a good enough model in the right workflow creates a business. he expects advantage to shift from model access to data, context, memory, tools and governance, and describes the leadership task as building the system that solves problems, focusing on a few non negotiable outcomes with clear ownership, and treating intelligence as a reusable capability embedded in daily decisions. the ai first telco a new formula for success turning ai into enterprise value beyond the core, bcg's strategic framework describes four plays that an operator can combine according to its ambition, assets and technical maturity. the ai first core telco is the mandatory baseline, reshaping network operations, customer service and decision making into a self learning, self healing system through predictive care, next best action management and closed loop network automation, with estimated ebitda gains of 5 15 percentage points within 12 18 months. ai monetization in consumer markets builds hyperpersonalized, ai native experiences that deepen loyalty and lift arpu, and sk telecom's a. assistant, which has passed 10 million monthly active users, is the cited proof that such products attract real usage. ai convergence repositions the operator as an end to end enterprise digital partner rather than a connectivity vendor, as in orange's combination of the orange cyberdefense acquisition, google cloud and microsoft partnerships and the orange business managed services platform. the sovereign ai infrastructure play uses operators' regulatory relationships and physical footprint to build ai ready data centers, gpu as a service platforms and compliance grade connectivity for governments and enterprises, as with singtel's nxera brand and nvidia partnered gpu service. four trends make these choices urgent, namely ai becoming the network's control system, data center and sovereign cloud capacity becoming the backbone of computing, hyperscaler competition in programmable network services, and on device ai assistants that could disintermediate operators from their own customers. ai talent and an ai first culture underlie all four plays. turning ai disruption into telcos’ growth engine sk telecom shows how an operator can pursue the ai company agenda through internal build and external alliances at once. it plans to triple the share of spend devoted to ai from 12% to 33% by 2028 and to reach usd 18.5 billion in ai revenue, up from usd 13 billion in 2022, so that ai makes up about a third of revenue. its ai pyramid strategy has an infrastructure layer of data centers, ai semiconductors through its sapeon subsidiary and a multilingual telecom language model, a transformation layer that applies ai across mobile, broadband, enterprise and new verticals such as healthcare and mobility with mid term goals of cutting service costs by 20 30%, and a service layer led by the a. chatbot assistant launched in 2022 and enhanced with microsoft azure's openai service. alongside this build out, sk telecom has invested in anthropic, allganize and imprimed, formed a 16 company domestic k ai alliance, and joined a global ai alliance with deutsche telekom, e& and singtel to develop telecom specific language models and ai platforms. deutsche telekom and sk telecom are also working with openai, google and meta on a telecom specific model to power a next generation digital customer assistant. ai native telco journey of sk telecom a new formula for success a second, more visible pattern is partnership with ai native companies, exemplified by perplexity. in 2024 sk telecom invested usd 10 million to co develop language models and integrate perplexity's search into a., and deutsche telekom and softbank followed within months, offering perplexity to a combined mobile and broadband base of more than 335 million users. by 2025 the arrangements had deepened from bundling free premium subscriptions into co development, including softbank's plan for an ai native phone priced under usd 1,000. operators justify the model through better customer engagement than traditional voice assistants, subscription revenue as legacy margins compress, first mover differentiation, ai native devices buying ai tools. telecom focused generative ai also reaches sales and it, where personalized sales emails generated from customer data free representatives for customer facing time and coding enthusiasm have not yet reached the balance sheet. the explanation lies mainly in how operators deploy the technology, since nearly three quarters use ai to support only minimal or moderate redesigns centralized, modular ai platform of reusable services, with which one north american operator built about fifty reusable services and cut new use case build time from months to roughly two weeks and disconnected teams. the sixth is a genuine partner ecosystem that treats vendors as partners, and the seventh is deliberate management of regulatory and ethical risk through guardrails and a responsible ai framework, on the logic that trust determines whether operators can monetize their customer and network data. scaling the ai native telco the same research sorts ai agents into five architectural forms that help leaders scope what a use case calls for. simple reflex agents act on preset rules, like current next best action systems that warn a customer nearing a data limit, and utility based agents weigh several options in context, for example deciding whether to auto reply to an unhappy customer or draft a response for a person. goal based agents work toward an explicit target such as an upsell revenue goal, hierarchical agents decompose a complex task into ordered subtasks, and multi agent systems have several agents work independently or cooperatively toward a shared objective, such as a centralized employee assistant that answers queries and completes field notes across network tasks. scaling the ai native telco to make scaling repeatable, mckinsey as propensity model blueprints. workforce and accountability follow the same logic. about 30% of telecom working hours could be automated by 2030, but 91% of sector jobs will need fundamental redesign, so the dominant effect is role redefinition with new roles such as ai workflow architect and ai risk manager rising as traditional devops and customer support roles decline. leading operators also tie ai initiatives to budget lines and adjust divisional budgets to enforce delivery, on the principle that if ai is not in the budget, it is not real. telcos’ ai inflection point while data traffic growth is slowing from over 30% toward 10% in some markets, which opens a path to lower capital intensity only if operators know which investments actually improve the customer perceived network experience. simulating the customer satisfaction effect of specific interventions such as new sites, spectrum additions and hardware upgrades, starting from a baseline of how satisfaction deteriorates without investment, has let operators optimize capital plans by 10 15%, repurpose up to 25% of planned spend and improve roi within as little as 12 months. one operator that simulated more than 1,000 planned interventions found a long tail, over 10% of its capital plan, that would move satisfaction only about one seventh as much as its best interventions, savings that engineering thresholds had missed. the approach depends on customer experience scores as an input, careful scoping because of the compute cost of simulation, and governance that involves the ceo and cfo rather than the technology function alone. pushing telcos' ai envelope on capital decisions two operator cases show the scaling elements in practice. kpn built an agentic voice ai customer care verification, order status and technician scheduling, while keeping humans in moments such as churn risk house moves. it designed for sub two second response latency and natural interruption, built a morning and shipped prompt fixes that evening, and trained employees as roles shifted, reaching an 86% adoption success rate and a target of agentic handling of 10 20% of service calls by 2027. how telecom-pricing-and-personalization: summary telecom operators are squeezed by slow revenue growth, rising costs and commoditized pricing, and two complementary responses can restore their ability to earn more from customers. pwc's five cs of convergence, customer experience, commercial innovation, cost excellence and complexity reduction target pricing power at the strategic level, while ai driven personalization uses the customer, billing and network data operators already hold to create new revenue through targeted offers, real time promotions and personalized billing. the personalization argument depends on a technology stack of a unified customer graph, real time charging, event detection and next best action engines, but the sources supply no documented deployment and do not address the regulatory and trust risks of monetizing behavioral data. highlights telecom revenue is projected to grow at only a 2.9% global compound annual rate from 2023 to 2028 while energy, labor and supply chain costs rise, and research across more than 50 mobile markets shows declining pricing differentiation and pricing power, worst in europe. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge major us and eu mobile carriers generated usd 171 billion of operating cash over 2019 2023 but spent usd 98 billion on capital expenditure and acquisitions and usd 72 billion on debt service and dividends, leaving almost nothing to fund innovation despite costly 5g rollout that has not meaningfully raised inflation adjusted arpu. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge the number of operators in a market, three or fewer versus four or more, shows little correlation with pricing differentiation, which challenges the regulatory assumption that an optimal number of mobile players determines competitive intensity. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge pwc's five cs for rebuilding pricing power are convergence, customer experience, commercial innovation, cost excellence and complexity reduction, presented as parallel levers rather than a staged roadmap. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge convergence bundles fixed, mobile and other services into one contract so that connectivity is treated as a non discretionary purchase like utilities, which raises share of wallet and reduces churn, while commercial innovation embeds third party content or insurance, as in verizon's customizable myplan. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge cost excellence and complexity reduction are illustrated by vodafone's global shared services hubs, rakuten mobile's virtualized cloud native network, and a european operator's three year agile program to retire legacy network, product and it assets. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge operators hold behavioral, billing and network data comparable to or richer than that of consumer platforms, so the missing piece for platform style monetization is applying ai, personalization engines and the right architecture rather than gaining data access. how telcos can monetize personalization with ai five proposed monetization mechanisms are behavior triggered add on campaigns, cross sell and up sell of devices and converged offers, event driven promotions, personalized billing paired with loyalty discounts, and next best action recommendations that anticipate needs. how telcos can monetize personalization with ai the supporting stack is a customer graph unifying billing, device, network and support history, real time charging through ocs and pcrf, complex event processing with deep packet inspection to detect micro events, next best action engines with generative ai that write the campaign copy, churn prediction and omnichannel delivery. how telcos can monetize personalization with ai concept telecom operators face a two sided profitability squeeze. on the revenue side, pwc projects industry growth of only 2.9% a year globally from 2023 to 2028, held back by slowing macroeconomic growth, saturation in core connectivity and uncertainty about how quickly newer streams such as 5g services and b2b iot will materialize. on the cost side, energy and labor costs are rising, and a widening east west technology supply chain divide reduces the scale efficiencies that equipment vendors can offer. research across more than 50 national mobile markets confirms the commoditization pressure, since arpu is declining in real terms in most markets, pricing differentiation between operators remains historically low, particularly in europe despite a slight recent improvement, and the number of competing operators shows surprisingly little correlation with how differentiated pricing is. that last finding challenges the long standing regulatory assumption that a particular number of mobile players determines competitive intensity, and it bears on whether regulators should reconsider restrictions on in market consolidation. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge the financial consequence is stark. major us and eu mobile carriers generated usd 171 billion of operating cash from 2019 through 2023, of which usd 98 billion went to capital expenditure and acquisitions and usd 72 billion to debt service and dividends, leaving almost nothing for innovation, even though years of costly 5g investment have largely failed to lift inflation adjusted arpu in most markets. pwc therefore organizes its advice for telecom chief executives around rebuilding pricing power, meaning the ability to influence what the company charges, as distinct from only managing costs or waiting for market conditions to improve. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge the first c, convergence, means bundling fixed, mobile and other services such as television into a single contract instead of separate contracts per connectivity type. it reinforces connectivity's status as a non discretionary purchase, since consumers keep paying for gas, food and power even as prices rise, and it increases share of wallet, deepens loyalty, extends customer lifetime value and reduces churn because customers with several bundled services are stickier. the second c, customer experience and service excellence, uses ai to reverse telecom's poor service reputation, first by avoiding incidents and outages through better predictive maintenance and then by cutting the time and friction of recovery, as in ai supported call center agents. charter communications' chief executive describes the tools as helping agents get to a better answer faster and show more empathy, with expected gains in customer and employee satisfaction, fewer costly service visits and lower churn. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge the third c, commercial innovation, enriches bundles beyond basic convergence by embedding often third party elements such as content, insurance or segment specific packages, for example a bundle of data, international calls and public transit tickets for short term visitors. verizon's myplan lets postpaid customers add or remove premium components such as video on demand and gaming for a fixed monthly fee, moving from a rigid one size fits all bundle to a customizable subscription that strengthened its competitive position. the fourth c, cost excellence, covers classic levers such as lowering average labor cost through global delivery models and centers of excellence in lower cost regions, reducing headcount through automation and ai that now extend from back office work into customer facing functions and even core network and software operations, and demand management and strategic sourcing on external spend. vodafone's vois centralized back office and technology functions into global shared services hubs, and rakuten mobile's fully virtualized, cloud native, ai automated network cut both capital and operating expense by minimizing reliance on proprietary hardware, showing cost excellence as a competitive differentiator and not merely a defensive measure. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge the fifth c, complexity reduction, targets a more structural cost, the variety of products, platforms and technology accumulated over decades, which compounds cost and slows the organization even when each item is well managed. pwc recommends legacy retirement, described as challenging and unglamorous but necessary to escape a self perpetuating cost spiral, guided by a technology architecture blueprint that decides which components to retire or modernize and favors modular, reusable ones. a large continental european mobile operator brought product and technology teams together in an agile, sprint based program to retire legacy network assets, product platforms and it systems, which took three years but produced internal and external cost reductions that more than justified the effort. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge personalization offers a second route to earning more from customers by building new revenue models rather than defending price. consumer platforms such as instagram, tiktok and google sustain engagement with algorithms that learn each user's moods, hobbies, intentions and emotional state, and the proposal is that operators sit on an equivalent or richer data asset of billing history, device data, real time network telemetry and support interactions that could be used the same way, not merely to improve service but to construct new revenue streams. how telcos can monetize personalization with ai five mechanisms each map a type of customer signal to a commercial action. add on campaigns respond to behavioral patterns with real time offers, such as a roaming pack for a frequent traveler or a tailored streaming bundle for a heavy streamer. cross sell and up sell extends to smart devices, gaming add ons, home automation and converged tv, mobile and broadband offers chosen from observed habits rather than a generic catalog. event driven promotions fire on momentary conditions, such as a low balance top up nudge or a discount when a customer is near a partner retailer, and need the system to act within a perishable window of relevance. personalized billing pairs usage insights with loyalty discounts to build trust while raising arpu, on the logic that a fair, individually relevant billing experience is itself a retention lever. next best action recommendations anticipate needs such as a retention plan or upgrade before the customer asks, an approach whose limits are critiqued in customer personalization strategy. how telcos can monetize personalization with ai each mechanism depends on a specific technical stack. at the base is an ai and machine learning customer graph that unifies billing, device, network and support history into one predictive profile per customer, without which the data sources stay siloed and mechanisms that combine signals, such as location with billing status for a balance aware local promotion, cannot work. real time charging through online charging systems and policy and charging rules functions lets a promotion trigger instantly instead of in a batch cycle hours later. complex event processing correlates streams of low level signals into meaningful micro events such as a location change, an app switch or a usage spike, and deep packet inspection supplies the network level visibility into what traffic consists of that the processing needs. next best action engines paired with generative ai decide the offer and the moment and also write the campaign copy in real time, which folds creative production into the decision loop, and predictive analytics on early signs of dissatisfaction trigger retention interventions before a customer cancels. omnichannel delivery through sms, email, app push and call center ensures that whatever the system decides can reach the customer in the channel they are using. how telcos can monetize personalization with ai the two threads converge on the same structural point. operators already hold the deep user data, real time behavioral triggers and billing intelligence that digital platforms would covet, and pwc's five cs show how bundling, experience, innovation and simplification can turn that position into pricing power, while the personalization proposal shows how the data itself can be monetized. the gap in both cases is not access to assets but the operating model, ai capability and architecture needed to capture value from them. five commercial imperatives to help telcos regain an edge how telcos can monetize personalization with ai related telecom telecom-regulatory-economics: summary jonathan nuechterlein and philip weiser explain the economic ideas that shaped a century of us telecommunications regulation, which are network effects, natural monopoly and the question of whether a monopolist will also monopolize adjacent markets. they trace the history from rate of return regulation before 1996, which gave incumbents an incentive to over invest and relied on implicit cross subsidies, through the telecommunications act of 1996, which gave new entrants rights to interconnect with incumbents and lease parts of their networks. they then follow the debates over open access and net neutrality that arose when broadband replaced dial up and marginalized independent internet service providers, and they explain how the internet's layered architecture, in which open protocols let developers innovate on top of the network, shaped those debates. highlights three economic phenomena justify most historical government intervention in telecom markets: network effects a network's value to each user rises or falls with the number of other users on it, which can tip an unregulated market toward a single winner , economies of scale and density larger carriers can undercut smaller ones on a per customer cost basis , and monopoly leveraging a dominant platform provider's incentive to extend market power into adjacent, unregulated markets . digital crossroads second edition the "one monopoly profit" principle holds that a platform monopolist ordinarily has little incentive to also monopolize an adjacent, complementary market, since it can already extract nearly all the value at stake by pricing the platform itself — meaning monopoly leveraging becomes a real regulatory concern mainly when the platform's own retail price is regulated removing that pricing lever or when the adjacent market itself carries independent scale or network effect advantages. digital crossroads second edition rate of return regulation historically let incumbent telephone companies recover costs plus a "reasonable" return, which created a perverse incentive to over invest in assets "gold plating" since a larger regulated asset base meant a larger allowable profit; price cap regulation later replaced this in many jurisdictions to remove that incentive. digital crossroads second edition implicit cross subsidies — geographic rate averaging, above cost business and second line rates funding below cost residential first line service — were politically convenient ways to fund universal service, but created an arbitrage opportunity: any new market entrant's first move was to "cherry pick" the specific customers paying the largest implicit taxes. digital crossroads second edition the telecommunications act of 1996 addressed all three economic concerns simultaneously: sections 251/252 addressed network effects and scale disparities by granting new entrants rights to interconnect with incumbents and to lease "unbundle" capacity on incumbent network facilities at regulated cost based rates telric , while section 271 addressed monopoly leveraging concerns by conditioning bell companies' entry into long distance on first satisfying local competition obligations. digital crossroads second edition the internet's layered architecture — physical, logical, applications, and content layers — is what enabled its explosive growth, because open protocols at the logical layer let independent developers innovate at the applications and content layers without needing to become a physical layer transmission provider themselves; this same layering is what later made "who controls the physical layer" a central platform leveraging policy question once broadband displaced dial up. digital crossroads second edition once broadband displaced narrowband dial up, the independent isp intermediaries that had previously buffered applications and content providers from physical layer carriers were marginalized, spawning three distinct regulatory responses to the resulting leveraging concern: multiple isp open access requirements, "net neutrality" rules constraining what content/applications a broadband provider can block, and continued unbundling obligations on the underlying physical layer facilities. digital crossroads second edition concept digital crossroads traces how three related economic phenomena — network effects, economies of scale and density, and monopoly leveraging — provided the analytical justification for roughly a century of us telecommunications regulation, and how the interplay of those same three phenomena continues to structure regulatory debate as the industry moved from circuit switched telephony through the 1996 telecommunications act to today's broadband internet. in the earliest era of telephony, the absence of any interconnection mandate meant markets tended to "tip" toward a single dominant network, since a network's value to each subscriber rises directly with the number of other subscribers already on it — the classic network effect dynamic. economies of scale and density compounded this tipping tendency, since a larger incumbent carrier could spread its fixed costs over more customers and undercut smaller rivals on price. the third phenomenon, monopoly leveraging, describes a dominant platform provider's potential incentive to extend its market power from a bottleneck platform market e.g. local telephone lines into an adjacent applications market e.g. long distance service or equipment . the book introduces an important qualifying principle here, the "one monopoly profit" rule: an unregulated platform monopolist typically has little independent incentive to also monopolize a complementary market, since it can already capture nearly all the available value by pricing the platform itself at the profit maximizing rate — which means monopoly leveraging concerns become most acute specifically when the platform's own price is regulated removing that pricing lever or when the adjacent market carries its own separate network effect or scale advantages. digital crossroads second edition for most of the twentieth century, us regulators managed incumbent local telephone monopolies through rate of return regulation, under which a carrier was permitted to set retail rates sufficient to cover its costs plus a "reasonable" return on its invested capital — a scheme that created a well documented perverse incentive to over invest in physical assets "gold plating" since a larger regulated asset base directly translated into a larger allowable profit. this system was also used to fund universal residential telephone service through deliberate, politically convenient implicit cross subsidies: geographic rate averaging, above cost rates for business customers and second lines, and above cost long distance access charges all subsidized below cost residential first line service. these cross subsidies created a structural vulnerability, however, since any prospective market entrant's most profitable first move was simply to "cherry pick" whichever specific customer segment was paying the largest implicit tax under the existing rate structure, undercutting the incumbent there while leaving the cross subsidized segments alone — a dynamic that repeatedly shaped where competition first emerged long distance, then large business special access well before the 1996 act formally opened local markets to competition. price cap regulation later displaced rate of return regulation in many jurisdictions specifically to remove the gold plating incentive, tying allowed rate changes to an efficiency improvement factor and inflation rather than to the incumbent's actual invested capital. digital crossroads second edition the telecommunications act of 1996 is analyzed as a systematic attempt to address all three original economic concerns simultaneously within the wireline telephone system. sections 251 and 252 addressed network effects and the scale disparity between incumbents and new entrants by granting entrants a statutory right to interconnect their own networks with an incumbent's, and — more consequentially — a right to lease "unbundle" capacity on the incumbent's own network facilities at regulated, cost based rates calculated under a methodology called telric total element long run incremental cost , which based rates not on the incumbent's actual historical network design but on what a hypothetical, maximally efficient carrier would need to spend to build an equivalent network today. section 271 separately addressed monopoly leveraging concerns specifically: it conditioned the regional bell companies' entry into the long distance market on first satisfying a checklist of local competition obligations, on the theory that allowing bell companies into long distance before genuine local competition existed would let them leverage their still dominant local bottleneck position to disadvantage long distance rivals. digital crossroads second edition the book's later chapters extend this same regulatory logic to the internet era, built on an account of the internet's layered architecture — physical the wires or spectrum , logical transmission protocols , applications browsers, servers , and content the actual words, images, and media exchanged — as the specific structural feature that enabled the internet's explosive growth: because the logical layer protocols were kept open and standardized governed cooperatively through bodies like the ietf and w3c rather than by any single company , independent developers could innovate freely at the applications and content layers without needing to become physical layer transmission providers themselves, achieving disaggregated competition and innovation at every layer simultaneously. this same layered structure is what later made "who controls the physical layer" the central platform leveraging policy question once broadband began displacing narrowband dial up access: dial up had relied on independent, unaffiliated internet service providers as intermediaries who buffered applications and content providers from the underlying telephone network monopoly, but broadband access — provided by a much smaller number of cable and telephone incumbents — threatened to marginalize those independent isp buffers entirely. three distinct regulatory responses emerged from this concern, corresponding to different layers of the stack: multiple isp "open" access requirements, aimed at preserving independent isps as competitive intermediaries at the logical layer; "net neutrality" rules, aimed more directly at constraining what content or applications a broadband provider can block or degrade at the applications and content layers; and continued unbundling obligations targeted at the physical layer itself, aimed at stimulating direct facilities based competition to reduce reliance on behavioral safeguards altogether. digital crossroads second edition related telecom ai technology — that concept covers contemporary telecom operator strategy; this concept supplies the regulatory economic history and vocabulary network effects, natural monopoly, monopoly leveraging underlying why telecom has historically been so heavily regulated compared to adjacent tech industries. platform business models — the "one monopoly profit" and platform leveraging concepts here directly parallel, and predate, the platform economics literature covered in that concept, applied specifically to regulated network industries. that concept shares the network effects vocabulary applied here to the specific historical case of telephone market tipping. open questions this vault's two digital crossroads sources first and second edition were consolidated into a single concept on the assumption that the second edition substantially updates and extends the first rather than presenting a materially different argument; a direct edition by edition comparison was not performed, so any differences between isn't purely about upfront cost — carbonet's coo bill schonbrun wasn't sure whether the total cost of building and maintaining his custom system was actually lower than an enterprise saas license — and gartner analyst adnan zijadic notes that many companies pursuing enterprise grade custom builds still end up working with a dedicated "vibe coding vendor" offering customizable templates and prebuilt components, rather than building entirely from scratch, precisely because scaling, securing, and maintaining a vibe coded application is harder than building the initial version. meet the companies vibe coding their own crms a first person account from a self described non engineer illustrates just how far this capability now extends beyond professional software teams. using claude cowork as a real time coding companion, the author built and now operates a fully automated production system — a daily ai news newsletter, a two host narrated podcast, and the website that publishes both — entirely in spare time over several weeks, without ever sketching an architecture diagram first. the build proceeded as a sequence of six "graduations," each triggered by hitting a concrete limitation and asking claude how to solve it: moving from unreliable claude scheduled tasks to google cloud run and cloud scheduler for dependable triggering; adding firestore as a minimal two document state store to make the pipeline idempotent safe to retry without duplicating a day's newsletter ; wiring the anthropic api directly into the pipeline via authenticated https calls rather than manual chat interaction; using the gmail api with oauth to send real email which incidentally created a natural human review window ; adding elevenlabs text to speech to generate the two host podcast audio, plus a suno generated jingle for polish; and finally building a public website on cloudflare pages, fed by a github repository the pipeline writes to directly through github's contents api. the resulting system makes four sequential claude api calls each morning — research claude sonnet with web search , writing claude opus, using a "golden copy" example newsletter as a style guide , self review the same model grading its own output against a quality threshold and rewriting if it falls short , and podcast transcript generation — with gemini used separately for image generation, since the author found its multimodal output currently stronger than claude's for visuals. the author also discovered and solved a recurring "drift" problem: claude cowork would periodically forget prior architectural decisions and suggest alternatives like vercel hosting already rejected weeks earlier, which the author fixed by building a persistent memory "skill" documenting the system's actual architecture, invoked at the start of every relevant session. most notably, the author deliberately trained himself out of a human in the loop approval gate that had initially required him to review and approve each day's newsletter and transcript manually: once a self review quality check module proved reliable enough — grading each draft on structure and depth, auto approving anything above a threshold, and emailing the author only when something failed the check — full automation became safe, illustrating a general pattern of starting with a human checkpoint and removing it only once the ai's own self assessment has proven trustworthy in practice. the author's own framing of the underlying lesson: "the question isn't whether ai is good enough to run unsupervised. it's whether you've built the workflow that lets it run unsupervised consistently." how i built a production ai system without writing the code bain situates both of these ground level shifts — professional developers working through claude code and non engineers vibe coding entire systems through cowork — within what it calls the "anthropic moment": a shift from point solution ai coding assistance toward ai capable of executing full end to end workflows, marking the transition from ai assisted to genuinely ai led software development. bain's own tracking shows executive expectations accelerating sharply: in its 2024 survey, leaders projected 20 30% productivity gains from ai in software development; by its 2026 survey, many now anticipate gains of 5x to 10x, and ai's role in the software development life cycle has moved from a meaningful contribution cited by roughly half of executives toward near universal adoption. bain's research nonetheless finds a persistent gap between these expectations and reality: most companies still report only single digit efficiency improvements, even as 63% report higher output per engineer and 53% report faster release cycles. bain identifies five recurring reasons transformation efforts stall short of their potential — optimizing a single activity like code generation rather than the full delivery chain which just moves the bottleneck elsewhere ; mistaking a proliferation of pilots for real adoption, since pilots don't automatically translate into sustained usage or business impact without new workflows, measurement, and guardrails; focusing too narrowly on code completion rather than combining tight loop development assistance with a broader agent mode for multistep work; underestimating organizational resistance to a genuinely new way of working, which requires enablement and reassurance rather than being treated as a simple tooling swap; and failing to measure or prove value in a way that supports a credible roi conversation, without which initiatives cannot scale past the pilot stage. bain's central structural claim is that ai is dissolving the long standing boundary between the product development life cycle defining what to build, based on customer needs and strategy and the software development life cycle the actual work of building it , because ai enabled teams can now define, build, test, and refine in a single continuous flow rather than in sequential handoffs between separate product and engineering functions — a shift that requires redesigning organizational structure, since developers increasingly move from being code executors to being "agent architects and orchestrators" who structure work for agents with fresh context windows at each stage and human review at critical junctures rather than writing every line themselves. bain's roadmap for this transition runs through three phases — design, pilot, and scale, with too many companies jumping straight to pilots without first defining the problem and prioritizing investment — and rests on six durable principles regardless of which specific tools are in use: context is king the best ai development platforms will be distinguished not by coding quality alone but by whether they supply full lifecycle context — product intent, architecture, code base conventions, telemetry, security posture, and customer signals — since without it agents remain simple task accelerators rather than genuine orchestrators ; shift left, hard clearer upfront intent, sharper acceptance criteria, and spec driven workflows like research plan implement matter more as execution itself compresses, since garbage inputs still produce garbage outputs regardless of execution speed ; close the loop software development is a uniquely multistep ai use case, and the process only achieves its goals by transferring context between stages and feeding runtime results back into planning — a place where ai often exposes pre existing product engineering dysfunction rather than creating new problems ; treat risk as a first class design constraint rather than an afterthought agents given real leverage over a product need a defined risk envelope: permissioning, policy as code guardrails, auditability, evaluation harnesses, secure secrets handling, and clear human checkpoints for high risk changes ; be intentional about buy versus build organizations should buy commoditized tooling and orchestration wherever it accelerates learning, reserving genuine build effort for the truly differentiating context layer, domain ontology, and guardrails specific to how their own software actually ships ; and measure outcomes, not just output traditional dora style engineering metrics were designed for a world where only humans wrote code, and in an agentic world raw velocity can mislead, since teams can ship faster while quietly accumulating more defects, more technical debt, and more risk — bain recommends segmenting metrics by human versus agent authorship, adding system level measures like end to end cycle time and human intervention rate, and elevating risk and control health to first class scorecard dimensions alongside speed . the rise of the ai development life cycle related managing technical debt in the ai era — bain's warning that rising velocity can mask growing technical debt, and the ft's "comprehension debt" concern, are the direct risk side counterpart to this concept's productivity gain narrative. enterprise ai token cost management — the same claude code adoption driving the productivity gains documented here is also the proximate cause of the token cost rationing microsoft limiting claude code access, uber's budget exhaustion documented there. agentic ai platform architecture — mcp, cited here as one of anthropic's two key breakthroughs, is the same interoperability protocol covered in architectural depth in that concept. open questions none of the four sources addresses how vibe coded, non professionally architected systems like the personal production system, or the smb crms will fare on security, compliance, or scalability once they reach a scale or sensitivity that demands professional software engineering discipline — salesforce's cited mit statistic internal builds failing twice as often as vendor partnerships is the only data point touching this, and it isn't broken down by company size or system criticality. it's unclear whether bain's 5x 10x productivity projections are based on realized outcomes at specific named companies or aggregate executive sentiment/expectation — the source distinguishes "benchmarks" from "expectations" but doesn't always make clear which figure is which. sources how anthropic achieved ai coding working-with-generative-ai: summary working well with generative ai depends on knowing where it helps and where it misleads, and on building deliberate habits of use rather than relying on access to the best model. mollick's co intelligence rules and the bcg and harvard field experiment show large gains in speed, quality and skill leveling inside the jagged frontier of ai capability, but worse performance outside it, which makes human judgment and centaur and cyborg working patterns essential. practical discipline includes self auditing sessions, consulting a virtual board of ai personas, saving successful sessions as custom assistants and moving from simple context rich prompting toward configuring agents that are directed rather than prompted. highlights mollick treats ai as a general purpose technology that acts as a co intelligence, with early studies showing 20 80% productivity gains, and gives four rules, invite ai to the table, be the human in the loop, treat it like a person but say what kind and assume this is the worst ai you will use. co intelligence hallucination is structural, since models generate plausible continuations rather than retrieve facts, are not only find the boundary by extensive hands on use. centaurs and cyborgs on the jagged frontier co intelligence on a task outside the frontier, unaided consultants were right 84% of the time while ai users fell to 60 70%, and recruiters using high quality ai grew lazier, a dynamic called falling asleep at the wheel. centaurs and cyborgs on the jagged frontier tasks can be allocated as just me, delegated or automated, and centaur work divides labor cleanly between human and ai while cyborg work interleaves effort within a task and also offsets the more homogeneous output that ai produces. co found was the condition under which ai access made people more creative. audit yourself to get more from genai a virtual personal board of directors of ai personas offers breadth, availability, cognitive diversity and psychological safety as a complement to real advisers, as in a build versus buy decision that surfaced integration costs, roadmap control and nostalgia bias. how i built a platform, experiment first, write second person instructions and add reference files. how to build your own ai assistant prompting has no secret formulas, and context, constraints, explicit step by step instructions and sustained interactive practice matter more than rituals, while prompt sharing and blueprints let non programmers build and spread innovations. a guide to prompting ai for what it is worth innovation through prompting directing intelligence configures agents by context, capabilities and orientation and runs several with different lenses against the same data, and agentic coding tools extend this to knowledge work with cautions about trusted folders and review of actions. stop prompting ai. start directing it putting ai to work concept co intelligence frames current generative ai as a general purpose technology comparable in scope to steam power or the internet, but argues its impact on work and education may exceed theirs, because it acts as a co intelligence that directly augments or substitutes for human thinking rather than mainly automating mechanical or physical labor. early studies finding productivity improvements of 20 80% across many job types are cited as evidence of scale, while noting that these gains fall within the plausible range for earlier general purpose technologies. the book proposes four rules for working with ai productively instead of avoiding it or over trusting it. the first is to always invite ai to the table, because with no instruction manual the only reliable way to learn its value and limits for a task is direct, repeated experimentation, including attempts that disappoint or unnerve, since even a failure shows where the technology's boundary lies for that work. the second is to be the human in the loop, since human judgment remains essential, in part because an ai implicitly optimizes to give an answer the user finds satisfying, which can outweigh accuracy and let a confident but fabricated answer persuade an insistent user. co intelligence the third rule is to treat ai like a person but tell it what kind of person it is. research cited in the book finds that models give better answers when a request is framed as personally consequential, such as important to the user's career, and that explicit guidance on the persona to adopt improves the interest and usefulness of output, although the framing carries real risk, since treating ai as a person can create unrealistic expectations, obscure its nature as software and shape emotional relationships in ways that may not serve well being, so the book offers it as a pragmatic heuristic rather than a claim of personhood. the fourth rule is to assume this is the worst ai you will ever use, which keeps today's limitations from being treated as permanent. hallucination is presented as a structural consequence of how models work rather than a solvable bug, because a language model has no ground truth store and generates each output as a statistically plausible continuation, so tasks needing exact recall are especially prone, models are generally not optimized to say they do not know, and a request to explain its reasoning after an answer yields another plausible piece of generated text rather than an account of the process that actually produced the answer, since the model has no introspective access to it. co intelligence the largest study of the question is a pre registered field experiment by social scientists from harvard, warwick, mit and wharton with boston consulting group, using 758 consultants, 7% of the firm's consulting force, on 18 realistic tasks spanning creative work such as proposing shoe ideas for an underserved market, analytical work such as market segmentation, writing and marketing work such as press releases and persuasion such as an inspirational internal memo. consultants were randomly given plain gpt 4, the publicly available version with no special fine tuning or prompting, or no ai, and human and ai graders who agreed closely rated completion, speed and quality. ai assisted consultants completed 12.2% more tasks, finished 25.1% faster and produced 40% higher quality output, consistently across every measure. ai also leveled skill, since the lowest scoring consultants on a baseline assessment gained most, by 43%, while top performers improved less, a pattern the source compares to the steam shovel erasing the difference between good and bad diggers and which it says changes what skill differentiation means. centaurs and cyborgs on the jagged frontier the study's central concept is the jagged frontier, the fact that ai capability is unevenly distributed across tasks of similar apparent difficulty. pictured as an irregular fortress wall with some towers jutting out and others folding back, it puts equally hard looking tasks on opposite sides of an invisible boundary, so gpt 4 handles open ended idea generation easily but reliably fails to write a poem of exactly 50 words because it works with tokens rather than words and has no native sense of word count. because the boundary does not track intuitive difficulty, users can learn where it lies for their own work only through extensive hands on use, and the authors say plainly that no one, including a model's developers, knows the full range of a frontier model's abilities in advance. co intelligence applies the same idea as the reason that familiarity from repeated use matters, since reasoning about the frontier in the abstract does not work. centaurs and cyborgs on the jagged frontier co intelligence the experiment included a task engineered to fall outside gpt 4's frontier by exploiting a known blind spot so that the model would give a wrong but convincing answer, which proved hard to construct because gpt 4 solved most attempts. unaided consultants got it right 84% of the time, whereas consultants using ai did worse, at 60 70% accuracy, while writing up their wrong answers in better prose, a direct overreliance effect. the source links it to a related study by a co author in which recruiters using high quality ai became lazier and less attentive and made worse hiring decisions than recruiters using low quality ai or none, a dynamic called falling asleep at the wheel, in which an ai good enough to seem consistently trustworthy removes the incentive to stay critically engaged. centaurs and cyborgs on the jagged frontier two patterns are proposed to capture the benefits while avoiding overreliance. centaur work keeps a clear division of labor between person and machine, routing whole tasks to whichever is stronger given where each falls relative to the frontier, as in choosing a statistical technique personally while delegating graph production to the ai. cyborg work blends effort at a finer grain within one task, such as having the ai complete a sentence the human began and moving back and forth across the frontier repeatedly, and the source recommends it for ai assisted writing. neither is exotic, since both emerge from sustained hands on use, which is how a person comes to perceive the shape of their own frontier, and combining human and ai effort also recovers variety, since ai output, while better on average, was more homogeneous across consultants. co intelligence recommends starting by inviting ai into everything, letting centaur style task switching emerge as the frontier sharpens and cyborg style blending develop organically after that, and it offers a task allocation framework along a spectrum of trust. just me tasks stay human either because ai is not yet useful or because a person chooses to keep them, such as raising children, making important decisions or expressing values, delegated tasks are assigned to ai and checked, typically tedious or low importance work although delegated does not mean low stakes, and automated tasks are left to ai entirely, still a small category but expected to grow in well bounded domains. centaurs and cyborgs on the jagged frontier co intelligence the book highlights an organizational risk in shadow ai use going unreported. a worker who discovers how to automate much of their own job has a rational reason not to disclose it, since the natural managerial response to a visible productivity breakthrough is often to fire people and save money rather than reinvest the capacity, so organizations that want to capture employees' bottom up discoveries must deliberately and visibly reduce the fear of disclosure through incentives and psychological safety, not merely permission. co intelligence personal discipline determines who gains. in mit sloan management review, vipin gupta describes building, after a year of daily use with no benchmark for whether his sessions were any good, a reusable macro prompt that audits a significant ai session against 30 habits under five goals. he grounds it in a randomized field experiment, including mit sloan's jackson lu, that assigned 250 employees at a chinese technology consulting firm to chatgpt or not and found that access made employees significantly more creative by supervisor and outside evaluator judgment, but only among those with strong metacognitive strategies, meaning the ability to reflect on their thinking, recognize gaps and adjust, so the audit is a way of installing metacognition where it does not occur naturally rather than of judging the ai's output. audit yourself to get more from genai the five goals are set up, refine, verify, own and systematize. setting up means passing the intern test, giving role, context, constraints and materials as if briefing a new hire, and the highest leverage and most skipped habit is stating negative constraints, such as no generic swot and no hedging. refining means iterating on your own instructions instead of just asking for a better answer, epitomized by asking what question you should be asking that you are not. verifying means treating fluent output as a new category of quality risk, illustrated by a near miss in which a summary of a familiar regulatory history came back beautifully written, logically structured and wrong on two key points and almost reached a committee meeting, countered with a temporal awareness check on the date of the model's latest information and a confidence stress test of each factual claim. owning means imposing a personal voice and position on output that defaults to hedged, generically competent prose, including through a virtual personal board of directors, and systematizing means converting a successful session into a reusable macro prompt template with variable placeholders rather than losing the accumulated context when the chat closes. applied to a usd 5 billion competitive due diligence analysis, the habits surfaced a material gap between a competitor's public narrative and its internal employee sentiment data and caught a usd 42 million enforcement action that the ai's own output had understated, evidence that the discipline rather than the model produced the value. audit yourself to get more from genai the virtual personal board of directors, developed in a multi persona prompts. the author's board includes a tactical persona modeled on sun tzu for power dynamics, an empathetic strategist modeled on former pepsico ceo indra nooyi, a bold realist modeled shaping a model's output through the wording, context and structure of the input. mollick argues against treating it as a discipline with secret techniques, since models are improving rapidly at inferring intent, heavily engineered prompts full of superlatives such as act as the smartest person ever do not outperform plain, direct requests, and the returns to prompt crafting should keep shrinking. what reliably helps is context and constraints. because models predict likely continuations, unconstrained prompts yield generic output that mirrors common training patterns, and telling the model what persona or perspective to take, what style to use, what to avoid and what source material to draw on breaks that default, although assigning a named identity such as bill gates does not confer that person's expertise, and pasting reference text, asking for a summary or extension, or using retrieval where available narrows the space of completions. a guide to prompting ai for what it bok/ai-01-foundations-of-ai: summary modern ai is software that learns patterns from data instead of following rules written by programmers. this chapter explains how that learning works, how it led to foundation models and the language models behind chatbots, and why those models still make mistakes that cannot be fully removed. it also covers what scaling can and cannot be expected to deliver, the new vocabulary of 2025, the state of the debate about artificial general intelligence, and two practical ways of thinking about where ai fits in a business, as cheap prediction and as a choice between analytical and generative tools. key ideas artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning are nested fields, and nearly all current ai comes from letting machines find patterns in examples. foundation models are trained once on broad data and then adapted to many tasks. the ones that work with text are called large language models. a language model produces text by predicting the next word fragment, so it can state falsehoods with confidence, and no current technique removes this entirely. better prediction has been the reliable result of scaling, while new abilities have not been predictable, and the supply of high quality training data is a limit. no system has shown human level general intelligence, although some researchers now expect ai to start improving itself within a few years. economically, ai makes prediction cheap, which raises the value of human judgment and of the data and actions that surround each prediction. foundations of ai from rules to learning traditional software follows instructions that a programmer wrote for every case. this works well for payroll and poorly for tasks such as recognizing a face, which people do easily but cannot describe as a list of rules. machine learning solves this by giving the computer examples and letting it find its own rules. arthur samuel defined the field in the 1950s as giving computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed. artificial intelligence is the broad goal of making machines perform tasks that normally need human thinking. machine learning is the main method used today, and deep learning is a branch of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. each layer learns a little more than the one before it, from simple features such as edges to complex ones such as faces. see ai and machine learning foundations. machine learning systems are trained in three ways. supervised learning uses examples that humans have labeled, and it is the most common method in business. unsupervised learning looks for groupings in unlabeled data. reinforcement learning improves by trial and error against a reward. the related field of data mining adds a standard project process, called crisp dm, and a set of common tasks such as classification and clustering. see data mining fundamentals. deep learning became practical only about a decade ago, when three things came together. researchers found a way to train networks layer by layer, large amounts of digital data became available, and graphics processors turned out to run neural networks far faster than ordinary chips. foundation models and language models a foundation model is a system trained on broad data and then adapted to many different tasks. stanford researchers coined the term in 2021. instead of building one model for each job, organizations start from one large model and adapt it, for example by training it a little further on their own examples. most of today's foundation models rely on the transformer, an architecture introduced by google researchers in 2017. its key idea is attention, which lets the model look at every part of a passage at once and decide which words matter most for understanding any other word. large language models, or llms, are the foundation models trained on text, and they power chatbots and writing assistants. scale brings both benefits and a risk. the largest models show abilities that smaller versions lack. because so many applications are built on the same few models, a flaw in one model is inherited by everything built on it. researchers also admit that nobody fully understands how these models work internally or exactly when they fail. what a language model does such a system does one thing repeatedly. it predicts the most likely next word fragment, called a token, adds it to the text and repeats. outside software controls when the loop stops. the model does not look anything up, and it does not learn from a single correction during a conversation. any apparent memory of earlier chats comes from a separate feature that feeds stored facts back into the next prompt. this design explains the main limits. the model generates text that sounds right, and it has no built in way to check whether a statement is true. a confident but false statement is called a hallucination. prompting, retrieval and fact checking reduce hallucinations, but they cannot guarantee that none occur, and the same is true of the sources a model cites. the limits go beyond facts. models can appear to reason without chaining logical steps reliably, can misread the structure of a question, and can write plans that sound sensible but ignore reality. a field experiment with more than 750 consultants at bcg showed the practical risk. consultants using gpt 4 on one reasoning task were wrong 23 percent more often than those without it, because the model's confident explanation persuaded them not to check. organizations therefore design around these limits. they keep a person in the loop, using sampling or risk based checks so that review stays affordable. they sometimes use a second model to check the first, remembering that the checker can also be wrong. they add other technologies, such as knowledge graphs and models trained on specialist data. see llm mechanics, limitations and scaling. grounding a model in company data a model knows only what was in its training data. a customer service chatbot built on a general model cannot see a customer's account or the company's current policies. retrieval augmented generation, usually shortened to rag, closes this gap. it works like a librarian. first, the company's documents are indexed so that their meaning can be searched. then, when a question arrives, the system finds the most relevant passages and gives them to the model, which writes an answer based on them and can cite them. rag is only as good as the data behind it. out of date or biased documents produce confidently wrong or biased answers. rag also stays useful when models can accept extremely long prompts, because too much material lowers quality, models pay less attention to the middle of a long prompt, and longer prompts cost more. see retrieval augmented generation rag . what scaling can and cannot deliver for years the path to better models seemed simple. more data, more computing power and bigger models reliably produced better next word prediction, and this regularity is called a scaling law. the difficulty is that users care about new abilities, not prediction scores, and new abilities do not follow any comparable law. tests that require a model to handle genuinely new kinds of tasks suggest that models may be better at working within patterns they have seen than at going beyond them. data is a nearer limit. developers have already used most high quality text, and even transcribing all of youtube would add less usable text than the 15 trillion tokens used to train llama 3. synthetic data, which is training material produced by other models, helps fill specific gaps but has not replaced human written data. as a result, developers have moved toward smaller models trained for longer, which are cheaper to run and often more capable than their larger predecessors. new vocabulary from 2025 four terms from 2025 describe how models are now built and judged. reasoning models work through problems in several steps, backtracking when needed, at a much higher computing cost. evals are automated tests that decide whether a model is safe and capable enough to release. synthetic data is training material made by one model for another, and it spreads the teacher model's mistakes if nobody supervises it. vibes refers to judging a chatbot by its feel, for example whether its answers are concise or pandering, instead of by benchmark scores alone. see 2025 ai industry vocabulary. how close is general intelligence? artificial general intelligence, or agi, means ai whose abilities match a human's across the board. the traditional test is the turing test, in which an observer cannot tell the machine from a person. no system has passed it rigorously. current chatbots, however fluent, are still narrow systems that predict answers to specific prompts. researchers have listed eight abilities that ai would need to combine, including perception, fine motor skills, language, problem solving, creativity and social engagement. most experts place agi decades away, and a few doubt it will arrive this century. a newer concern is that ai is starting to help build ai. anthropic co founder jack clark estimates a 60 percent chance that a system will be able to create its own successor without human involvement by the end of 2028. executives are advised to treat agi as a long term question to monitor, while investing in today's narrow ai. see artificial general intelligence. two practical ways to think about ai in business the first is economic. the book prediction machines argues that what has become cheap is prediction, which means using the data you have to fill in information you lack. when something becomes cheap, people use more of it, and the things that go with it become more valuable. prediction goes with data, judgment and action. a decision has three parts, which are predicting what will happen, judging how much each outcome matters and acting. machines take over the first part, so human judgment becomes more valuable, not less. a common pattern is prediction by exception, in which the machine handles routine cases and sends unusual ones to a person. see prediction machines. the second is a choice of tool. analytical ai, such as forecasting and fraud detection, suits narrow decisions that have clear goals, good data and quick feedback. generative ai suits broad, ambiguous decisions, such as repositioning a brand, where it helps people see assumptions and options but should not make the decision. for narrow decisions it works best as an accelerator around an analytical core, for example by turning complaint transcripts into data a forecasting model can use. mckinsey's 2025 survey found that 88 percent of companies use ai, yet only about 40 percent see a positive effect on profit, which the research links to applying one kind of ai to every problem. see matching ai type to decision type. go deeper ai and machine learning foundations — the vocabulary and history of ai, deep learning, foundation models and the transformer. llm mechanics limitations and scaling — how language models generate text, why they fail and what scaling can deliver. retrieval augmented generation — how models are grounded in an organization's own documents. data mining fundamentals — task types, the crisp dm project process and overfitting. ai industry vocabulary 2025 — reasoning models, evals, synthetic data and vibes. artificial general intelligence — what agi would require and how close it may be. prediction machines — the economics of cheap prediction. matching ai type to decision type — choosing between analytical and generative ai.
bok/ai-02-industry-and-economics-of-ai: summary the ai industry is spending far more on infrastructure than it earns, and the central question is whether that gap will close. this chapter explains the arguments for and against calling the spending a bubble, why vendors price ai below its cost, and how forecasts of ai's economic effect differ. it also covers the concentration of power in a few companies and leaders, the rise of chinese and sovereign ai, the pressure on software as a service businesses and the new problem of managing the cost of ai inside a company. key ideas spending on ai infrastructure is roughly six times ai revenue, and the chips involved lose value within a few years. whether this is a bubble depends on how the spending is financed, how fast revenue grows and whether losses could reach the banking system. vendors charge less than ai costs to run, and the models themselves are becoming commodities, which makes pricing the core business problem. forecasts of ai's economic effect differ because they measure different things, such as spending on technology or gains in national output. power is concentrated in nvidia and a few frontier labs, and governments are responding with sovereignty policies and regulation. inside companies, ai costs are variable and easy to underestimate, so they need to be measured task by task. industry and economics of ai the spending gap technology companies are building ai infrastructure at a pace without precedent. in 2025 they were on track to spend $300 to $400 billion, while ai revenue was about $60 billion by a conservative estimate. that is a gap of roughly six to one. the chips make this spending unusual. railroads and fiber optic cable keep their value for decades, even if they sit unused for a while. graphics processors lose value within about three years, so much of the spending must be repeated. about half of the data center budget goes to these chips. is it a bubble? the sources give two main answers. one side points to how the spending is financed. companies increasingly move data centers into separate legal structures funded by private credit, which keeps the debt off their own balance sheets. that reduces transparency, and opaque funding was the trigger in about half of 18 historical bubbles. nvidia adds to the concern, because its guarantees and financing for customers could oblige it to pay more than $300 billion, so a downturn could concentrate losses in one company. the other side applies a strict test. by this test a bubble needs a market fall of 40 to 50 percent that lasts for years, and a similar fall in the investment behind the boom. neither has happened. generative ai also has real users, unlike many dot com sites, and chatgpt was projected to reach about $10 billion in annual revenue faster than facebook or tiktok did. nvidia funds its commitments from cash and operating profit rather than debt, which makes it different from cisco in the dot com years. a third view in the harvard business review changes the question. it asks how a bust could hurt the economy, through spending stopping, falling stock wealth or a credit crunch. it finds the boom smaller than headlines suggest, about 1 percent of national output, and concludes that systemic damage is unlikely while losses stay outside the banking system. the buildout is also limited by physical supply, not only by money. memory chips are sold out through 2026, advanced packaging is fully booked, gas turbines have backlogs to 2030 and grid connections can take four to seven years. local opposition blocked or delayed at least 75 projects in the first quarter of 2026 alone. this is the opposite of the dot com fiber glut, when capacity sat idle until demand arrived. see ai investment bubble and capital rotation. why vendors cannot price ai profitably every prompt costs real computing power, so ai has high variable costs. revenue per user is low. andy wu of harvard business school calls a bubble a time when everyone can see the value being created but no one is thinking about how to capture it. flat monthly subscriptions are in practice capped usage plans, and the usual $20 price does not cover the cost of heavy users. models are also becoming commodities. weak intellectual property protection lets well funded entrants such as deepseek approach the leaders with far less investment, which limits how far any vendor can raise prices. some investors argue that prices are too low for the value delivered. the venture firm a16z advises pricing at the highest layer of value that can be measured, such as credits for recognizable units of work or outcomes, instead of per token. see ai vendor pricing and profitability. competing forecasts of ai's economic effect estimates differ because they measure different things. bain projects that spending on ai hardware and software will reach $780 to $990 billion by 2027. economist daron acemoglu estimates that ai will raise us output by only about 1 percent over a decade, because only a small share of tasks across the economy can be done profitably by ai today. neither is wrong. one measures how much money is spent on the technology, and the other measures the gain in output. labor economists add a geographic point. even a modest overall effect could help some us cities and hurt others, especially midsize metropolitan areas. see the ai economic impact gap. a related argument is that the direction of ai matters. automation tends to favor owners of capital, while ai that creates new tasks raises the value of human expertise. see pro worker ai and labor displacement. power and geopolitics the economist compared ai's best known leaders with the industrial tycoons of 11 earlier technology waves. the people closest to ai models rank lower than might be expected, because model making needs few employees and none of them has full control of their company. nvidia's jensen huang has gathered a different kind of influence, through his supply chain position, his popularity in taiwan and his offers of sovereign ai to governments. the economist treats april 7, 2026 as a turning point. on that day anthropic announced that it would withhold its mythos model from general release because of its ability to find software vulnerabilities, and political pressure for regulation increased. see ai power concentration and new tycoons. china shows a second path. deepseek's r1 model in january 2025 matched leading us chatbots at a fraction of the reported training cost and was released as open source. the harvard business review reads this as classic disruption, in which a cheaper product that is good enough moves up the market. it advises companies to decide deliberately which model providers to use. see deepseek and china's ai ecosystem. sovereign ai means ai capability under national or organizational control. mckinsey estimates that sovereignty requirements could influence 30 to 40 percent of global ai spending, a market of $500 to $600 billion by 2030. sovereign offerings cost 10 to 30 percent more, and most initiatives stall because sovereignty is treated as a checklist. organizations
